Initially created: 2025-12-17T20:45:57.293+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: *Liáng Shū* 1, Annals of Tàizǔ (Commentary: The original annals in Xuē Shǐ,
as recorded in the *Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn*, are complete.
However, the original volume of the Annals of Liáng Tàizǔ has been lost.
Of the scattered entries found in various rhyme categories,
only sixty-eight articles were obtained.
Supplementing these with those cited in *Tōngjiàn Kǎoyì* and *Tōngjiàn Zhù*,
another twenty-one articles were obtained.
The beginning and end are incomplete,
and it has not been possible to compile them into a coherent piece.
Examining the deeds of Zhū Liáng recorded in the Usurper's Section of *Cèfǔ Yuánguī*,
all are based on the original text of Xuē Shǐ,
and are quite detailed from beginning to end.
By adopting them article by article,
a compilation is still possible.
We have respectfully followed the precedent of our predecessors, who used Wèi Dàn's book and Gāo Shì Xiǎoshǐ to supplement the missing chapters of the *Běi Wèi Shū*.
We have adopted the events of Liáng Tàizǔ from *Cèfǔ Yuánguī*,
arranging them chronologically by year and day,
and ordering them sequentially
to make up for the omissions,
hoping to restore something of the original Xuē Shǐ.
Furthermore, the original book's volume and chapter number are noted under each article,
for cross-referencing.
Tàizǔ Shénwǔ Yuánshèng Xiàohuángdì,
whose surname was Zhū,
personal name Huàng,
originally Wēn,
(*Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn*, Volume 8687.
) was a native of Dàngshān, Sòngzhōu.
His ancestors were descendants of Shùn's Sītú Hǔ.
His great-great-grandfather was Àn,
great-grandfather Màolín,
grandfather Xìn,
and father Chéng.
The Emperor was the third son of Chéng,
and his mother was Wénhuì Wáng Huánghòu.
(*Cèfǔ Yuánguī*, Volume 182.
Commentary: According to *Wǔdài Huìyào*: Liáng Sùzǔ Xuānyuán Huángdì, personal name Àn,
was the forty-second generation descendant of Shùn's Sītú Hǔ.
In the seventh month of the first year of Kāipíng,
he was posthumously honored as Xuānyuán Huángdì,
with the temple name Sùzǔ,
and buried in Xīngjí Líng.
Jìngzǔ Guāngxiàn Huángdì, personal name Màolín,
was the eldest son of Xuānyuán Huángdì,
and his mother was Xuānxī Huánghòu Fàn Shì.
In the seventh month of the first year of Kāipíng,
he was posthumously honored as Guāngxiàn Huángdì,
with the temple name Jìngzǔ,
and buried in Yǒng'ān Líng.
Xiànzǔ Zhāowǔ Huángdì, personal name Xìn,
was the eldest son of Guāngxiàn Huángdì,
and his mother was Guāngxiào Huánghòu Yáng Shì.
In the seventh month of the first year of Kāipíng,
he was posthumously honored as Zhāowǔ Huángdì,
with the temple name Xiànzǔ,
and buried in Guāngtiān Líng.
Lièzǔ Wénmù Huángdì, personal name Chéng,
was the eldest son of Zhāowǔ Huángdì,
and his mother was Zhāo yì Huánghòu Liú Shì.
In the seventh month of the first year of Kāipíng,
he was posthumously honored as Wénmù Huángdì,
with the temple name Lièzǔ,
and buried in Xiánníng Líng.
) In the sixth year of Dàzhōng of Táng, the year being Rénshēn,
on the night of the twenty-first day of the tenth month,
he was born in Wǔgōu Lǐ, Dàngshān County.
That night,
a red aura rose above the dwelling where he lived.
The villagers, seeing it,
all ran in alarm,
saying:
"The Zhū family's house is on fire!"
When they arrived,
the dwelling stood intact.
After entering,
a neighbor announced the birth of a child,
and everyone found it extraordinary.
(*Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn*, Volume 16019.
Commentary: The above is also found in *Cèfǔ Yuánguī*, Volume 182.
From this, one can infer
that *Cèfǔ Yuánguī*'s citations of events from the Five Dynasties era are mostly based on Xuē Shǐ.
) The three brothers
were orphaned before reaching adulthood.
Their mother (Commentary: In *Cèfǔ Yuánguī*'s citation of this passage,
the character "母" (mother)
is followed by the characters "王氏" (Wáng Shì).
) took them to live with Liú Chóng, a native of Xiāoxiàn.
When the Emperor grew up,
he did not apply himself to earning a living,
but considered himself heroic and brave,
which most villagers disliked.
Chóng, seeing his laziness,
often rebuked and flogged him.
Only Chóng's mother, who had pitied him since childhood,
personally combed his hair,
and often warned her family, saying:
"Zhū Sān is no ordinary person.
You all should treat him well."
When her family asked for the reason,
she replied:
"I once saw him, while in deep sleep,
transform into a red snake."
However, the others did not believe her.
(*Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn*, Volume 5949.
During the Qiánfú era of Táng Xīzōng,
Guāndōng suffered continuous famine,
and bandits gathered.
Huáng Cháo took advantage of this to rise in Cáo and Pú.
Tens of thousands of famine victims wished to join him.
The Emperor then left Chóng's home,
and together with his elder brother Cún, joined Huáng Cháo's army.
Due to his repeated victories in battle,
he was promoted to duìzhǎng (隊長, squad leader).
On the *jiǎshēn* day of the twelfth month of the first year of Guǎngmíng of Táng,
Huáng Cháo captured Cháng'ān.
He dispatched the Emperor to lead troops and garrison at Dōngwèiqiáo.
At this time,
Zhūgě Shuǎng, the Jiédùshǐ of Xiàzhōu, led his division to garrison at Lìyáng.
Cháo ordered the Emperor to persuade Shuǎng to surrender,
and Shuǎng subsequently submitted to Cháo.
In the second month of the first year of Zhōnghé,
Cháo appointed the Emperor as Dōngnánmiàn Xíngyíng Xiānfēngshǐ (Southeast Front Mobile Camp Vanguard Commander),
ordering him to attack Nányáng,
which he captured.
In the sixth month,
the Emperor returned to Cháng'ān,
and Cháo personally welcomed him at Bàshàng.
In the seventh month,
Cháo dispatched the Emperor to the west to resist the armies of Bīn, Qí, Fū, and Xià at Xīngpíng,
achieving merit wherever he went.
In the fifth month,
the former Tang Dynasty chancellors Zhāng Wénwèi and Yáng Shè were both appointed as Ménxià Shìláng and Píngzhāng Shì.
Yùshǐ Dàfū Xuē Yíjǔ was appointed as Zhōngshū Shìláng and Píngzhāng Shì.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 199.)
When the Emperor first received the abdication,
he was especially eager to govern well.
He entrusted the chancellors with seeking out and finding virtuous and capable individuals.
If there were those of lower rank who possessed talent and ability but had long been unable to achieve their ambitions,
they were to be specially promoted and employed.
If there were those who understood the principles of good and bad governance and could offer remedies for the ills of the time,
they were allowed to submit memorials.
The Emperor would personally review and select them, considering their benefits and drawbacks before implementation,
and then reward them with titles and ranks.
If there were those who lived in obscurity in rural areas, not seeking fame or advancement,
the local officials were ordered to invite them with full courtesy,
hoping to leave no talent undiscovered or overlooked.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 213.)
Zhāng Quányì, Yǐn of Hénán and concurrently Jiéduéshǐ of Héyáng, was promoted and enfeoffed as Wèi Wáng.
Qián Liú, Jiéduéshǐ of Liǎngzhè, was promoted and enfeoffed as Wúyuè Wáng.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 196.)
On the Xīnsì day,
the relevant authorities memorialized
that the Emperor's birthday should be designated as Dàmíng Jié,
with one day of holiday before and after.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juǎn 16187.)
On the Rénwǔ day,
Zhū Yǒuqīan, Jiéduéshǐ of Bǎoyìjūn, presented two hundred sets of robes for civil and military officials.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 197.)
On the Yǐyǒu day,
the Emperor's elder brother Quányù was enfeoffed as Guǎng Wáng,
his son Yǒuwén as Bó Wáng,
Yǒuguī as Yǐng Wáng,
Yǒuzhāng as Fú Wáng,
Yǒuyōng as Hè Wáng,
and Yǒuhuī as Jiàn Wáng.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juǎn 16628.
Note: According to Ouyáng Shǐ, his nephews Yǒuliàng were enfeoffed as Héng Wáng,
Yǒunéng as Huì Wáng,
and Yǒuhuì as Shào Wáng.)
On the Xīnmǎo day,
the old residence in the Eastern Capital was converted into Jiànchāng Gōng,
and the supervisor of Jiànchāng Yuàn was renamed Jiànchāng Gōng Shǐ.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juǎn 12113.)
Initially,
when the Emperor was establishing his enterprise,
due to the numerous records of soldiers and granaries in the Four Garrisons,
he established the Jiànchāng Yuàn to oversee them.
Now, it was changed to a palace,
evidently to emphasize its importance.
(Tōngjiàn Zhù, citing Xuē Shǐ.)
On the Jiǎwǔ day,

an imperial edict was issued that all official names of subordinate offices and prefectures and counties across the empire that contained characters forbidden by the imperial ancestral temple's personal names
should be changed: Chéngmén Láng was changed to Ménjú Láng;
Mào Zhōu was changed to Wèn Zhōu;
Guì Zhōu Mùhuà Xiàn was changed to Guīhuà Xiàn;
Pān Zhōu Màomíng Xiàn was changed to Yuèsháng Xiàn.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 189.
Note: Wèi Tài's Dōngxuān Bǐlù states that in the capital, areas outside the city were called Zhōudōng, Zhōuxī, Zhōunán, Zhōuběi,
and counties like Wéichéng, Xiāngchéng, and Zuòchéng
were simply called Wéi Xiàn, Xiāng Xiàn, and Zuò Xiàn,
which was a continuation of the taboo practices from the Liáng period.)
An edict was issued that the Shūmì Yuàn should be renamed Chóngzhèng Yuàn,
with Jìng Xiáng, who was in charge of the Yuàn, as Yuànshǐ.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juǎn 12113.)
Wénsī Yuàn was changed to Qiánwén Yuàn,
and Tónghé Yuàn was changed to Zuǒluán Yuàn.
(Note: Wǔdài Huìyào states: In the fifth month,
Yùshí Shǐ was changed to Sīshàn Shǐ,
and Xiǎomǎfāng Shǐ was changed to Tiānjì Shǐ.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
The residence north of Shuǐběi in the Western Capital was made Dàchāng Gōng.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 196.)
The Tàiqīng Gōng in Yōng Zhōu was abolished,
and the Tàiwēi Gōng in the Western Capital and the Tàiqīng Gōng in Bó Zhōu were both changed to Guàn,
while all Zǐjí Gōngs in various prefectures were changed to Lǎojūn Miào.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 194.)
The monk Zhìxuān from Quán Zhōu returned from the Western Regions,
presenting the relics of Pratyekabuddhas and Buddhist scriptures in Sanskrit manuscripts.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juǎn 21175.)
On the Bǐngshēn day,
the Emperor held a banquet at Xuándé Diàn to reward the military commanders Liú Hàn, Fú Dàozhāo, and others,
granting them gifts of varying amounts.
In this month,
the Jiéduéshǐs of the three garrisons of Qīng Zhōu, Xǔ Zhōu, and Dìng Zhōu requested private banquets,
and each was bestowed with local products.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juǎn 16746.)
Hán Jiàn, Jiéduéshǐ of Qīng Zhōu, was appointed Shǒu Sītú
(Qīng Zhōu was
mistakenly written as
"Qīng Zhōu"
in the original, now corrected according to the context.
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān)) and Píngzhāng Shì.
The Emperor considered Hán Jiàn to have both civil and military talents,
and to be knowledgeable about the benefits and harms of agriculture, military affairs, and the planning of expenses.
Wishing to consult him fully on these matters,
his favor and grace were exceptionally rare at the time,
with few comparable.
He was immediately appointed as the prime minister,
and bestowed with very generous gifts.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 199.)
Wáng Rú, Cìshǐ of Sù Zhōu, presented a white rabbit.
Tú Jiāhé, Cìshǐ of Pú Zhōu, presented auspicious grain and sweet wheat.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 202.)
Guǎng Zhōu presented many rare treasures and precious medicines
of various categories.
Zhāng Quányì, Yǐn of Hénán, presented an excess of 100,000 strings of cash, 6,000 bolts of silk, and 300,000 liǎng of cotton from before the first year of Kāipíng,
and further requested that the annual tribute quota be fixed at 30,000 bolts of silk per year,
to be a permanent custom.
Gāo Jìchāng of Jīngnán presented several dozen auspicious tangerines,
whose quality and taste
The two characters
"bǎi wèi"
should, in terms of meaning, be
"gān wèi."
However, Wǔdài Huìyào also has
"bǎi wèi."
For now, we retain the original.
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān)) greatly surpassed the usual tribute.
Moreover, tangerines usually ripen in winter,
but now it was midsummer.
People at the time found this unusual,
and thus called it an auspicious sign.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 197.
Note: Wǔdài Chūnqiū states: In the fifth month,
Lǐ Sī'ān and the Jìn people fought at Lù Chéng,
and Lǐ Sī'ān's army was defeated.
Cèfǔ Yuánguī, citing Xuē Shǐ,
states that Lǐ Sī'ān was only appointed as commander in the eighth month.
The Wǔdài Chūnqiū recording Lǐ Sī'ān's defeat in the fifth month
is likely erroneous.
For now, the record from Wǔdài Chūnqiū before the sixth month is retained
for reference.
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān))
In the sixth month,
the Emperor visited Qiányuán Yuàn,
where he hosted a banquet for the chancellors, academicians, and tributary envoys from various circuits.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juǎn 16746.)
On the Jǐhài day,
the Emperor presided at Chóngyuán Diàn.
Eight sets of jade tablets and seals, bearing the posthumous titles for the four ancestral temples, were brought out from within the palace.
The chancellors, civil and military officials, imperial guards, and musicians escorted them to the Tàimiào for the ceremony.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
the Imperial Astronomical Bureau memorialized:
"The character 'Wù'
is found in the solar term 'Wùchén,'
we request it be changed to 'Wǔ'."
This was approved.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 189.
Note: Róngzhāi Xùbǐ thought that
"Wù"
resembled the character
"Chéng,"
so the Sītiān (Astronomical Bureau) flattered him.
Little did he know that
"Wù"
was used to avoid the personal name Màolín, the great-grandfather of the Liáng founder,
and not because it resembled
"Chéng."
Yúngǔ Zájì had already clarified this.
The monument for Chóngfú Hóu Miào, erected in the second year of Kāipíng,
correctly uses 'Wǔchén,'
which shows the practice of taboo at that time.)
On the Guǐhài day,
an edict was issued concerning former court officials
who had been banished to the southern wilderness,
and whose cases had not been cleared for many years.
Among them, some possessed talent and ability but were envied by their contemporaries,
and had suffered deep injustice.
It was ordered that their names be recorded,
all their official ranks be restored,
and that all circuits be notified to send them to the capital.
If they had already died,
they were permitted to be reburied,
to demonstrate imperial grace.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 191.)
As the road north of Huī'ān Mén in the Western Capital was too close to the inner palace walls
and inconvenient for the people,
it was ordered to be relocated from Yúlín directly to the south of Duānmén.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 196.)
Bào'ēn Chányuàn in Yào Zhōu was changed to Xìngguó Sì.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 194.)
Mǎ Yīn memorialized that he had defeated the Huái bandits.
Qū Yù, Jiéduéshǐ of Jìnghǎijūn, died.
He also swept away the left Fēng,
and suppressed Xiànshǒu.
Thus, with the barbarians outside and the Huáxià culture within,
(“內夏” (nèi xià, Huáxià culture within)
was originally written as
“內憂” (nèi yōu, internal worries);
it has now been corrected according to the context.
(From a sticky note in the Yǐngkù copy)) it was further known where Heaven’s
mandate truly lay;
all creatures, great and small,
jointly recognized the eternal stability of the imperial foundation.
Looking up, mindful of the auspicious blessings,
yet lacking a means to repay them.
Therefore, on the day of the Winter Solstice,
he personally performed
the ritual at the Yuánqiū.
This great celebration,
must reach the common people,
thus extending a private act of generosity
to bestow fortune upon the weary and weak.
It is hoped that recovery will gradually be achieved,
and peace quickly established.
Alas!
Since I ascended the throne,
the years have been few,
the dark mists not yet dispelled,
and punitive expeditions still frequent.
Arms and soldiers require discussion regarding provisions,
and flying
transport frequently burdens the registered households.
These matters are unavoidable,
and the worry is like falling into a pit.
It is appropriate that local officials
redouble their efforts in pacification,
clearly admonish and instruct,
and for each official department to recruit
corvée labor,
while prohibiting corrupt officials from excessively extorting and seeking gain.
This is to prevent people from becoming scattered and destitute,
and from suffering and being unable to cope.
It is appropriate to order the officials of the Hénán Fǔ, Kāifēng Fǔ, and all circuits’ Guānchá
Shǐ to strictly supervise and control,
and for Cìshǐ and Xiànlìng not to exploit circumstances for taxation,
or to unduly disturb the people.
For all ordinary lawsuits,
it is hoped that light penalties will be applied.
Only when the use of
the military ceases
should preferential provisions be immediately discussed.
If there are any omissions in the benevolent decrees and regulations,
the relevant departments should be ordered to categorize and present proposals based on precedents.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 190
On the day Jǐhài,
Luó Tíngguī, a Lángzhōng of the Sīmén, was appointed Fùshǐ of the Wèibó Jiédù,
acting as the head of the prefecture,
and his name was changed to Zhōu Hàn.
At that time, Yèwáng Shào wēi's illness worsened daily,
and concerned about future affairs,
he thus submitted this request.
(Tōngjiàn Kǎoyì quotes Xuēshǐ.)
)On the day Xīnchǒu,
he visited Gǔshuǐ.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 205.)
)On the day Wùwǔ,
he held court at Míngwén Diàn,
and appointed Tàifù Zhāng Zōngshì as Tàibǎo. After Hán Jiàn received the appointment
(Note: The original text is suspected of being corrupted or having omissions.)
the guards of the Jīnwú led him to ascend the imperial carriage,
and the ceremonial procession guided him to pay homage at the Tàimiào. After this,
he proceeded to the Shàngshū Shěng for the official appointment.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 199.)
)He visited Yúlín Pō to inspect the troops,
and trained the infantry and cavalry of all commands.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 214.)
)An imperial edict renamed Qiánwén Yuàn to Wénsī Yuàn,
Xíngcóng Diàn to Xīng’ān Diàn,
Qiúchǎng to Xīng’ān Qiúchǎng,
and also renamed Gōngjiàn Kù Diàn to Xuānwēi Diàn
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 196.)
)Língzhōu reported that
Liú Zhījùn, a rebel general from Fèngxiáng, led forces from Bīn, Qí, Qín, and Jīng to invade and press upon the prefectural city.
The Emperor dispatched Kāng Huái Yīng from Shǎnzōu and Kòu Yànqīng from Huázhōu to lead troops to attack Bīn and Níng,
to relieve the pressure from the bandits of Shuòfāng.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 216.
Note: According to Wǔdài Chūnqiū: in the eleventh month
the Qín people came to invade Língzhōu.
Kāng Huáiyīng from Shǎnzōu invaded Qín,
and captured Níng, Qìng, and Yǎn prefectures.
When the Qín people attacked,
Huáiyīng's army was defeated at Shēngpíng.)
)On the day Yǐchǒu in the twelfth month, the Lày (Winter Solstice sacrifice) was held,
and a hunt was conducted at Gānquán Yì.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 205.)
)Given that Púzhōu was the place where he first established his foundation,
and also for the purpose of strategizing for Fū and Yán,
he toured the area for several months.
During his leisure time, he traveled to Jiāolídìan,
where he recounted past events,
remembered Wáng Chóngróng’s former merits,
and issued an edict to praise, commend, and honor him.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 211.)
)The Guózǐ Jiān reported:
“We propose to construct a temple for Wénxuān Wáng,
and further request to levy a monthly
tax of fifteen cash per string of coins
from the salaries of officials currently serving in the court and throughout the realm,
to cover the cost of construction materials.”
This was granted.
In this year,
the temple of Wénxuān Wáng was repaired using the levied salaries of officials.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 194.)
)Wáng Shěnzhī, the Jiédù Shǐ of Fújiàn, reported
that he donated money to build a monastery,
and requested an imperial plaque for it.
An edict named it Dàliáng Wànsuì Zhī Sì,
and permitted forty-nine monks to be ordained there.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 194.)
)Wáng Rénsì, the Láolìang Shǐ, was posthumously granted Sīkōng;
Shǐ Zhào, the former Yāyá of Tóngzhōu, was granted Yòu Púshè;
Yāyá Wáng Yànhóng, Gāo Hànquán, Qiū Fèngyán, and Qiú Qióng were all granted Xíngbù Shàngshū;
and Wáng Yún was granted Yùshǐ Sīxiàn.
Initially,
when Zhījùn was about to rebel,
he conspired to gather the generals and inquire what should be done.
Rénsì and others upheld righteousness and did not yield,
and all suffered his cruelty.
At this time, they were posthumously praised and honored.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 210.)
)Liú Shǒuguāng reported
that he fought his brother Shǒuwén west of Jìzhōu,
and captured Shǒuwén alive.
(Tōngjiàn Zhù quotes Xuēshǐ.)
On the day Rénchén, the first day of the first month of the fourth year of Kāipíng,
the Emperor held court at Cháoyuán Diàn,
receiving congratulations from all officials,
using ritual and music
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 197.)
)Edict:
“Public affairs are difficult to delay,
and residences are all quite distant.

Therefore, the Zhōngshū Shèrén on daily duty, and the Lángguān responsible for seals in the Lìbù and Sīfēng, the Shàofǔ Jiān, and the scribes and clerks responsible for carving seals, documents, and writing appointment scrolls,
should all take turns lodging in the vicinity of the Zhōngshū.”
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 191.)
)The Emperor exited through the Shīzǐ Mén
and went to the foot of Yúlín Pō to inspect and train.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, juǎn 214.)
)On the day Rényín,
he visited Bǎoníng Qiúchǎng,
and hosted a banquet for the prime ministers and all civil and military officials.
The prime minister Zhāng Zōngshì and others were given additional gifts,

Also, Ouyáng Shǐ's biography of the second concubine, née Guō, states: In Tiānfú 3 of the Jìn,
an imperial edict ordered that the heads of criminals previously stored in the Grand Temple
be released for relatives to collect and bury.
Then, the head of Mòdì was exhumed,
and the Right Guard General Ān Chóngruǎn was dispatched to bury it with the concubine.
The concubine had died in Luòyáng.
Páng Yuánbīng's Wénchāng Zá Lù states: Liáng Jūnwáng
was first buried in the Tiānfú era of Jìn,
and thus his former concubine, née Zhāng, alone survived.
Kǎogōng Yuánwài Shāng Péng composed an epitaph saying:
"There was a seven-month appointment,
but the concubine who longed for the mausoleum was not seen;
Jiǔyí lost its color,
leaving only the consort who wept by the bamboo."
Now, the commentary states: Mòdì's Défēi, née Zhāng, died early,
and was later buried with Mòdì.
However, the second concubine, née Guō,
was still alive during the Tiānfú era.
Ouyáng Shǐ did not explicitly state which concubine was buried with him,
and Wénchāng Zá Lù mistakenly assumed that the surviving one was the former concubine, née Zhāng.
This is likely an error based on hearsay.
Although Xuē Shǐ's biography of empresses and concubines of Liáng is missing,
by referencing the annals of Mòdì of Liáng and Gāozǔ of Jìn,
it is determined that Défēi, née Zhāng, was buried with him.
Also, the Wǔdài Shǐ has no biographies of imperial relatives by marriage.
Wǔdài Huìyào states: The eldest daughter of Liáng Tàizǔ, Princess Ānyáng,
married Luó Tíngguī,
and was posthumously enfeoffed in the 8th month of Kāipíng 2.
Princess Chánglè
married Zhào Yán,
and was enfeoffed on the 11th day of the 5th month of Kāipíng 1.
Princess Pǔníng
married Zhāozuò Wáng Shì,
and was enfeoffed on the 11th day of the 5th month of Kāipíng 1.
Princess Jīnhuá
was enfeoffed in the 10th month of Kāipíng 2.
Princess Zhēnnìng
was enfeoffed on the 5th day of the 10th month of Gānhuà 3.
Shàodì's eldest daughter, Princess Shòuchūn,
was enfeoffed on the 5th day of the 4th month of Gānhuà 3.
His second daughter, Princess Shòuchāng,
was enfeoffed on the 23rd day of the 9th month of Zhēnmíng 1.
Now, examining the Tōngjiàn Kǎoyì's citation of the Biographies of Meritorious Officials of Liáng, it states: Luó Tíngguī married Princess Ānyáng,
and also married Princess Jīnhuá.
Xuē Shǐ's biography of Luó Shàowēi also records that in Kāipíng 4,
an imperial edict ordered Princess Jīnhuá to become a nun.
Thus, Princess Jīnhuá indeed married into the Luó clan,
but Wǔdài Huìyào does not record this,
which is also a textual omission.

Hè Délún,
his ancestors were people from a Hexī部落.
His father, Huáiqìng,
was a junior officer in the army of Huázhōu.
Délún was a yájiàng of Huá in his youth.
When Tàizǔ commanded the Four Circuits,
Délún followed with his own army,
and successively rendered military service,
progressing through císhǐ and liúhòu,
then promoted to Jiédùshǐ of Pínglú Circuit.
When Yáng Shīhòu of Wèibó died,
the imperial court appointed Délún to replace him.
On the night of the 29th day of the third month of Zhēnmíng First Year (915 CE),
the Wèi army mutinied,
captured Délún,
imprisoned him in a separate lodge,
and killed all his subordinates.
Forced by Zhāng Yàn, the leader of the rebellion,
they sent envoys to pledge allegiance to Tàiyuán.
The Jìn King descended east from Huángzé Lǐng,
and reached Línqīng.
Délún secretly sent his aide, Sīkōng Tíng, to the Jìn King,
to complain about Zhāng Yàn's insults and humiliation.
When the Jìn King arrived at Yǒngjì,
he executed Yàn and eight others,
and then entered Wèi.
Délún immediately presented his seals and tallies to the Jìn King.
(According to Zīzhì Tōngjiàn: After the Jìn King entered,
Délún presented his seals and tallies,
requesting the King to concurrently lead the Tiānxíong Army.
The King firmly declined,
saying:
"I heard that the Biàn bandits were pressing your domain,
so I personally led my army,
traveling far to rescue you;
I also heard that the city has recently suffered terribly,
so I temporarily entered to offer comfort.
If your Excellency does not trust me,
but pushes the seals and tallies upon me,
this is truly not my original intention."
Délún bowed again and said:
"Now the enemies are close,
and the military city has just undergone a great change.
People's hearts are uneasy,
and Délún's core subordinates and administrators have been almost entirely killed by Zhāng Yàn.
Isolated and weak,
how can I command the army!
If trouble arises,
I fear I will betray your great kindness."
The King then accepted it.

Supervisor Zhāng Chéngyè detained him and did not let him proceed.

Wáng Tán attacked Tàiyuán with a surprise army.
Many of Délún's subordinates fled,
and Chéngyè feared he would cause trouble,
so he executed Délún,
and killed all his retainers and troops.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 17467.)

Shīhòu moved his military camp to below the city walls,

In the third month of Tiānfù Fourth Year (904 CE),
