when Lùzhōu was attacked,
Cúnjié was made Commander of Cavalry and Infantry for the Campaigning Army.
In the second month of the second year of Kāipíng
he was transferred from Senior General of the Right Supervisor of Gates Guard to Commander of the Right Dragon Tiger Guard,
stationed in Luòyáng.
That year,
the imperial army was defeated at Shàngdǎng.
The Jìn people, capitalizing on their victory, pressed on towards Zézhōu,
and the city was on the verge of falling.
Zhāng Quányì, the Defender of Hénán, consulted with Cúnjié.
Consequently, Cúnjié led his own army, together with the Right Dragon Tiger Guard and Yǔlín Guard, to support Shàngdǎng.
When the army reached Tiānjǐng Pass,
Cúnjié said to his generals:
"Although this expedition
is not by imperial decree,
this strategic location
must not be lost."
At that time, the Jìn people, having just won a victory,
were in high spirits.
Cúnjié led his troops forward,
silently arriving at Zézhōu by night.
They happened to encounter the wall guards who had already set fire and raised a clamor
to respond to the outer army.
The Administrator was defending the yáchéng [official residence city],
not knowing what to do.
Cúnjié had barely entered
when the Jìn army arrived.
He then distributed his forces for defense.
The Jìn army attacked from all four sides,
digging tunnels to enter the city.
Cúnjié also responded with counter-tunnels,
fighting underground.
The Jìn army could not advance.
He also used powerful crossbows to shoot them,
piercing both men and horses.
After thirteen days,
the Jìn army suffered many casualties,
burned their camps, and retreated.
The prefecture was thus saved.
(Note: Cúnjié, after serving in the Lùzhōu campaigning army, became Commander and was
stationed in Luòyáng.
Later, during the defeat at Jiāchéng,
Cúnjié was never in the army.
Ouyáng Shǐ, however, says: When the Jìn army had already broken Jiāchéng,
Cúnjié returned with his remaining troops,
and upon reaching Tiānjǐng Pass,
he went back to rescue Zézhōu.
The Kǎoyì of the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn has already pointed out this error.
(Kǎoyì of the Old History of the Five Dynasties)) Tàizǔ repeatedly praised and admired him.
In the fifth month,
he was promoted to Commander of the Left Dragon Tiger Guard,
and concurrently served as Commander-in-Chief of all Cavalry and Infantry of the Six Armies.
In the tenth month,
he was appointed Administrator of Jiàngzhōu.
In the third year of Qiánfú (876 CE),
the imperial court appointed Duàn Wénchǔ as the Supervisor of Water and Land Transport for Dàiběi and the Defender of Yúnzhōu.
At that time, the region suffered successive famines,
and Wénchǔ gradually reduced the army's rations.
All the armies harbored resentment.
Wǔhuáng was a border defense commander in Yúnzhōng,
and his subordinates repeatedly complained that army rations were insufficient.
Border commanders Chéng Huáisù,
Wáng Xíngshěn, Gài Yù, Lǐ Cúnzhāng, Xuē Tiěshān, Kāng Jūnlì, and others
then escorted Wǔhuáng into Yúnzhōu,
with a crowd of nearly ten thousand people.
They encamped at Dòují Tái.
Wénchǔ was shackled and brought out of the city,
to respond to the situation outside.
The generals submitted a memorial,
requesting to bestow the staff and axe upon Wǔhuáng.
The imperial court did not agree,
and summoned troops from various circuits to suppress them.
(Note: According to the Old Book of Tang, Annals of Yìzōng: In the twelfth month of Xiántōng thirteen (872 CE),
Lǐ Guóchāng's young son Kèyòng killed Duàn Wénchǔ, the Defender of Yúnzhōng,
occupied Yúnzhōu,
and proclaimed himself Acting Defender.
The New Book of Tang, Annals of Xīzōng:
On the guǐyǒu day of the second month of Qiánfú five (878 CE),
Lǐ Kèyòng, the Garrison Commander of Yúnzhōng, killed Duàn Wénchǔ, the Defender of Dàtóng.
Ōuyáng Shǐ follows the Old Book of Tang,
while Zīzhì Tōngjiàn follows the New Book of Tang.
Xuē Shǐ states Qiánfú three,
which differs from other books.
According to Zīzhì Tōngjiàn Kǎo Yì, quoting Zhào Fèng's Hòutáng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù, it is indeed Qiánfú three.
Zhào Fèng was a Tang chancellor,
not far from Wǔhuáng's time,
and his observations are more reliable,
thus it should be trustworthy.)
In the fifth year of Qiánfú (878 CE),
Huáng Cháo crossed the Yangzi River,
and his power spread.
The Son of Heaven then realized the seriousness of the matter,
and appointed Wǔhuáng as the Military Governor of Dàtóng Jūn,
(Note: Ōuyáng Shǐ states that Kèyòng was appointed as the Defender of Dàtóng Jūn;
the New Book of Tang states that Guóchāng was appointed as the Defender of Dàtóng Jūn;
Zīzhì Tōngjiàn states that Guóchāng was appointed as the Military Governor of Dàtóng Jūn;
all differ from Xuē Shǐ.)
and acting Minister of Public Works.
In winter, Xiànzǔ led an army to attack the Dǎngxiàng.
The Tǔhún Hèlián Duó took advantage of the void to seize Zhènwǔ,
and the entire clan was captured by the Tǔhún.
Wǔhuáng went to Dìngbiān Jūn to welcome Xiànzǔ back to Yúnzhōu,
but the defending general of Yúnzhōu refused them entry at the pass.
Wǔhuáng raided the areas of Wèi and Shuò,
gained three thousand men,
and encamped at Xīnchéng in Shénwǔ Chuān.
Hèlián Duó attacked and besieged them day and night.
Wǔhuáng and his three brothers responded to the rebels from four sides.
Soon after, Xiànzǔ arrived with an army from Wèizhōu,
and the Tǔhún retreated.
From then on, the army's power revived.
The Son of Heaven appointed Hèlián Duó as the Military Governor of Dàtóng Jūn,
and moreover ordered him to advance and attack Wǔhuáng.
In the spring of the sixth year of Qiánfú (879 CE),
the imperial court appointed Lǐ Jūn, the Military Governor of Zhāoyì, as the Northern Pacification Commissioner.
He led the armies of Shàngdǎng and Tàiyuán across Shílíng Guān,
and encamped at Dàizhōu.
He joined Lǐ Kějǔ of Yōuzhōu and Hèlián Duó to jointly attack Wèizhōu.
Xiànzǔ defended it with one army,
while Wǔhuáng went south with another army to Zhēlǔ Chéng to resist Lǐ Jūn.
That winter, there was heavy snow,
bowstrings and crossbow strings broke,
and the southern army suffered from the bitter cold.
They were greatly defeated in battle,
and fled back to Dàizhōu.
Lǐ Jūn died from a stray arrow.
In the spring of the first year of Guǎngmíng (880 CE),
the Son of Heaven again ordered Marshal Lǐ Zhuó
(Note: Ōuyáng Shǐ states "Pacification Commissioner Lǐ Zhuó";
Zīzhì Tōngjiàn also states
"Zhuó";
which differs from Xuē Shǐ. (Old History of the Five Dynasties Examination of Differences))
to lead an army of several tens of thousands and encamp at Dàizhōu. Wǔhuáng ordered Army Commander Fù Wéndá to raise troops in Wèizhōu.
Gāo Wénjí, the Prefect of Shuòzhōu, along with the generals of Xuēgě and Ānqìng
(Note: The New Book of Tang states "Mǐ Hǎiwàn, leader of the Sàgě, and Ānqìng."
(Old History of the Five Dynasties Examination of Differences) Xuēgě and Ānqìng
were originally written as "Xuē Hé, Nǚ Dù."
Now, having examined Xuē Shǐ as quoted in Cèfǔ Yuánguī, and also the New Book of Tang and Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, all state Xuēgě and Ānqìng.
This has now been corrected.
(Photographic copy sticky note)),
bound Wéndá and sent him to Lǐ Zhuó.
In the sixth month, Lǐ Zhuó led a large army to attack Wèizhōu.
Xiànzǔ fared poorly in battle,
and so he led his clan to flee to the Dádá tribe.
After staying for several months,
the Tǔhún Hèlián Duó secretly sent people to bribe the Dádá to sow discord against Xiànzǔ,
and gradually suspicion and obstruction arose.
Wǔhuáng knew of this.
He would often summon their chieftains to hunt in the wilderness,
sometimes competing with them in a hundred-pace horse-riding archery contest using a whip,
or using a suspended needle on a tree leaf as a target.
He hit it with divine skill.
Because of this, the hearts of the tribesmen were subdued,
and they dared not secretly rise up.
Soon after, Huáng Cháo crossed north from Jiāng and Huái.
Wǔhuáng slaughtered oxen and poured wine,
feasting their chieftains.
As the wine flowed,
he explained to them,
"My father and I have been slandered and estranged by treacherous officials,
with no means to repay the country.
Now I hear that Huáng Cháo is invading Jiāng and Huái from the north,
which will surely become a disaster for the Central Plains.
One day, if the Son of Heaven grants amnesty and pardon,
and issues an edict to levy troops,
I and you gentlemen will march south to pacify the empire.
This is my wish.
Life in this world,
how brief it is!
How can we grow old in the sand dunes forever!
Gentlemen, strive hard."
The Dádá knew he had no intention of staying,
and were all relieved with no objections.
In the eleventh month of that year,
Huáng Cháo raided Tóngguān.
The Son of Heaven ordered Chén Jǐngsī, the eunuch supervisor of Hédōng, to be the Commander for Raising Troops in Dàiběi,
to gather troops and defeat the rebels.
In the twelfth month,
Huáng Cháo attacked Cháng'ān,
and Xīzōng fled to Shǔ.
Chén Jǐngsī and Lǐ Yǒujīn led five thousand cavalry from the Shāzhū tribes south to the capital.
Yǒujīn was Wǔhuáng's paternal cousin.
(Note: According to Zīzhì Tōngjiàn,
Yǒujīn initially surrendered to Lǐ Zhuó along with Gāo Wénjí,
and thus was able to go south to the capital with Chén Jǐngsī.
Xuē Shǐ does not record this.)
I was shocked and dismayed beyond measure.
Tears soaked my lapel,
doubly deepening the melancholy of Shēn Xū;
sweat poured down my back,
as if I had heard the words of Jiǎng Jì.
(Jiǎng Jì,
originally written as
「Jiǎng Yǎn」,
now
corrected according to the Cèfǔ Yuánguī (sticky note in the photocopy edition)). I, your servant, have served two dynasties,
received grace from three generations,
was honored with the positions of general and minister,
and my lineage is tied to the imperial clan.
I was granted an axe to lead punitive expeditions,
and asked for fragrant grass as a sign of tribute when I went to punish a state.
I have
battled in the field,
for over twenty years,
yet ultimately failed to sever Xīn Mǎng's head,
or break Chī Yóu's shoulder and thigh,
leading to the overthrow of the imperial court,
and wolves and tigers running rampant.
Moreover,
having been entrusted with duties and shared responsibilities,
enjoying honor and favor,
if the precious jade is destroyed in its box,
whose fault is that?
Reflecting on these points,
I am filled with immense shame.
However, there is no constant
position for rulers and ministers;
mountains and valleys undergo transformations.
Perhaps one might whip the long river into submission,
or seal Hángǔ Pass with mud,
as times change and affairs alter,
principles also vary in countless ways.
Just like the fierce competition at the end of the Zhōu dynasty,
or the tripod
dominance at the beginning of the Wèi dynasty.
Sūn Quán and his son
did not receive explicit conferment of grace from Hán;
Liú Bèi and his ministers
rose from humble beginnings in Zhuō Jùn.
To gain it is not to be indebted to family lineage;
to lose it does not
diminish one's achievements.
When it is the season for chasing the deer,
why regret the loss of embroidered robes?
Only I, your servant, have enjoyed imperial favor for successive dynasties,
(enjoyed favor,
originally written as
「yīng chǒng」,
now corrected
according to Cèfǔ Yuánguī.
(sticky note in the photocopy edition)) and generations have shown loyalty,
humbly bearing the words of instruction,
and roughly preserving family traditions.
A good chess player first adheres to strategy;
one who cultivates a path through a field must
not remove the ox.
I swear in this life
never to lose my integrity.
Relying on the imperial victory,
may the enemies be swiftly annihilated.
If events do not accord with my wishes,
then to roam with Zāng Hóng in the
underworld
would also be without regret.
You alone are a great statesman of the state;
Sōng and Héng mountains bestow their blessings upon you.
You govern the superior lands of the Nine Provinces,
and possess the immense talent of an era.
At this time,
seek your own greater fortune.
The good news I have received
does not align with my deepest convictions.
What will the world say of me?
Having a state is not my principle.
This humble and sincere plea
does not express everything.
In the fifth month,
Liáng Zǔ dispatched his general Kāng Huái'īng to lead a hundred thousand troops to besiege Lùzhōu.
Huái'īng led his soldiers and populace,
building ramparts around the city,
cutting off all communication to the city.
Wǔ Huáng sent Zhōu Déwēi with troops to reinforce.
Déwēi's army encamped at Yúwú,
leading the vanguard to challenge,
capturing prisoners daily.
Huái'īng dared not engage in immediate battle.
Liáng Zǔ, seeing Huái'īng's lack of success,
then replaced him with Lǐ Sī'ān.
(Note: Lǐ Sī'ān replacing Huái'īng is recorded in Tōngjiàn as occurring in the seventh month, which differs from Xuē Shǐ's record of the fifth month.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) Sī'ān led his army to encamp at Lùchéng.
(Lùchéng,
originally written as
「Zéchén」,
considering that Tōngjiàn, Ōuyáng Shǐ, and Wǔdài Chūnqiū all record Lǐ Sī'ān besieging Lùchéng,
it is now corrected.
(sticky note in the photocopy edition)) Zhōu Déwēi attacked him with five thousand cavalry,
and the Liáng army suffered a major defeat,
beheading over a thousand.
Sī'ān retreated to a strong defensive position,
and additionally built outer fortresses,
calling them
「Jiázhài」,
to resist our reinforcing army.
Liáng Zǔ mobilized the people of Shāndōng to supply provisions.
Déwēi daily attacked them with light cavalry,
making the supply routes difficult and dangerous,
and the morale of the populace grew increasingly fearful.
Lǐ Sī'ān then built a covered passage from the southeast mountain pass,
connecting to the Jiázhài,
to facilitate the transport of provisions.
From then on, the Liáng army firmly defended the Jiázhài.
In the winter, tenth month,
Wǔ Huáng fell ill.
At this time, the city wall of Jìnyáng mysteriously collapsed on its own,
which the diviners considered an ill omen.
On the *wùzǐ* day, the first day of the first month of the fifth year of Tiānyòu,
Wǔhuáng's illness worsened.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
he passed away in Jìnyáng,
at the age of fifty-three.
His dying wish was for a simple burial,
and that mourning clothes be removed twenty-seven days after the announcement of his death.
Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
and posthumously honored him as Emperor Wǔ (Wǔhuángdì),
with the temple name Tàizǔ.
His mausoleum is in Yànmén.
(From *Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn* scroll 7154.
*Wǔdài Shǐbǔ* says: Tàizǔ Wǔhuáng
was a descendant of Zhūyē Chìxīn,
a man of the Shātuó tribe.
His senior was born in a vulture's nest.
The chieftain, seeing his unusual birth,
had him raised by various tribes.
Thus,
"Zhūyé"
was taken as his surname,
meaning he was not raised by a single father.
Later, the pronunciation became corrupted,
and "Zhū"
was changed to
"Zhū,"
and "Yé"
to
"Yē."
When
Tàizǔ
was born, he was blind in one eye.
As he grew, he became brave and skilled,
excellent at riding and archery,
unrivaled wherever he went.
At the time, he was called
"Dúyǎnlóng" (One-Eyed Dragon),
which was greatly resented by the tribes.
Fearing disaster,
Tàizǔ
led his entire clan to surrender to the Táng dynasty.
He was appointed Cìshǐ of Yúnzhōu,
bestowed the surname Lǐ,
and named Kèyòng.
When Huáng Cháo attacked Cháng'ān,
he led troops from the north to respond to the crisis.
After achieving success,
he was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Tàiyuán
and enfeoffed as King of Jìn.
When Wǔhuáng held Hédōng,
his prestige and reputation greatly increased.
Yáng Xíngmì of Huáinán often regretted not knowing his appearance.
He then sent a painter, disguised as a merchant,
to Hédōng to sketch him.
When the painter arrived,
not long after,
someone who knew of his plot
captured him.
Wǔhuáng was initially very angry,
but then he said to his close associates,
"Since
I am naturally blind in one eye,
let us summon him and have him paint me,
to see what he does."
When the painter arrived,
Wǔhuáng
slapped his knee and sternly said,
"Huáinán sent you to paint my portrait.
You must be an excellent painter.
If you fail to capture me to a tenth of my likeness,
then beneath these steps shall be your death."
The painter bowed twice and began to draw.
It was the height of summer,
and Wǔhuáng held an eight-cornered fan.
The painter depicted the fan's corner partially covering his face.
Wǔhuáng said,
"You flatter me."
He immediately ordered him to paint again.
The painter responded instantly and drew
him holding a bow and nocking an arrow,
with one eye slightly closed to check the arrow's straightness.
Wǔhuáng was greatly pleased,
and generously rewarded him with gold and silk before sending him away.
*Wǔdài Shǐ Quēwén* says: It is said that when Wǔhuáng was near death,
he gave three arrows to Zhuāngzōng and said,
"One arrow is for attacking Liú Réngōng.
If you do not first conquer Yōuzhōu,
Hénán cannot be planned.
One arrow is for striking the Qìdān.
A Bǎojī and I clasped hands and swore an oath,
becoming brothers,
vowing to restore the Táng imperial house.
Now he has broken his promise and allied with the rebels.
You must attack him.
One arrow is for annihilating Zhū Wēn.
If you can fulfill my ambition,
I will die without regret."
Zhuāngzōng hid the three arrows in Wǔhuáng's ancestral temple.
When attacking Liú Réngōng,
he ordered his staff officer to make a modest sacrifice at the temple,
request one arrow,
place it in a brocade pouch,
and have a trusted general carry it as the vanguard.
On the day of triumph,
along with the captives and spoils, the arrow was returned to the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
The attacks on the Qìdān
and the annihilation of the Zhū clan were handled similarly.
Also,
Wǔhuáng was blind in one eye,
and was called
"Dúyǎnlóng."
He enjoyed killing,
and if his attendants committed even a minor fault,
he would surely put them to death.
Initially, he concealed his blindness,
and no one dared to offend him.
Once, he ordered a portrait.
The painter depicted him in the act of nocking an arrow,
with one eye slightly closed.
When the painting was finished and presented,
Wǔhuáng was greatly pleased,
and rewarded him handsomely.
The historian says: Wǔhuáng began his career in Yīnshān,
responded to the Táng court's distress,
chased away the jackals from the imperial palace,
and eradicated the ominous influences from Qínchuān.
He was granted the imperial surname and enfeoffed,
coming to possess Fén and Jìn.
He can be said to have rendered meritorious service.
However, despite his great efforts in aiding the emperor,
he was not without the awe-inspiring power that overshadowed his lord.
When the red banners of his army camped by the Wèiqū,
allowing the imperial carriage to have the good fortune of passing through Shímén,
compared to the assistance rendered to the Zhōu dynasty by Huán and Wén,
was he not somewhat ashamed?
But then he lost support in Pú and Jiàng,
and long struggled in Bìng and Fén.
If not for the exceptional talent of his successor,
how could there have been such a flourishing imperial enterprise?
Moreover, his accumulated merits and virtues
do not compare to those of Zhōu Wén;
his founding of the dynasty
is still inferior to that of Wèi Zǔ.
To be posthumously honored as
"Wǔ"
is indeed fortunate.
(From *Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn* scroll 7154.
) Collation notes
*Tángshū Sān Zhuāngzōng Jì Dìyī*
Observers, defenders, militia commanders, and other envoys, as well as Cìshǐ (刺史), Jiānyā (監押), Xíngyíng Jiàngxiào (行營將校), etc.,
are hereby granted an imperial edict
no changes or alterations shall be discussed.
They shall continue to use their old titles,
awaiting separate new appointments.
The way to govern a state
is none other than to pacify the people;
the rule for encouraging industry
should be to lighten taxes.
May the hope of relief be realized,
and the folk rhyme of contentedness be achieved.
Therefore,
the households of all circuits
should be exempted from corvée labor,
and each should focus on farming.
The outstanding arrears of taxes,
and all accumulated annual taxes and levies overdue for many years,
as well as public and private debts,
etc.,
within Biànzhōu (汴州) city,
from the day of its recovery onwards,
are all exempt from collection;
for other circuits,
all outstanding amounts from the twelfth month of the Rénwǔ (壬午) year onwards
are remitted.
Běijīng (北京) and Héběi (河北) had previously, due to ongoing calamities,
been ordered to procure warhorses.
If there are any cases where the official funds have not yet been repaid
or horses could not be procured in time,
these
can be exempted.
All imperial clan members and civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court,
who were innocently slaughtered by the Zhū (朱) clan,
shall all be posthumously honored.
If any of their descendants or the individuals themselves
fled and are scattered in various places,
the local authorities shall be ordered to search for them
and provide them with travel expenses to the capital.
Righteous men and chaste women,
filial sons and obedient grandsons,
shall have their households honored and proclaimed,
and be given appropriate
relief.
Orphaned, widowed, or solitary individuals
who have nowhere to turn,
the local authorities shall be instructed to discuss means of rescue.
Citizens over eighty years of age
shall have one son exempted from military service.
Those who
previously submitted to the rebel regime as generals, officers, or officials,
shall all be left unquestioned.
On the Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,

Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜), the Pīmìshǐ (樞密使), Jiǎnjiào Tàibǎo (檢校太保), Shǒu Bīngbù Shàngshū (守兵部尚書), and Tàiyuánxiàn Nán (太原縣男), was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Shǒu Shìzhōng (守侍中), Jiānxiū Guóshǐ (監修國史), concurrently Zhēndìng Yǐn (真定尹), and Chéngdéjūn Jiédùshǐ (成德軍節度使),
retaining his former titles of Pīmìshǐ (樞密使) and Tàiyuánjùn Hóu (太原郡侯),
and was moreover granted an iron certificate.
On the Yǐwèi (乙未) day,
an imperial edict ordered Zǎixiàng Dòulú Gé (宰相豆盧革) to provisionally oversee the senior personnel selection of the Lìbù (吏部),
and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Lǐ Déxiū (御史中丞李德休) to provisionally oversee the eastern and western personnel selections.
On the Bǐngshēn (丙申) day,
Duàn Níng (段凝), the Huázhōu Liúhòu (滑州留後) and Jiǎnjiào Tàibǎo (檢校太保), was confirmed as Huázhōu Liúhòu (滑州留後),
and was moreover granted the surname
Shàoqīn (紹欽).
(Shàoqīn (紹欽)
was originally written as
"Shào Kēng (紹鏗)",
but after consulting the Tōngjiàn and Ōuyáng Shǐ, it is consistently written as
"Qīn (欽)",
so it has now been corrected.
(Sticky note in the photographic archive copy)) Dù Yànqiú (杜晏球), the Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫), Jiǎnjiào Sīkōng (檢校司空), and Shǒu Huīzhōu Cìshǐ (守輝州刺史), was appointed Jiǎnjiào Sītú (檢校司徒),
retaining his former title of Huīzhōu Cìshǐ (輝州刺ǐ史),
and was moreover granted the surname
Shàoqián (紹虔).
An imperial edict ordered the execution of Xià Yànlǎng (夏彥朗), the Suíjià Bīngmǎ Dōujiān (隨駕兵馬都監), outside the Héjǐng Mén (和景門).
At that time, eunuchs, relying on imperial favor,
were extensively encroaching upon the residences of commoners.
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) reported this matter,
and Yànlǎng (彥朗) was then executed as a warning.
On the Dīngyǒu (丁酉) day,
officials were granted two thousand bolts of silk and two million coins,
and administrative personnel one thousand bolts of silk and one million coins.
On the Wùxū (戊戌) day,
Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源), the Jiézhōng Qǐyùn Kuāngguó Gōngchén (竭忠啟運匡國功臣), (Kuāngguó (匡國)
was originally written as
"Zhāngguó (章國)" to avoid the Sòng (宋) taboo,
but has now been corrected according to Ōuyáng Shǐ.

(Sticky note in the photographic archive copy)) Tiānpíngjūn Jiédùshǐ (天平軍節度使), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Jiǎnjiào Tàifù (檢校太傅), concurrently Shìzhōng (侍中), Fānhàn Mǎbù Zǒngguǎn Fùshǐ (蕃漢馬步總管副使), and Lǒngxījùn Hóu (隴西郡侯), was appointed as Jiǎnjiào Tàifù (檢校太傅) and concurrently Zhōngshūlìng (中書令) and Tiānpíngjūn Jiédùshǐ (天平軍節度使) and Tèjìn (特進),
ennobled as Kāiguógōng (開國公),
with increased actual fiefdom,
and the rest remaining as before.

Lǐ Jìjí (李繼岌), the Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Jiǎnjiào Tàifù (檢校太傅), Běidū Liúshǒu (北都留守), Xīngshènggōng Shǐ (興聖宮使), and Pàn Liùjūn Zhūwèi Shì (判六軍諸衞事), was appointed Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi (檢校太尉) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事),
and made Tōkyō Liúshǒu (東京留守).
An imperial edict to the Yùshǐ Tái (御史臺) stated:
Within the official ranks, those who wish to seek external posts
or request to be assigned to separate offices
are all permitted to submit their petitions to the Zhōngshū (中書) for imperial review.
On the Jǐhài (己亥) day,
a banquet was held for meritorious officials in Chóngyuán Diàn (崇元殿),
and former generals of the Liáng (梁) dynasty were all present.
When the Emperor was in high spirits,
he said to Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源):
"The guests at today's banquet
were all my formidable enemies just a few days ago,
and now they are gathered together;
this is all due to the strength of your vanguard."
Liáng (梁) generals Huò Yànwēi (霍彥威) and Dài Sīyuǎn (戴思遠), etc., all prostrated themselves and kowtowed at the imperial steps.
The Emperor then bestowed imperial robes and wine vessels upon them,
and the banquet concluded in great merriment.
Mèng Qiú (孟璆), the Qízhōu Cìshǐ (齊州刺史), submitted a memorial requesting death,
but an imperial edict pardoned him.
Qiú (璆) had initially served the Emperor as a cavalry general.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānyòu (天祐),
when the Emperor and Liú Xún (劉鄩) were confronting each other at Xīnxiàn (莘縣),
Qiú (璆) led seven hundred cavalry and defected to Liáng (梁).
Now he came to ask for punishment.
The Emperor replied to him:
"When I was in dire straits,
you led seven hundred cavalry to defect to the enemy.
How dare you face me!"
Qiú (璆) was terrified and begged for death,
but the Emperor forgave him.
Soon after,
he was transferred to be Bèizhōu Cìshǐ (貝州刺史).
(Bèizhōu (貝州)
was originally written as
"Yuèzhōu (月州)",
but has now been corrected according to the text.
(Sticky note in the photographic archive copy)) On the Gēngzǐ (庚子) day,
the Emperor hunted on the southern bank of the Biànshuǐ (汴水).
On the first day of the eleventh month, Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
the officials concerned memorialized:
"The prefectures and counties in Hénán (河南) are currently using fake seals;
we request that they be recalled, destroyed, and re-cast."
This was granted.

Lǐ Cúnwò (李存渥), the Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫), Jiǎnjiào Tàifù (檢校太傅), Zuǒ Jīnwú Shàngjiāngjūn (左金吾上將軍) concurrently Líng Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Jūnshì (領左龍武軍事), and Fénzhōu Cìshǐ (汾州刺史), was appointed Huázhōu Jiédùshǐ (滑州節度使),
and given the additional titles of Tèjìn (特進) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事);
Lǐ Shàoróng (李紹榮), the Zázhǐhuī Sànyuán Dōubùshǔ (雜指揮散員都部署), Tèjìn (特進), Jiǎnjiào Tàifù (檢校太傅), and Xīnzhōu Cìshǐ (忻州刺史), was appointed Xúzhōu Jiédùshǐ (徐州節度使);
Lǐ Shàoqīn (李紹欽), the Huázhōu Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (滑州兵馬留後) and Jiǎnjiào Tàibǎo (檢校太保), was appointed Yǎnzhōu Jiédùshǐ (兗州節度使).
On the Rénwǔ (壬寅) day,
Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞), the Fèngxiáng Jiédùshǐ (鳳翔節度使) and Qínwáng (秦王), sent an envoy to congratulate on the recovery of the empire.
On the Guǐmǎo (癸卯) day,
Zhū Yǒuqiān (朱友謙), the Hézhōng Jiédùshǐ (河中節度使) and Xīpíngwáng (西平王), came to court.
(Xīpíngwáng (西平王)
was originally written as
"Xīlái (西來)",
but after consulting the biography of Zhū Yǒuqiān (朱友謙) in Ōuyáng Shǐ,
Yǒuqiān (友謙) was enfeoffed as Xīpíngwáng (西平王),
so it has now been corrected.
(Sticky note in the photographic archive copy)) On the Yǐsì (乙巳) day,
Yǒuqiān (友謙) was granted the imperial surname
and his name was changed to Jìlín (繼麟).
The Emperor ordered his imperial son Jìjí (繼岌) to treat him as an elder brother.
Kāng Yánxiào (康延孝), the Pěngrí Dōuzhǐhuīshǐ (捧日都指揮使) and Bózhōu Cìshǐ (博州刺史), was appointed Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ (鄭州防禦使) and Jiǎnjiào Tàibǎo (檢校太保),
and was granted the surname
Shàochēn (紹琛).
Yuán Xiàngxiān (袁象先), the Sòngzhōu Jiédùshǐ (宋州節度使), Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi (檢校太尉), and Píngzhāngshì (平章事), was confirmed as Sòngzhōu Jiédùshǐ (宋州節度使),
and was moreover granted the surname
Shào'ān (紹安).
Wēn Tāo (溫韜), the Xǔzhōu Kuāngguójūn Jiédùshǐ (許州匡國軍節度使), Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi (檢校太尉), and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), was confirmed as Xǔzhōu Jiédùshǐ (許州節度使),
and was moreover granted the surname
Shàochōng (紹冲).
In the summer, fourth month, on the day of Xīnsì (the first day of the month),
Fáng Zhīwēn reported:
“On the twenty-first day of last month,
the garrison soldiers at Lútái rebelled,
harming Wū Zhèn, Deputy Pacification Commissioner and Jìedùshǐ of Níngguó Army.
Subsequently, I, along with Ān Shěntōng, put the rebellious soldiers to the sword.”
(Note: The Wǔdài Chūnqiū states that when the Lútái garrison rebelled,
Fáng Zhīwēn pacified it.
According to the biography of Fáng Zhīwēn in Xuē Shǐ and the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn,
Zhīwēn initially incited the garrison soldiers to rebel.
Later, fearing the endeavor would fail,
he then conspired with Ān Shěntōng to suppress the rebellious soldiers.
What is written in the Wǔdài Chūnqiū is quite contrary to the facts.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) Upon hearing this, the Emperor
suspended court for one day,
and posthumously granted Wū Zhèn the title of Tàifù.
The state of Xīnluó sent envoys to offer tribute of local products.
On Dīnghài,
Liú Yàncóng, acting as Liúhòu of Huázhōu, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of that prefecture.
On this day,
the Emperor went to Huìjiéyuán to feast with his close ministers.
On Jǐchǒu,
Cuī Jūjiǎn, Bīngbù Shìláng, was made acting Shàngshū Zuǒchéng;
Wáng Quán, Hùbù Shìláng, was made Bīngbù Shìláng;
Péi Bō, Lǐbù Shìláng, was made Hùbù Shìláng;
and Lǐ Yú, Hànlín Chéngzhǐ and Shǒuzhōngshū Shèrén, was made Lǐbù Shìláng with full duties.
On Gēngyín,
the Yùshǐtái reported:
“On the third day of this month, during the meal in the corridor,
when the hundred officials were seated,
officials from the Two Provinces only then arrived,
and those of the fifth rank and below rose up.”
The Emperor decreed:
“Every time one attends the corridor meal,
it is as if attending an imperial banquet.
To observe private etiquette
is to lose court decorum.
Each shall be fined half a month's salary.”
(Note: Wǔdài Huìyào states: Edict of the fifth month, third year of Chángxīng: For the two civil and military ranks,
whenever they enter the palace for a bestowed meal,
formerly the officials of the Yùshǐtái and other court officials all dined in the two corridors outside Fūzhèngmén.
Only the officials of the Northern Province sat separately inside Fūzhèngmén.
Being separated by a gate,
they could not see each other,
leading to unevenness in sitting and standing,
making it difficult to maintain solemnity.
Henceforth, whenever they enter the palace for a bestowed meal,
officials of the Northern Province should also set up their seats in the eastern corridor outside Fūzhèngmén,
with the north end being the place of honor,
awaiting the full attendance of their ranks before sitting simultaneously.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
The Emperor decreed:
“The three thousand five hundred men from the nine commands, including Yèdū Fèngjié, belonging to Lóng Zhì’s division of the Lútái rebellious army,
(Lóng Zhì,
originally written as
now corrected according to the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān))
and their entire families, including wives, children, and relatives in the camp, shall be executed.”
The troops under Lóng Zhì
were originally recruited and stationed by Yáng Shīhòu, the late Jìedùshǐ of Wèibó from the Liáng dynasty.
They were all brave and valiant men from across the land,
and their division was called Yínqiāng Xiàojié (Silver Spears of Efficacious Loyalty), numbering just eight thousand men.
When Shīhòu died,
Hè Délún could not control them.
They welcomed Zhuāngzōng from the west into Wèi,
followed him on campaigns along the Hé River,
and were successful wherever they went.
After Zhuāngzōng unified the realm,
although he frequently bestowed rewards,
they became arrogant and insatiable.
At the end of Tóngguāng,
they abducted Zhào Zàilǐ from Bèizhōu
and occupied Wèibó.
When the Emperor succeeded to the throne,
Zàilǐ hoped to escape disaster
and secretly petitioned to attend the imperial court.
Thus, Prince Cóngróng was appointed commander,
and they were ordered to defend against the Qìdān in the north.
On this expedition,
they did not carry armor,
only banners on long poles to mark their formation.
Therefore, they marched swiftly with bowed heads.
On the way, they heard that Lǐ Yán had been killed by Mèng Zhīxiáng,
and believing Jiànnán to be cut off,
they incited each other.
When they were stationed at Lútái,
it happened that Wū Zhèn replaced Fáng Zhīwēn as commander,
which only increased the baseless rumors.
Zhèn
and Fáng Zhīwēn were gambling in the eastern camp.
At noon,
a great clamor rose outside the camp.
Zhīwēn mounted his horse and exited the gate,
where he was surrounded by armored soldiers.
They said:
“If you do not lead us, the young men,
where else will you go?”
Zhīwēn deceived them, saying:
“The cavalry are all on the west of the river;
what can the infantry do alone!”
Thus, he managed to leap onto his horse and board a boat,
crossing to the western bank.
Ān Shěntōng restrained the cavalry from moving.
Zhīwēn conspired with Shěntōng to seize an opportunity to attack them,
ordering the rebellious soldiers to pack their armor and march south.
The cavalry advanced slowly,
their ranks disciplined and orderly.
The rebels looked at each other in dismay,
lit torches, and marched through the night,
exhausted in the desolate marsh.
At dawn,
he secretly ordered the troops from other prefectures to march separately.
Zhīwēn and others then attacked the rebellious army,
leaving corpses strewn across the fields.
The remaining rebels fled back to their old camp,
only to find it already burned.
The next day,
they were all slaughtered.
Only two or three out of ten escaped through dense grass and irrigation ditches.
By night, they fled into the mountains and valleys,
gradually escaping to Dìngzhōu.
By the time Wáng Dū was defeated,
there were no survivors left.
On Guǐsì,
Fáng Zhīwēn, Jìedùshǐ of Yǎnzhōu, was granted the additional title of Shìzhōng;
Ān Shěntōng, Fángyùshǐ of Qízhōu, was granted the additional title of Jiǎnjiào Tàifù.
Both were rewarded for their achievements at Lútái.
On Dīngyǒu,
the usurper Wú Yáng Pǔ sent Léi Xiàn, a transferred aide from Yòuwēiwèi Jiāngjūn, to present tribute of Dūanwǔ ritual silks.
(Léi Xiàn,
recorded as Léi Guān in Jiǔguó Zhì,
and still as ‘現’ in Shíguó Chūnqiū.
We follow the old usage.
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān))
On Xīnchǒu,
Zhāng Jìngxún, former Jìedùshǐ of Lìzhōu, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Yúnzhōu.
Kǒng Xún, Pīmìshǐ, was dispatched to the city of Jīngnán,
because Liú Xùn, the Pacification Commissioner, was ill.
On Jiǎchén,
Hán Yànhuì, Hùbù Shìláng, was appointed Mìshūjiān.
On this day,
the Emperor visited the residences of Shí Jìngtáng and Ān Chónghuǐ.
On Bǐngwǔ,
Lǐ Sì'ēn, late Jìedùshǐ of Zhènwǔ, was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi.
Yán Zhì, Sīfēng Lángzhōng and acting Shūmìyuàn Zhíxuéshì, was made Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū with full duties.
Liáng Wénjǔ, Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū, submitted a memorial, stating:
“Since the pacification of Shǔ,
soldiers have plundered a great many people from Xīchuān,
separating families.
This may harm harmony.
I request permission for them to be reunited.”
The Emperor’s benevolence was always profound;
prompted by Wénjǔ’s memorial,
he decreed that those from Hénán and Héběi who had been captured and separated due to war and fire
should all be allowed to be recognized and reunited.
On this day,
Yǐngzhōu presented a white magpie.
In the fifth month, on Guǐchǒu,
Wáng Yánjūn, Liúhòu of Fújiàn, Jiǎnjiào Tàifù, and Císhǐ of Shūzhōu, was appointed Jiǎnjiào Tàishī and Shǒuzhōngshū Lìng,
also serving as Fújiàn Jìedùshǐ and Prince of Lángyá Commandery.
Xiāo Qǐng, Tàicháng Qīng, was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
On this day,
Huáizhōu presented a white magpie.
On Wǔwǔ,
the court was suspended due to the death of Zhāng Gé, Sānsī Fùshǐ and Shǒu Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
Dòu Mèngzhēng, Hànlín Xuéshì, Jiàbù Lángzhōng, and Zhīzhìgào, was made Zhōngshū Shèrén with full duties.
On Guǐhài,
Zhāng Yánlǎng, Xuānhuīshǐ, was dispatched to coordinate the dispatch of grain from commanderies and counties to the city of Jīngnán,
and was to deal with matters according to military law.
Cuī Gōngshí, Yòu Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn, was made Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn.
Gāo Xíngzhōu, former Císhǐ of Fùzhōu, was made Yòu Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn.
Guǒzhōu was assigned to another commandery.
On Yǐchǒu,
the usurper Wú Yáng Pǔ presented tribute of new tea.
Cāngzhōu presented a white crane.
On Gēngwǔ,
an edict ordered the recall of the Jīngnán army.
Afterwards, the soldiers were allowed to plunder residents before returning.
An edict stated:
“All civil and military officials, and Jìedùshǐ and Císhǐ of various circuits,
who still have living parents,
shall each be granted special favors.”
Rèn Yuán, Zǎichén, submitted a memorial resigning from his duties in the Three Departments.
Therefore, Mèng Hú, Pīmìyuàn Chéngzhǐ, was made Sānsī Fùshǐ to temporarily preside over the affairs.
In the spring of the fourth year of Tiānchéng (929 CE), in the first month, on the day Rénshēn, the first day of the month,
the Emperor held court in the Chóngyuán Hall to receive congratulations,
with the imperial guards arranged as usual.
Zhào Déjūn, Jiedushi of Yōuzhōu, reported:
“My grandson, Zàn,
is five years old.
He can silently recite the Analects and the Classic of Filial Piety.
(Note: Sòng Shǐ states Zàn was seven years old
and could recite twenty-seven scrolls of texts.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) He is eligible for the child prodigy examination
and requests to take the preliminary examination in Biànzhōu.”
(Yōuzhōu was
originally written as
“Bīnzhōu”;
Lúnyǔ (Analects) was
originally written as
“Hélún”;
it is now corrected according to Cèfǔ Yuánguī.
(Yǐngkùběn Niánqiān)) An imperial edict stated:
“The son of a Dūwèi and
the grandson of a Tàiwèi,
who can recite Confucian classics,
clearly demonstrates the family's teachings.
There is no need for him to take the examination;
he is specially granted recognition.
He shall be bestowed a special imperial decree of passing the examination
and be included in this year's spring imperial roster.”
(Note: Sòng Shǐ states: He was specially granted passing as a child prodigy
and included in the Ministry of Rites' spring roster of the third year of Chángxīng.
Xuē Shǐ states it was the spring roster of the fourth year of Tiānchéng,
which differs from Sòng Shǐ.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) On the day Wùzǐ,
the autumn taxes owed from the first year were remitted.
Ān Chóngruǎn, Left Guard Grand General, was appointed Jiedushi of Qiánnán.
On the day Rénchén,
the five Uighur envoys, including Chèbō, were each granted the title of Huáihuà Sīgē and sent back.
Féng Yūn, Deputy Resident Administrator of Běijīng, was appointed Xuānhuī Shǐ and Supervisor of the Three Bureaus.
On the day Wùxū,
the unauthorized use of provisional official titles was forbidden throughout the realm.
Mèng Zhīxiáng of Xīchuān reported:
“I request permission to appoint my relatives as Cìshǐ in my own circuit.”
In the second month, on the day Yǐsì,
Wáng Yànqiú reported
that Dìngzhōu had been recaptured on the third day of this month.
(Note: Ōuyáng Shǐ states that on the day Guǐmǎo of the second month,
Wáng Yànqiú conquered Dìngzhōu,
which aligns with Xuē Shǐ.
Tōngjiàn states Guǐchǒu.
Upon examination, Guǐchǒu was not the third day of the second month;
this is suspected to be a copying error.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) Wáng Dū’s head was captured,
and over two thousand Khitan troops, including Tūněi, were taken alive.
All officials offered congratulations.
An imperial edict ordered the imperial carriage to return to Dōngjīng on the twenty-fourth of this month.
On the day Xīnhài,
Wáng Yànqiú, Commissioner for Campaigns against the Northern Frontier and Jiedushi of Sòngzhōu, was appointed Jiedushi of Yùnzhōu
and additionally granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
Lǐ Cóngmǐn, Deputy Commissioner for Campaigns against the Northern Frontier and Jiedushi of Cāngzhōu, was appointed Jiedushi of Dìngzhōu.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo, Supervisor of the Northern Frontier Campaign Army and Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu, was appointed Jiedushi of Cāngzhōu.
Zhào Déjūn, Jiedushi of Yōuzhōu, was additionally granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Zhào Jìngyí, Privy Council Commissioner, was appointed Acting Governor of Biànzhōu.
(Zhào Jìngyí was
originally written as
“Jìngyí”;
it is now corrected according to Ōuyáng Shǐ.
(Yǐngkùběn Niánqiān)) On the day Bǐngchén,
Xíngzhōu reported
that the false Crown Prince Lǐ Jìtáo, sent from Dìngzhōu,
had been dealt with.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the Emperor presided from the Xián'ān Tower to receive the captives and trophies from Dìngzhōu.
All officials were arranged in formation.
A manifesto was proclaimed in front of the tower.
After the ceremony,
Wáng Dū’s head was offered to the Grand Altar of Land and Grain.
Wáng Dū’s four sons and one brother,
and Tūněi and his son,
were all dismembered in the marketplace.
(Note: Wǔdài Huìyào states: The Shàngshū of the Ministry of War proclaimed the manifesto in front of the tower.
After the proclamation,
Zhāng Wénbǎo, Shàngshū of the Ministry of Punishments, reported:
“I request that the head of the rebel Wáng Dū be handed over to the appropriate department.”
Xiāo Xīfǔ, Grand Justice, received it and brought it out
to offer it at the suburban altars.
Wáng Dū’s sons and the barbarian generals were dismembered at Kāifēng Bridge.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) At that time, the style of the manifesto
resembled that of imperial edicts.
This was due to an error by the scribe,
which was mocked by discerning individuals.
Zhào Jìngyí, Privy Council Commissioner, died
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàifù.
Zhào Fèng, Scholar of the Duānmíng Hall, was appointed Acting Governor of Biànzhōu.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the imperial carriage departed from Biànzhōu.
On the day Bǐngyín,
it arrived at Zhèngzhōu.
Zhèng Yù, Left Chief Minister Emeritus, was granted 200,000 cash.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Cuī Xié, Chancellor, died,
and an imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Shàngshū Yòupúshè.
Lǐ Qí, Resident Administrator of Dōngdū and Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince, and others reported
that they had gone to Yǎnshī County to welcome the Emperor.
At that time, Lǐ Qí’s memorial contained the phrase:
“defeated the fierce faction of the Khitan
and broke the rebellious city of Zhēndìng.”
An imperial edict stated:
“If the Khitan are indeed a fierce faction,
Zhēndìng is not a rebellious city.
Lǐ Qí is fined one month's salary.”
On the day Gēngwǔ,
the imperial carriage arrived from Biànzhōu.
In the third month, on the day Jiǎxū,
Féng Dào submitted a memorial requesting appointment as Chancellor.
On the day Bǐngxū,
an imperial edict demoted Lǐ Cóngcàn, Imperial City Commissioner, to Sīhù Cānjūn of Fángzhōu
and ordered his immediate execution.
Cóngcàn was
one of the Emperor’s nephews.
Previously,
when the Emperor was on an imperial tour to Biànzhōu,
Cóngcàn was left behind to guard the imperial palace.
Cóngcàn, however, went to a banquet in the Huìjié Garden.
(Huìjié was
originally written as
“Zēngyún”;
an examination of the Tōngjiàn commentary states: Huìjié Garden was in Luòyáng city.
Zhāng Quányì resided in Luòyáng for many years;
his private residence was in Huìjié Ward.
Its buildings, rooms, and gardens
were magnificent for that era.
They were surrendered to the government
and became the Huìjié Garden.
It is now corrected.
(Yǐngkùběn Niánqiān)) In his drunkenness,
he playfully climbed onto the imperial couch.
Ān Chónghuǐ reported this,
and thus he was subjected to the law.
On the day Rénchén,
the Central Secretariat reported:
“From now on, if any of the officials request leave to visit their parents,
please grant them an appropriate amount of tea and medicine.”
This was approved.
On the day Yǐwèi,
Fú Xí, former Jiedushi of Yùnzhōu, was appointed Jiedushi of Biànzhōu.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
an imperial edict announced that the people within the jurisdiction of Yèdū, Yōu, Zhèn, Cāng, Xíng, Yì, and Dìng prefectures,
in addition to regular taxes,
would be exempted from all miscellaneous levies and impositions,
due to their labor in transporting supplies during the campaign against Wáng Dū.
Empress Zhēnjiǎn Cáo of Emperor Wǔ,
was the mother of Zhuāngzōng.
She was from Tàiyuán,
and as a daughter of a respectable family, she became a concubine of Emperor Wǔ.
Her appearance and demeanor were serene and beautiful,
her nature was humble and retiring yet discerning,
and she was greatly esteemed by the Lady of Qín Guó.
She often calmly said to Emperor Wǔ:
"I observe that Cáo Jī is an extraordinary woman,
Your Majesty should treat her generously."
Emperor Wǔ had many imperial favorites.
In the early years of Qiánníng,
after subduing Yān and Jì,
he acquired Lady Zhāng, wife of Lǐ Kuāngchóu.
(Note: The original text avoided the Sòng taboo and wrote Lǐ Chóu;
now added based on the Fānzhèn Biographies of the Xīn Tángshū.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) Her beauty was unmatched,
and her favor was peerless.
At that time, there were many concubines filling the chambers,
and she rarely had the opportunity to be presented to the emperor,
only the Empress Dowager's favor remained undiminished.
Emperor Wǔ's nature was severe and stern;
if his attendants made a mistake,
he would certainly punish them harshly,
and no one dared to speak,
only the Empress Dowager would calmly intercede,
and he would then soften his expression.
When Zhuāngzōng was born,
his physique and appearance were extraordinary and outstanding.
Emperor Wǔ found him unusual and doted on him,
and the Empress Dowager became even more cherished and honored.
All the other ladies were beneath her,
and the Empress also diligently provided internal assistance,
praised by those around her.
When Emperor Wǔ passed away,
Zhuāngzōng succeeded to the throne of the Prince of Jìn.
At that time, Lǐ Kèníng and Lǐ Cúnhào plotted rebellion,
and the people's morale was fearful and uneasy.
The Empress Dowager summoned the監軍 Jiānjūn Zhāng Chéngyè,
pointed to Zhuāngzōng and said to him:
"The late emperor held your arm and entrusted this child to you.
If you hear of external plots
and wish to betray this trust,
you all only need to secure a place for my son and me,
do not let us beg for food in Biàn,
that would be fortunate enough."
Chéngyè then executed Cúnhào and Kèníng,
to clear the internal troubles.
Zhuāngzōng was skilled in music and enjoyed the jests and frivolity of actors,
and the Empress Dowager often tugged his ear to instruct him.
In the seventh year of Tiānyòu,
Zhèn and Dìng requested aid.
Zhuāngzōng hastily ordered the preparation of troops,
but the Empress Dowager said:
"My teeth are gradually decaying,
it is fortunate if my son merely does not lose the legacy of his ancestors.
Why must you brave the wind and rain,
and leave me morning and evening!"
Zhuāngzōng replied:
"I received the late king's dying wish
that I must eliminate our enemies.
Regarding the matters in Shāndōng,
the opportunity must not be lost."
When he departed,
the Empress Dowager saw him off at Fénqiáo,
(Note: The original text wrote
"Wèiqiáo";
now corrected based on the annotations in the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
and was overcome with grief.
After Zhuāngzōng pacified Zhào and Wèi,
he stationed himself in Yèchéng.
Within a year,
he would return to visit his mother four or five times,
and the people and officials admired his filial piety.
The Empress Dowager was initially enfeoffed as Lady of Jìn Guó.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he ordered the Chancellor Lú Sǔn to present the imperial edict to confer the venerable title of Grand Empress Dowager.
That year, after pacifying Hénán,
he traveled west to Luòyáng,
and ordered his imperial brother Cúnwò and imperial son Jìjí to go to Tàiyuán to escort her.
Zhuāngzōng personally went to Huáizhōu
to welcome her back to the Chángshòu Palace.
The Empress Dowager had always been on good terms with Grand Consort Liú.
After their separation,
she was depressed and unhappy.
Soon, she heard that the Grand Consort was ill.
Imperial physicians and palace eunuchs
came continuously to inquire about her health.
Later, she said to Zhuāngzōng:
"My affection for the Grand Consort is like that of siblings.
She has been ill for years;
just seeing my face
would be comforting to her heart.
I will temporarily go to Jìnyáng,
and return with her in ten days or a month."
Zhuāngzōng said:
"The weather is currently hot and poisonous,
and the mountain roads are rugged.
There is no need for you to travel back and forth.
We can order Cúnwò and others to welcome and attend to the Grand Consort."
So, she stopped.
When the news of her death arrived,
the Empress Dowager wept bitterly for several weeks,
and from then on was unwell,
soon collapsing and dying in the Chángshòu Palace.
In the tenth month of the winter of the third year of Tóngguāng,
she was posthumously granted the title Empress Zhēnjiǎn.
She was buried in Shòu'ān Líng.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 19304.
Grand Consort Liú,
was the principal wife of Emperor Wǔ.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 1266.
Note: The complete biography of Grand Consort Liú
is missing from the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn.
According to Běimèng Suǒyán, Lady Liú, wife of Lǐ Kèyòng, Prince of Jìn,
often accompanied the army.
Regarding military strategies,
she contributed greatly.
Previously,
there was a disturbance at Shàngyuányì in Biànzhōu.
The Prince of Jìn was enraged
and wanted to turn his army to attack it.
The Lady said:
"Your Highness is suppressing bandits for the state,
but if you attack the city due to a personal grudge over a cup of wine,
the fault will lie with us.
It is better to withdraw the army;
there is still the imperial court where this can be discussed."
Thereupon, the army withdrew.
In the Tiānfù period,
Zhōu Déwēi was defeated by the Biàn army,
and the entire army scattered.
The Biàn army pursued us.
The Prince of Jìn was in great danger and fear,
and discussed with Lǐ Cúnxìn
the possibility of fleeing to Yúnzhōu for safety.
The Lady said:
"Cúnxìn was originally a shepherd boy from the north;
how can he care about success or failure!
Your Highness often laughed at Wáng Xíngyú for abandoning his city and losing power,
being slaughtered by others.
Now you want to follow his example,
why?
Years ago, Your Highness sought refuge beyond the frontier,
and nearly suffered harm,
relying on the imperial court being preoccupied with many matters,
only then were you able to return.
Now if you suddenly leave the city,
there will be unforeseen changes,
how can you reach a distant place!"
The Prince of Jìn stopped his intended journey.
After several days,
the scattered and dispersed soldiers reassembled,
and the military city was stable.
This was due to the efforts of the Lady.
Wǔdài Huìyào states: In the fourth month of the first year of Tóngguāng,
she was formally designated as Imperial Grand Consort.
Ōuyáng Shǐ states: When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he honored Cáo Shì as Grand Empress Dowager,
and designated his嫡母 dímǔ (legal mother) Liú Shì as Imperial Grand Consort.
The Grand Consort went to express gratitude to the Empress Dowager,
who showed a look of shame.
The Grand Consort said:
"I wish that my son may enjoy the kingdom endlessly,
and that I may have the fortune to die on earth to join my late lord,
what more can I say!"
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng and entered Luò,
he sent people to welcome the Empress Dowager back to Luò,
where she resided in Chángshòu Palace,
while the Grand Consort alone remained in Jìnyáng.
In the fifth month of the third year of Tóngguāng,
the Grand Consort passed away.
Chóng Tāo served diligently and gave his utmost,
assisting and supporting the royal house.
During the difficult beginnings,
his accomplishments were unparalleled.
He pacified Bāshǔ in the west,
extending the imperial prestige.
On the day of his death,
both Chinese and barbarians mourned him.
However, commentators believed that although Chóng Tāo had many merits,
his authority was too great.
He was unable to know his place and assess his strength,
and listened to the misguided schemes of petty men,
wishing to attain the security of Mount Tài,
like hastily trying to avoid traces,
which only quickened his downfall.
His nature was also rigid and stubborn;
he would act impulsively when encountering matters.
He neither knew the successes and failures of previous generations,
nor did he understand the sentiments of the people at the time.
He took the whole world as his responsibility,
which was extremely reckless.
When his power overshadowed the four seas,
and carriages filled his gate,
scholars flattered him,
and distinctions between different ranks gradually emerged.
His colleague Dòu Lú Gě said to Chóng Tāo (Note: The twelve characters from
"distinctions between different ranks gradually emerged"
to this point were missing from the original text;
they are now inserted from the Cèfǔ Yuánguī.)
said:
"Fényáng Wáng was from Dàiběi,
and moved his family to Huáyīn.
Since the Shìzhōng's family has always been in Yànmén,
is it not due to his ancestral virtue?"
Chóng Tāo replied:
"Due to the chaos, the genealogical records were lost.
My ancestors often said they were four generations removed from Fényáng Wáng."
Gě said:
"Thus, it is ancestral virtue."
Because of this, he began to distinguish between different ranks,
promoting unworthy individuals
and entrusting them with his confidence;
while discarding
all the old meritorious officials who had supported the founding of the dynasty.
When an old subordinate sought advancement,
Chóng Tāo said to him:
"Although you are an old retainer from the prince's residence,
your family has no eminent status.
I deeply appreciate your talents and skills,
but I dare not promote you hastily,
for fear that renowned scholars might mock me."
During the expedition to Shǔ,
he paid respects at the tomb of Shàngfù Zǐyí in Xīngpíng.
He once casually said to Jìjí:
"After Shǔ is pacified,
Your Highness will be the crown prince.
When a thousand autumns and ten thousand years pass (i.e., when you ascend the throne),
and the divine artifact is in your hands,
you should completely abolish eunuchs,
and treat the scholar-gentry with courtesy.
Not only should you ostracize and dismiss eunuchs,
but even castrated horses should no longer be ridden."
(Note: The Tōngjiàn writes "shànmǎ."
Upon checking Hú Sānsheng's commentary, it quotes Xuē Shǐ as also writing "shànmǎ."
Therefore, we retain the original.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) Internally, the court musicians and close attendants
gnashed their teeth in anger;
externally, old colleagues and veteran generals
pointed fingers and grieved deeply.
His family's extermination was thus inevitable.
Furthermore, his sons were arrogant and lawless.
After Shǔchuān was pacified,
they transported precious goods
to their residence in Luòyáng.
On the day of confiscation,
the mud seals were still wet.
Although Zhuāngzōng was misled by petty men in his later years,
leading to the tragic end of a meritorious official,
it was also Chóng Tāo who brought disaster upon himself.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 22160.)
The historian says:
Indeed, when one serves a lord,
gains position, and encounters a favorable time,
one cannot fail to strive for achievements,
nor can one fail to establish a reputation.
However, when achievements are made and reputation is established,
then prestige becomes great and one's person is endangered.
Slander then takes shape,
and precious jade is broken first because of it.
Therefore, Chóng Tāo's execution
was precisely for this reason.
Thus, we know that when the powerful Wú was destroyed, Fàn Lǐ departed;
when the unified Qí fell, Yuè Shēng fled.
If not for their wisdom,
who could avoid disaster?
Intelligent and discerning individuals
should take heed of this!
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 22160.)

) Guāngyìn (光胤) served the Liáng (梁) dynasty,

When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) pacified Biàn (汴) and Luò (洛),
Lú Chéng (盧程) was dismissed due to his arrogance,
and Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) was appointed from among the meritorious officials.
Debaters thought that for the ceremonial precedents and institutions of the current dynasty,
it was necessary to consult famous scholars of previous generations.
All said that Guāngyìn (光胤) had the makings of a chancellor.
Xuē Tíngguī (薛廷珪) and Lǐ Qí (李琪), when Wǔ Huáng (武皇) was King of Jìn (晉),
