At that time, everyone said they should be placed in the highest offices.
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇tāo) adopted the views of those who spoke up, saying,
"Tíngguī (廷珪) is old and decrepit, superficial and lacks the qualities of a chancellor;
although Qí (琪) has high literary accomplishments,
he is treacherous and lacks the demeanor of a scholar.
Neither can be a chancellor."
So, the matter was dropped.
In the eleventh month of Tóngguāng (同光) first year,
Guāngyìn (光胤) and Wéi Shuō (韋說) were both appointed Grand Councilors.
Guāngyìn (光胤) was born at the end of a dynasty,
and was gradually influenced by the prevailing customs.
Although he wished to rise high and emulate his predecessors,
his talent and strength were insufficient,
and he could not achieve far-reaching goals.
Whenever the court had discussions on rituals, music, institutions, or proposed reforms,
he took it upon himself to handle them.
His colleagues were not widely learned,
and seeing his superficial and rambling arguments,
none could fathom him.
Although Dòulú Gé (豆盧革) relied on his family background,
his official career in the current dynasty was still minor.
Having long served in the princely court,
he was not deeply familiar with court protocols and ceremonies.
Whenever Guāngyìn (光胤) put forth an argument,
Gé (革) merely nodded in agreement.
Later, when Gé's (革) memorials and proposals were sometimes appropriate,
Guāngyìn (光胤) said to the officials,
"The discussion we had yesterday,
the gentleman in the front seat said something fairly appropriate.
Recently, he has made some progress.
How can scholars give up!"
Such was his arrogance.
Initially,
Dòu Lúgé and Wéi Shuō incurred displeasure.
The executive council discussed appointing a chancellor.
The privy councilor Kǒng Xún did not wish for someone from Héshuò to hold the chancellorship.
Rèn Yuán wished to appoint Lǐ Qí as chancellor,
but Zhèng [Wángyù] was not on good terms with Qí.
Kǒng Xún also disliked Qí.
He said to Ān Chónghuì:
“Lǐ Qí is not without artistic and scholarly talent,
but he is not incorruptible.
In court discussions, no one is better than Cuī Xié.”
Chónghuì agreed with this,
and subsequently proposed the selection of a chancellor.
Míngzōng said:
“Who is suitable?”
He then presented Xié.
Rèn Yuán memorialized, saying:
“Chónghuì has been deceived and betrayed by others.
Someone like Cuī Xié
has little knowledge of written characters.
People of the time called him ‘the illiterate stele.’
I myself was formerly ignorant of letters,
and advanced without talent,
already making myself a laughingstock to the world.
How can there be
another object of ridicule within the Central Secretariat!”
Míngzōng said:
“Wéi Sù, the Prefect of Yìzhōu,
is said by people to be from a prominent family,
and has always treated me well.
What about placing him in this position?
If Sù is not yet suitable,
then Clerk Féng was a judicial officer in the previous court.
(Clerk Féng,
originally written as
“bǐjì” (note),
is now corrected according to Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
(Sticky note in the image library copy)) He is called a virtuous elder,
and does not compete with others.
He can be a chancellor.”
Dào had once served as Zhūangzōng's personal secretary in his military government,
which is why Míngzōng called him that.
After the court session ended,
the chancellors and privy councilors rested under the eaves of the Zhōngxīng Hall.
Kǒng Xún brushed his robes and left,
saying:
“In affairs of state, it’s first Rèn Yuán,
second Rèn Yuán.
If Cuī Xié dies suddenly, so be it;
if he doesn't die, he will certainly hold this position.”
Chónghuì privately said to Yuán:
“Now the chancellorship is vacant,
can Xié be acceptable for now?”
Yuán said:
“The court has Lǐ Qí,
whose learning reaches heaven and man,
and whose family has held high office for generations.
In terms of talent and skill,
he can rival a hundred of his peers.
Yet slandering scoundrels skillfully obstruct him,
jealous of his ability.
To surely abandon Qí and appoint Xié as chancellor
would be like discarding a pill of sūhé
(Sūhé,
originally written as
“sūquán”,
is now corrected according to Zīzhì Tōngjiàn and Ōuyáng Shǐ.
(Sticky note in the image library copy)) and picking up a beetle’s droppings.”
Chónghuì smiled and stopped.
However, Chónghuì and Xún held the same office,
and Xún daily spoke of Qí's shortcomings and Xié's strengths.
Therefore, Chónghuì eventually yielded to him.
After Xié was appointed to office,
he had others write his court memorials,
borrowing others' hands.
The court considered the affairs of the National Academy important,
and ordered Xié to concurrently oversee the duties of the Grand Minister of Sacrifices.
Xié memorialized that two hundred students should be admitted to the academy each year as a fixed number.
Public opinion condemned this.
(Note: Běimèng Suǒyán records: Míngzōng asked Chancellor Féng Dào:
“Does Lú Zhì drink recently?”
He replied:
“Zhì once visited my residence,
and also drank a few cups.
I advised him not to overdo it,
as affairs are also like wine:
excess leads to trouble.”
Cuī Xié forcefully interjected from his seat, saying:
“I heard in the Shí Yī Xīn Jìng [Medical Mirror of Diet]
that wine is extremely good;
without adding medicines,
it is enough to calm the mind and spirit.”
Those on the left and right, seeing his superficiality,
could not help but smile.
(Kǎo Yì of Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ)) In the spring of the fourth year,
the emperor returned to the capital from Yímén.
Following him to Xūshuǐ驛,
he suddenly died of a stroke.
An edict posthumously granted him the title of Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
with the posthumous name Gōngjìng.
His sons were Qí, Sòng, and Shòu Zhēn.
Only Sòng served the imperial court,
reaching the office of Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū,
and ended his career as Fūzhōu Xíngjūn Sīmǎ.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juan 2740.)
Lǐ Qí,
courtesy name Táixiù.
His fifth-generation ancestor, Chéng,
at the end of Tiānbǎo, was the Lǐbù Shàngshū and Dōngdū Liúshǒu.
When Ān Lùshān captured the eastern capital,
he was killed,
and was successively posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi,
with the posthumous name Zhōngyì.
Chéng's grandson, Cǎi,
during the Yuánhé era,
rose to the position of Jǐshìzhōng.
Cǎi's son, Jìngfāng,
during the Wénzōng era, was a Jiànyì Dàfū.
Jìngfāng's son, Gǔ,
during Guǎngmíng,
served as the Dūtǒng Pànkuān for Jìn Gōng Wáng Duó.
(Note: Tàipíng Guǎngjì, citing the preface to Lǐ Qí's collection, states his father was Jìng,
who assisted Wáng Duó in the Huázhōu advisory staff.
However, Lǐ Qí's grandfather was named Jìngfāng,
so his father could not be named Jìng.
It is suspected that this is an error in the transmission of Tàipíng Guǎngjì.
(Kǎo Yì of Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ)) He became a Jiànyì Dàfū
due to his achievements in recovery.
Qí was Gǔ's son.
At thirteen years old,
his rhymed prose and poems
were greatly admired by Wáng Duó,
though he also suspected they might have been ghostwritten.
One day,
Duó invited Gǔ to a banquet at his official residence.
(“Zhào Gǔ”,
originally written as
“míng Gǔ”,
is now corrected according to the context.
(Sticky note in the image library copy)) He secretly sent someone to Qí's residence to test him with the topic of the “Ode to Hàn Zǔ Gaining the Three Heroes.”
Qí picked up his brush and completed it instantly.
The end of the ode said:
“One prospers by gaining scholars;
one does not share with the unworthy.
Friends of the dragon's head are precious;
ministers forming a tripod are weighty.
How fitting was Xiàng Shì's defeat and downfall,
for he could not even employ one Fàn Zēng.”
Duó read it and was astonished,
saying:
“This child is a great talent;
he will monopolize literary fame.”
(Note: Tàipíng Guǎngjì records: When Qí was a boy, he called on Duó.
Duó looked at him and said:
“A decree just arrived from Shǔ,
appointing Tuòbá Sīgōng of Xiàzhōu as Commander-in-Chief for recovery.
Can you compose a poem?”
He immediately took up his brush and composed it,
saying:
“Flying cavalry passes through the Bā棧,
vast imperial grace reaches Xiàtái.
Generals will ascend to heaven,
people will come from the sun's edge.
This place is far from the Golden Gate,
when will the Jade Carriage return?
Quickly pacify the bandits west of the pass,
do not wait for the imperial edict to urge.”
Duó was even more impressed,
and taking Qí's hand, said:
“This is truly the phoenix's feather.”
At that time, he was fourteen.
The following year,
he observed mourning for his mother,
and consequently became a wanderer in Qí and Lǔ.
Burning husks for light,
he turned night into day, reading thousands of volumes,
and occasionally composing poetry and rhymed prose.
When Táng Xīzōng fled again to Liáng and Yáng,
he secretly composed an ode, saying:
“In sorrow and pain no edict is issued,
who submits memorials to ascend Mount Tàishān?”
(Kǎo Yì of Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ))
Yào Yànchóu,
was a man from the three Shatuo tribes.
As a youth, he served Míngzōng with his skill in riding and archery,
and was successively promoted to the rank of battalion commander.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he was made Cǐshǐ of Chéngzhōu
and Dū Jiāng of the Cavalry and Infantry in Héyáng.
He followed Wáng Yànqiú to suppress Wáng Dū in Dìngzhōu,
and after it was pacified,
he was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Shòuzhōu and Shìwèi Bùjūn Dū Yúhòu.
When Yáng Yànwēn, the Zhīhuīshǐ of Hézhōng, rebelled,
Yànchóu was redesignated Shìwèi Bùjūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ
and appointed Fù Zhāotǎoshǐ of Hézhōng,
(Note: Ōuyáng's history records him as Zhāotǎoshǐ.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) and led troops to suppress him.
Not long after,
the Dǎngxiàng raided the Huíhú envoys on their way to court.
An edict ordered Yànchóu to garrison Shuòfāng,
to suppress the rebellious Dǎngxiàng,
and to search for bandits.
He recovered all the horses and precious jade offered by the Huíhú,
captured their leaders, and returned.
Soon after, he was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Bīnzhōu.
He was dispatched to assemble troops to regulate Yánzhōu;
the Fān Róng fled,
and he recovered over a thousand people, both scholars and commoners, who had been captured by the Fān,
and sent them back to their hometowns.
He received an edict to, along with the Jiédùshǐ of Yánzhōu,
(Note: The original text has a lacuna;
Ōuyáng's history records Língwǔ Kāng Fú.
) attack Xiàzhōu.
After several months, it was not taken,
so the troops withdrew and returned to their garrisons.
When Mǐndì succeeded to the throne,
he joined Wáng Sītóng in attacking Fèngxiáng,
serving as Fù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
When the imperial army collapsed,
Yànchóu intended to flee downstream,
but was captured by soldiers and handed over.
At that time, Mòdì had already reached Huázhōu,
and ordered him imprisoned
and executed.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he and Wáng Sītóng were jointly posthumously granted the title of Shìzhōng.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Vol. 18129.)
Sòng Lìngxún,
his origin is unknown.
When Mǐndì was still a prince,
he was appointed Kèjiàng.
He was learned and delighted in goodness;
all his actions followed etiquette.
During the Chángxīng period,
Mǐndì successively held positions as a grand prince,
and Lìngxún was promoted to Dū Yāyá.
(Dū Yāyá,
originally written as
"Xiáyá,"
but the Qìdān Guó Zhì states:
"Sòng Wáng's former Yāyá, Sòng Lìngxún, hearing of the rebellion,
hanged himself and died."
The original character
"Xiá"
was a scribal error,
now corrected.
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān)) He assisted in the administration of the frontier,
and was highly reputed at the time;
Mǐndì deeply trusted him.
When Mǐndì succeeded to the throne,
Zhū and Féng held power,
and did not want Mǐndì's former retainers to be by his side,
so Lìngxún was sent out as Cǐshǐ of Cízhōu.
When Mǐndì was in distress in Wèi,
Lìngxún daily sent people to inquire.
When he heard the Emperor had been harmed,
he grieved greatly for half a day,
then hanged himself and died.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Vol. 13044.)
The historiographer says: He who cuts for the great carpenter
still wounds his hand,
how much more so he who holds the reins of reward and punishment for the Son of Heaven!
Therefore, ancient sages,
when entrusted with great responsibilities and holding great power,
all humbled themselves,
gave credit to others rather than themselves,
broadened the path of public service,
and cut off selfish desires;
only then could they preserve themselves and escape calamity.
But what kind of person was Zhònghuǐ?
How could he escape death?
An ancient saying goes:
"Do not be the head of power,
lest you suffer its blame."
This applies to Zhònghuǐ, does it not!
From Hóngzhāo downwards,
their strength could not protect the state,
their schemes could not secure the country,
and they perished one after another.
Whom else should we blame?
Only Lìngxún, moved by the old grace of his former lord,
committed suicide out of great sorrow.
To lose his life in this manner
is enough to leave a lasting name.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Vol. 13044.)
Collation Notes
Táng Shū, Vol. 43, Biographies No. 19
Dòulú Gé,
his ancestral home.
His grandfather was Cǐshǐ of Tóngzhōu.
His father, Zàn,
was Cǐshǐ of Shūzhōu.
(Xuānhé Shūpǔ states: His lineage is lost.
(Diànběn)) Gé, as a youth, lived through times of rebellion and upheaval,
and sought refuge in Fū and Yán,
then moved into Zhōngshān.
Wáng Chǔzhí treated him with respect,
(Wáng Chǔzhí,
originally written as
"Chǔzhēn,"
now corrected according to the Xīn Táng Shū.
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān)) and appointed him to his staff,
where he earned renown for his memorials.
At a peony banquet, he composed a poem
that satirized Chǔzhí, implying he should focus on the welfare of his people,
his words were ancient and elegant.
Chǔzhí gradually held him in high regard,
and he was promoted to Jiédù Pànguān.
However, he managed his household without principles,
and once he alone requested an audience with Chǔzhí.
Chǔzhí, fearing there might be shortcomings in his governance
and expecting advice,
arranged his tablet and went out to meet him,
only to find that Gé was pleading for a military position for his favorite.
At the end of Tiānyòu,
Zhuāngzōng was about to ascend the throne and
sought capable ministers.
Lú Zhì recommended Gé, as he was from a renowned family,
and he was summoned and appointed Xíngtái Zuǒ Chéngxiàng.
In the early Tóngguāng period,
he was appointed Píngzhāngshì.
Upon entering the court,
many matters were confused,
especially regarding the deliberation of official ranks,
which were reversed,
and repeatedly corrected by Xiāo Xīfǔ, a clerk in the Censorate.
Gé accepted the corrections
without difficulty.
When Zhuāngzōng first pacified Biàn and Luò,
Gé recommended Wéi Shuō,
hoping that he understood matters of state
and would share his achievements.
After Shuō was appointed,
he again became involved in the categorization of officials,
his conduct was frivolous and unrestrained,
and resentment fell upon Gé.
Furthermore, the sons of both Gé and Shuō were appointed Shíyí,
fathers and sons serving in the same office,
which drew criticism,
so they were reassigned as Yuánwàiláng.
Gé requested that Shuō's son, Tāo, be made Hóngwénguǎn Xuéshì,
and Shuō requested that Gé's son, Shēng, be made Jíxián Xuéshì.
This exchange of favors
was like a marketplace,
and those who understood deemed it shameful.
After Gé became a minister,
he did not focus on recommending the worthy or encouraging the capable,
but only on cultivating himself
and seeking methods of immortality.
He once consumed cinnabar,
vomited blood for several days,
and nearly died but recovered.
Zǐ Shìmíng
served in the Zhōu,
ending his career as the Yìzǎi.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 5225.)
Yào Zòngzhī,
a native of Tàiyuán,
was a scholar in his youth.
When Míngzōng was the Cìshǐ of Dàizhōu,
he was appointed Jūnshì Yázhuī.
He followed Míngzōng to garrison Xíngzhōu,
where he served as Zhǎngshūjì,
and successively held the posts of Jiédù Fùshǐ for the Tiānpíng and Xuānwǔ Circuits.
When Míngzōng garrisoned Chángshān,
Yào Zòngzhī was ill and did not follow.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
Zòngzhī met him in Luòyì.
Ān Chónghuì was angered by his wait-and-see attitude,
and he remained unappointed for a long time.
Míngzōng said:
"During Déshèng's military campaigns,
(Déshèng was originally written as
"得勝" (Déshèng) in the original text.
According to Xuē Shǐ and the biographers of the Liáng and Táng emperors,
it is uniformly written as Déshèng,
so it has now been corrected.
(From a sticky note in the Yǐngkù edition.)) Zòngzhī accompanied me through hunger and cold,
never leaving my side.
Now that I possess the realm,
who is not rich and noble?
Why should Zòngzhī alone be abandoned?"
After ten days,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Cízhōu.
After more than a year,
he was promoted from Hùbù Shìláng to Lìbù Shìláng.
However, he was completely ignorant
of the methods of selection and compilation.
At the beginning of Chángxīng,
he became Cìshǐ of Cáozhōu.
In the ninth month of the first year of Qīngtài,
he was relieved of his post due to illness and died.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 21617.)
Jiǎ Fù
was the Pànguān of Wáng Róng, the former Jiédùshǐ of Zhènzhōu.
His family possessed three thousand scrolls of books,
which he personally collated and edited.
When Zhāng Wénlǐ assassinated Wáng Róng,
Zhuāngzōng had not yet ascended the throne.
Wénlǐ sent Fù to Yèdū to persuade him to assume the imperial title.
He then stayed in Yèxià,
residing in a postal inn.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Jiǎ Fù as Hónglú Shàoqīng.
Later, he retired as Hónglú Qīng,
returned to Zhènzhōu,
built a thatched hut in his villa,
and taught his children and grandchildren to farm and herd for a living.
Fù had initially served successively as a magistrate in the subordinate districts of Zhèn and Jì.
Wherever he governed, he demonstrated administrative ability.
He was naturally calm and indifferent,
and did not contend with others.
He was considered an outstanding scholar of Zhènzhōu.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 11714.)
Mǎ Gǎo
was fond of scholarly pursuits in his youth,
and passed the Míngjīng examination,
also attaining the Bácuì degree.
He served in the Liáng as Tàicháng Xiūzhuàn,
successively held the post of Shàngshū Láng,
participated in the affairs of the Lǐyuàn,
and was promoted to Tàicháng Shàoqīng.
When the various princes of the Liáng dynasty took consorts
and princesses married out,
they all performed the rites of bowing and yielding at the palace gate.
Mǎ Gǎo considered this improper,
and submitted a memorial to stop it,
which public opinion deemed correct.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 22605.
Note: There are missing texts below.
(Diànběn)) In the fourth year of Chángxīng,
he became Hùbù Shìláng.
Mǎ Gǎo was already eighty years old at that time.
By the time he became Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
he was over eighty.
(Note: The biography of Mǎ Gǎo was originally incomplete.
Ouyáng Shǐ states that he died at eighty and was posthumously appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū.
According to Xuē Shǐ,
Mǎ Gǎo was already over eighty when he was Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
which differs from Ouyáng Shǐ.
Furthermore, Zhízhāi Shūlù Jiětí states:
Zhonghuá Gǔjīn Zhù was written by Mǎ Gǎo,
Tàixué Bóshì of the Later Táng.
However, Ouyáng Shǐ's miscellaneous biographies do not record Mǎ Gǎo as Tàixué Bóshì.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
His spirit showed no decline.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, Volume 784.)
He often forgot things concerning current affairs,
stating that Yuán Zhěn should not have passed the Jìnshì examination
because his father, Yuán Lǔshān,
had the same given name (進).
There were many such instances.
He also submitted a memorial:
"In ancient times, there was no mourning attire for a sister-in-law.
Wénhuáng innovated,
believing that due to the closeness of siblings,
there should not be no mourning attire,
and thus proposed 'xiǎo gōng' (lesser mourning).
Now, the current legal text on mourning attire stipulates 'dà gōng' (greater mourning) for a brother's wife.
I do not know who proposed this change
and placed it in the legal text."
The various academicians refuted this, saying:
"Laws and ordinances are the great principles of the state.
When Mǎ Gǎo was in charge of the Lǐyuàn,
he never discussed or settled this.
Now to suddenly submit a memorial refuting the legal statutes
is an offense."
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, Volume 954.
Note: The biography of Mǎ Gǎo was originally incomplete,
and only a general outline remains now.
Xǔ Jì,
courtesy name Xiánxián.
His grandfather Mì
was renowned in Kuàijī.
From a young age, Xǔ Jì had a fondness for mountains and waters,
broadly studied the classics and histories,
mastered the Sānshì (Three Divinatory Arts).
(The Sānshì,
it is suspected there is an error.
An examination of the Cèfǔ Yuánguī also renders it as
"Sānshì,"
so for now we retain the original,
and note it here.
(Adhesive note in the Yingku bản)) He was especially clear on the Yì [Jīng] hexagrams.
(Note: Tàipíng Guǎngjì states: Jì studied the Yì [Jīng] with a Jìn zhēngjūn.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) He long dwelled in Mount Sìfēng [Sìmíngshān]
and did not seek contemporary fame.
Zhāozōng heard of his name,
summoned him to the palace,
and granted him an audience in the inner hall.
It happened that Zhāozōng was then harmonizing with musicians on the bífì,
and after the performance was over,
he ordered Xǔ Jì to sit and bestowed fruits upon him,
asking about the meaning of the Yì [Jīng].
After his departure,
Xǔ Jì said to others:
"The sovereign indulges in sound,
not in governance.
I have heard that a ruler of men
should illuminate virtue and prevent transgression
to oversee the hundred officials,
who may emulate him.
Now, without disdaining ignoble matters,
he seeks proficiency himself,
the way of a ruler has declined."
Soon after, he requested to return to the mountains,
residing temporarily in Jiānglíng,
subsisting on *zhī* mushrooms and abstaining from grains,
living according to his nature.
At the end of Tiānyòu,
the Jìdùshǐ Zhào Kuāngníng and his brothers treated him with deep respect,
receiving from him instruction on the Dao of self-preservation.
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
he was appointed Jiànguān,
but did not take office.
People in Hànnán called him Zhēngjūn.
When the Liáng attacked Xiāngyáng,
Kuāngníng and his brothers abandoned their post and fled to Shǔ,
and Xǔ Jì accompanied them.
After more than a year,
the Shǔ ruler Wáng Jiàn treated him with the respect due to a teacher,
and he rose to the position of Shǔ Xiàng.
At the end of Tóngguāng,
when Shǔ was pacified,
he traveled east with Wáng Yǎn,
was appointed Gōngbù Shàngshū and retired,
settling in Luò.
At this time, Xǔ Jì was already old,
but his spirit was still vigorous,
he was calm and spoke little,
sometimes uttering in the Shǔ dialect
"how strange, how strange"
and no one knew his ultimate meaning.
He died in the sixth month of Qīngtài three (936 CE),
at over eighty years of age.
His descendants reached the position of Shěngláng.
During the Tóngguāng era,
among those known for their esoteric arts,
there was also the monk Chénghuì.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 10625.
Chénghuì is attached to the biography of Xǔ Jì.
The Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn cut and divided the entry;
now we reconnect them
to restore the original.
(Adhesive note in the Yingku bản)) Chénghuì first became a monk on Mount Wǔtái,
was able to observe the precepts,
and was said to understand the three destinies of "skin, bone, and flesh."
People initially gravitated towards him,
his fame gradually spread,
and many came from all directions to offer provisions,
traveling thousands of *lǐ*.
He claimed he could command venomous dragons,
and bring forth wind and rain,
his followers called him Jiànglóng Dàshī.
When the capital suffered a drought,
Zhuāngzōng welcomed him to Luòxià,
personally bowing to him,
the six palaces paid respects,
scholars and commoners looked up to him,
believing he could bring sweet rain morning or evening.
After praying for several tens of days,
there was no sign of a response.
Someone suggested that if the official prayer for rain yielded no results,
he would be burned.
Chénghuì feared this and fled.
Upon his death,
he was given the posthumous title Fǎyǔ Dàshī,
and his stupa was named Cíyún zhī Tǎ.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 925.)
Zhōu Xuánbào,
(Zhōu Xuánbào,
Jǐnxiù Wànhuāgǔ renders it as
"Cuī Xuánbào,"
which is a transcription error.
An examination of Ouyáng Shǐ and Tōngjiàn both render it as
"Zhōu,"
so we retain the original.
(Adhesive note in the Yingku bản)) was originally a native of Yān,
whose family had for generations served as Cóngshì.
Zhōu Xuánbào became a monk in his youth,
his master had the ability to discern people.
He followed his master for over ten years,
enduring hardships without complaint,
and his master, knowing he was teachable,
imparted to him the arts of Yuán [Tiāngāng] and Xǔ [Jì].
Broadly, he described people's appearances,
comparing them to turtles, fish, birds, and beasts,
making intuitive judgments based on sight,
all reaching the truth of the matter.
Upon returning to his hometown,
he reverted to secular life.
Initially,
Lú Chéng, wearing humble clothes, traveled in Yān,
and visited him with two like-minded companions.
Zhōu Xuánbào said to the local man Zhāng Yīnjǔn:
"Of these two gentlemen,
next year, when the flowers bloom,
both will be among the deceased;
only that Daoist priest
will be very noble in future years."
The following year,
the two men indeed died.
Another twenty years later,
Lú Chéng rose to prominence in Yèxià.
Zhōu Xuánbào returned to Jìnyáng,
where Zhāng Chéngyè greatly respected him,
and his predictions were often accurate.
Zhāng Chéngyè ordered Míngzōng to change his clothes and stand among the various officers,
and used another person to impersonate him,
but Zhōu Xuánbào pointed to Míngzōng at the end of the line and said:
"Is not the bone structure that of the Nèiyá Tàibǎo?"
(Note: The above is suspected to have omissions or errors.
Běimèng Suǒyán states: "The bone structure is extraordinary;
is this the Nèiyá Tàibǎo!"
) Everyone marveled at his unusual insight.
When asked about Míngzōng's fortune and longevity,
he only said that in the end he would become the Zhènzhōu Jiédùshǐ;
at that time Míngzōng was Nèiyá Dūxiào,
only concurrently holding the position of Zhōumù.
Zhāoyì Empress Xià was serving as a concubine,
and accidentally offended Míngzōng,
who severely chastised her.
Zhōu Xuánbào saw her and said:
"This person has the position of a Fānhóu Fūrén,
and will give birth to noble sons."
Míngzōng's furious anger consequently subsided,
and later his words proved true.
Tàiyuán Pànguān Sīmǎ Kuí visited Zhōu Xuánbào,
who said to Sīmǎ Kuí:
"Within five days, you will undertake a ten-thousand-li mission,
and there is no foreseen return date."
A few days later,
Sīmǎ Kuí, while intoxicated,
was strangled by his collar and died.
Zhuāngzōng appointed Zhōu Xuánbào as Běijīng Xún'guān.
The year after Míngzōng's enthronement,
he one day said to his attendants:
"The Daoist Zhōu Xuánbào once made several predictions about me that have proven true;
he should be summoned from Běijīng Jīnzhi to the palace."
Zhào Fèng submitted a memorial, saying:
"What Zhōu Xuánbào excels at,
the arts of Yuán [Tiāngāng] and Xǔ [Jì],
is that Your Majesty's nobility is beyond words.
Now that it has been proven,
there is nothing else to ask.
If he is summoned to the palace,
then ambitious and competing individuals
will flock to ask about good and ill fortune,
which I fear verges on sorcery and delusion."
So Míngzōng stopped the order.
He ordered that Zhōu Xuánbào be generously rewarded with gold and silk,
and appointed Guānglù Qīng and allowed to retire.
He soon died in Tàiyuán,
at over eighty years of age.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 8997.)

On the *jǐmǎo* day of the fifth month,
the Emperor's late eldest sister was posthumously enfeoffed as the Grand Princess of Wúguó.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
the Emperor's niece, the County Princess Yǒngfú, passed away.
Court was suspended for three days, and
she was posthumously enfeoffed as the Commandery Princess Píngchāng.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the Emperor's second grand-uncle, the posthumously granted Grand Mentor Wàn Yǒu, was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín;
the Emperor's third grand-uncle, the posthumously granted Grand Commandant Wàn Quán (note: the original text reads
now corrected to "銓" following Ōuyáng Shǐ), was

posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Sòng;
the Emperor's paternal uncle, the posthumously granted Grand Commandant Fúwáng Dé, was posthumously granted Grand Mentor and

The relevant department was further ordered to select an auspicious day for the investiture.

Wáng Yìjiǎn, Censor-in-chief, was appointed Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs;
Zhāng Yǔn, Vice Minister of Rites, was appointed Censor-in-chief;
Wú Chéngfàn, Scholar of the Central Secretariat, was appointed Vice Minister of Rites;

Wáng Sōng, Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Vice Minister of Personnel;
Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn, Vice Minister of War, was appointed Vice Minister of Personnel;
Lǚ Qí, Vice Minister of Revenue, was appointed Vice Minister of War;
Wéi Xūn, Vice Minister of Justice, was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue;
Lǐ Xiáng, Vice Minister of Public Works, was appointed Vice Minister of Justice.
On the *guǐsì* day,
the Chief Ministers and others were ordered to go separately to temples and monasteries to pray for rain.
On the *jǐhài* day,
flying locusts came from the north, obscuring the sky and moving south.
Lǐ Duō, Guest of the Crown Prince, died.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Of all criminals currently imprisoned in various circuits, prefectures, and subprefectures,

excluding those guilty of the Ten Abominations, Five Rebellions, robbery and murder, counterfeiting seals, manufacturing poisons, or officials committing embezzlement, whose sentences shall each be reduced by one degree,
all others shall be released."
At this time, there were droughts and locusts everywhere,
hence this edict was issued.
On the *yǐsì* day,
the Emperor went to the Xiàngguó Temple to pray for rain.
On the *gēngxū* day of the sixth month,
due to the harm caused by armyworms and locusts,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, Commander-in-chief of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry, was ordered to go to Gāomén to offer sacrifices and make announcements.
Furthermore, seven people, including Liáng Jìnchāo, an envoy of various departments, were dispatched to the Kaīfēng Prefecture area to capture them.
(Note: Ōuyáng Shǐ records it as *guǐhài* day,

which differs from Xuē Shǐ.)
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Ān Shěnhuī, Commander of the Left Yǔlín Army, was appointed Military Governor of Lùzhōu.
Sùzhōu reported that
flying locusts clung to grass and died from dryness.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Bèizhōu reported that
there were a total of three thousand seven hundred runaway households.
Wèi Yántāo, a palace attendant, was dispatched to Sōngshān to cast a dragon tablet and pray for rain.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Mǎ Cóngbīn, Protector of Xījing, was appointed General-in-chief of the Left Jiānmén Guard.
Flying locusts in the Kaīfēng Prefecture area died on their own.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Hénán Prefecture reported that
a great swarm of flying locusts descended,
covering mountains and fields everywhere.
Grass, seedlings, and tree leaves were all consumed,
and many people starved to death.
Wú Chéngfàn, Vice Minister of Rites, died.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
for the impending investiture of the Empress Dowager,
Wáng Yìjiǎn, Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, was sent to report to Heaven and Earth.
Shǎnzōu reported that
locusts flew into its territory,
damaging and eating the five grains and bamboo and tree leaves.
There were a total of eight thousand one hundred runaway households.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Fú Méng, Remonstrance Official, was appointed Vice Minister of Rites;
Péi Tǎn, Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left, was appointed Remonstrance Official.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
twenty-eight court officials and external officials were dispatched to various circuits, prefectures, and subprefectures to borrow millet and wheat.
(Note from *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*: On the *jǐchǒu* day of the seventh month,
an edict stated that due to famine and
insufficient national resources,
over sixty envoys were dispatched to various circuits to collect grain from the people.
This differs from Xuē Shǐ.)
At this time, the envoys, eager to please,
established very harsh laws.
Private mills and grindstones were sealed with mud,
and those who concealed their numbers were all put to death.
Consequently, people could not make a living, and
there was widespread resentment.
In this month,
there were great locust swarms in various prefectures and commanderies,
consuming all vegetation wherever they went.

On the *dīngchǒu* day, the first day of the seventh month in the eighth year of Tiānfú,
the capital experienced rainfall three *chǐ* deep.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Lǐ Cóngwēn, Military Governor of Xǔzhōu, came to court and
was advanced to Duke of Chǔguó.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Huángfǔ Yù, former Military Governor of Héyáng, was appointed Commander of the Right Lóngwǔ Army.

On the *guǐsì* day,

the Empress Dowager was formally invested in the main hall.
Chief Minister Lǐ Sōng served as the envoy, and
Lǐ Shènyí, Right Court Gentleman for Scrutiny, served as his deputy.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
the Emperor went to Nánzhuāng,
summoned accompanying officials to practice archery, and
farmers by the roadside were each given a cloth shirt and straw sandals.

Yáng Sīquán, General-in-chief of the Right Guard, died
and was posthumously granted Grand Tutor.
On the *xīnhài* day,
thirteen court officials were separately dispatched to various prefectures to inspect drought-affected seedlings.
Jīng, Qīng, Cí, and Yè all reported a total of five thousand eight hundred and ninety runaway households.
Five county magistrates and assistants, citing natural disasters and starvation,
resigned their posts by surrendering their official seals.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
Lǐ Cóngmǐn, former Military Governor of Zhāoyì, was appointed Commander of the Left Lóngwǔ Army.
wind and frost,
disregarding hunger and thirst,
are all things that Huárén cannot do.
These are five points that cannot be contended with.
The Róng people are all horsemen,
who benefit on flat terrain;
Zhōngguó
uses infantry,
who prefer narrow and treacherous paths.
North of Zhào and Wèi,
south of Yān and Jì,
within a thousand *lǐ*,
the land is as flat as a whetstone.
The advantages for infantry and cavalry
are clearly
discernible.
If the state were to engage in a standoff with Qìdān,
it would certainly have to station troops on the border.
If too few, one would fear the enemy's strength,
and thus must fortify walls to ensure self-preservation;
if too many, one would suffer
the hardship of supply transport,
and must pursue the enemy swiftly and return quickly.
When we return, they arrive;
when we go out, they withdraw.
Thus, the valiant warriors of the imperial guards
would be exhausted by constant deployments,
and the border regions of Zhèn
and Dìng
would be left with almost no inhabitants.
These are six points that cannot be contended with.
Some argue that Your Majesty's provisions for Qìdān
constitute waste and depletion,
and Your Majesty's humble concessions
constitute humiliation.
This humble subject's view
is that this is not so.
Moreover, even the heroic Hànzǔ
still sent tribute to Mòdú;
Shényáo, with his martial strategies,
still called himself a subject to the Kèhán.
This is called understanding adaptability,
and being skilled at bending and extending.
What is lost is minor,
what is gained is great.
If, however, this leads to conflict,
and ultimately to
animosity,
then from then on, year after year there will be conscriptions,
day after day there will be transportation of supplies,
distressing the people of the realm,
and emptying the state's treasuries.
This is what is called waste and depletion,
is it not
excessive!
Once war begins,
generals will wield arbitrary power,
military officials and meritorious subjects
will demand excessive indulgence,
border provinces and distant commanderies
will become arrogant,
strong externally and weak internally,
the superior will
transgress the inferior,
this is what is called humiliation,
and is it not even more so!
These are seven points that cannot be contended with.
May Your Majesty consider the grand strategy for the state,
adopt the good counsel of the generals and chancellors,
not listen to Fán Kuài's empty words,
but rather heed Lóu Jìng's unpleasant advice.
Then,
train and pacify the soldiers,
nurture the common people,
accumulate grain and gather men,
encourage agriculture and practice warfare,
to await a time when the state has nine years of reserves,
and the army is ten times stronger.
When the ruler has no internal
worries,
and the people have surplus strength,
then one can observe their changes,
await their decline,
use one's own strengths,
attack their weaknesses,
conquer all without fail,
and achieve
success in every endeavor.
This is the best strategy.
May Your Majesty ponder it deeply.
Your subject also believes that Yèdū commands rivers and mountains,
and presents a strategic advantage,
with fertile plains,
and abundant household taxes.
It is a famous principality of Héshuò,
and indeed a great
bulwark of the state.
Currently, the commanding general has gone to the capital,
and the military headquarters are without a leader.
Your subject secretly considers the saying "careless storage invites thieves,"
and fears it is not the intention of a brave man to keep it tightly shut.
I beg Your Majesty to reconsider
deeply,
to prevent treacherous schemes from arising.
I wish to implore Your Majesty to briefly prepare the imperial carriage,
and make arrangements for a tour.
Although it involves enduring wind and rain,
which would impose hardship on Your sacred person;
yet to nip problems in the bud and prevent
minor issues,
it truly relies on Your sagacious strategy.
To inspect the regions and display righteousness,
now is the time.
Your subject has received profound imperial grace,
and his concern for the state is urgent.
His wisdom is small, but his plans are grand;
his reasoning is shallow, but his words are many.
Prostrate, I only fear exceeding my bounds,
but perhaps I might contribute one in ten thousand.
I humbly risk death to submit this.
The memorial was presented,
but kept within the palace and not released.
Gāozǔ summoned an attendant to the inner chambers,
and conveyed a secret imperial edict to Wéihàn, saying:
"I have recently served the north with feelings of
frustration and displeasure.
Now, having reviewed your memorial,
I feel relieved as if awakening.
My decision is made,
you need not worry."
In the summer of the seventh year,
Gāozǔ's imperial carriage was at Yèdū.
Wéihàn came to court from his garrison,
and was reappointed as Jìnchāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Shàodì ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be appointed Shìzhōng,
and Supervisor of National History.
He repeatedly submitted proposals to make peace with Qìdān,
but was rejected by the commanding general Jǐng Yánguǎng.
The following year,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn provoked Qìdān,
leading to the Battle of Chányuān.
All orders for repelling the enemy and issuing commands
came from Yánguǎng,
and Wéihàn and the other chancellors had no part in them.
When Qìdān retreated,
Wéihàn had close associates who were favored by Shàodì
secretly recommend him,
saying:
"If Your Majesty wishes to control the northern barbarians and bring peace to the realm,
only Wéihàn can do it."
(Note: Ōuyáng Shǐ writes that Wéihàn secretly sent someone to persuade the Emperor,
which is consistent with Xuē Shǐ.
Tōngjiàn writes that someone said to the Emperor:
"To bring peace to the realm,
only Sāng Wéihàn can do it,"
which differs from Xuē Shǐ.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) Shàodì then sent Yánguǎng to guard Luò,
and appointed Wéihàn as Zhōngshūlìng,
again serving as Shūmìshǐ and Hóngwénguǎn Dàxuéshì,
and subsequently enfeoffed as Wèiguógōng.
Matters great and small,
all were entrusted to him.
Within a few months,
all affairs gradually became orderly.
However, as his power and position grew heavy,
bribes and gifts from all directions
piled up at his door.
Thus, within a few years,
he accumulated vast wealth,
which led to envious individuals slandering him.
Soon after,
the Nèikèshěngshǐ Lǐ Yàntāo and Duānmíngdiàn Xuéshì Féng Yù, both of whom held power due to their connections,
were at odds with Wéihàn.
Slanderous remarks gradually reached the emperor,
and Wéihàn increasingly fell out of favor and was viewed with suspicion.
He was about to be dismissed,
but was saved when chancellors Liú Xù and Lǐ Sōng memorialized, saying:
"Wéihàn is a founding hero,
and moreover has no obvious fault.
It is inappropriate to lightly advance or dismiss him."
Shàodì then stopped.
Soon after, Féng Yù was made Shūmìshǐ,
to divide Wéihàn's power.
Zhèng Yúnsǒu’s
original name was Áo,
Yúnsǒu was his courtesy name.
Due to the naming taboo of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng,
his courtesy name was thus passed down through the generations.
He was originally from Nányàn.
(Comment: Ōuyáng’s history states he was from Bǎimǎ, Huázhōu.
(Old History of the Five Dynasties, Examination of Differences)) In his youth, he loved learning
and was upright and unyielding.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng,
he once took the imperial examinations for jinshi,
but did not pass.
He then wished to take his wife and children to live in reclusion in the mountains and valleys,
but his wife disapproved,
and refused to go.
Yúnsǒu then traveled briefly through various prefectures,
acquiring several hundred strings of cash to support his family,
bid them farewell, and departed.
Soon after, he entered Mount Shàoshì,
(Comment: Ōuyáng’s history states he entered Shàoshì to become a Daoist priest.
(Old History of the Five Dynasties, Examination of Differences)) and composed thirty-six chapters of “Poems on Simulating Peaks,”
to guide his interests,
which many people circulated.
Later, his wife sent a letter expressing her wishes,
urging him to return home.
Yúnsǒu never glanced at it,
but threw it entirely into the fire;
such was his detachment from worldly ties.
Presently, he heard that there was a five-needled pine on Mount Xīyuè
whose resin had accumulated for a thousand years,
and could remove the Three Corpses,
so he resided in Huàyīn.
He was good friends with Lǐ Dàoyīn and Luó Yǐnzhī;
people at the time called them
“Three High Gentlemen.”
Dàoyīn had a technique for fishing,
using a hook but no bait,
and could also transmute gold and stone;
there was nothing he couldn’t do.
Yúnsǒu constantly witnessed these things,
believed them, but did not seek them for himself.
Yúnsǒu was on good terms with the powerful minister Lǐ Zhèn of the Liáng dynasty.
Zhèn wished to offer him a salary,
but he refused and did not accept.
When Zhèn was demoted to the south,
Yúnsǒu walked a thousand li to visit him;
those who knew him highly esteemed this.
Later, his wife and children successively passed away.
Each time he heard the sad news,
he would cry once and then stop.
At that time, only two young boys in green robes, a qín, and a crane
accompanied him wherever he went.
He enjoyed the game of qísài,
and when he met companions, he would play day and night.
Even in cold wind and heavy snow,
he would sit by the eaves playing a game;
though his hands and feet cracked,
he showed no weariness.
During the Tiānchéng era of Táng,
he was summoned and appointed Zǔo Shíyí,
but he did not take up the post.
He spent his days and nights with Luó Yǐnzhī.
Yǐnzhī profited from medicinal arts,
while Yúnsǒu supported himself with mountain fields.
Both were fond of wine and skilled in poetry,
and adept at long whistles.
He had a large gourde,
which he claimed could ward off cold and heat.
He kept wine in it,
and its flavor did not spoil for a long time.
He carried it daily to places with flowers, trees, water, and stones,
taking a sip and reciting a poem.
Once, in a drunken state, they composed a linked verse.
Zhèng said:
“One pot, a famous thing in heaven;
Two people, carefree in the world.”
Luó said:
“Apart from the drunken Yǐnzhī and Yúnsǒu,
I wonder where true innocence is found.”
When Emperor Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he heard of his reputation,
and sent an envoy with a letter to show respect,
summoning him to be Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū.
Yúnsǒu claimed illness and did not rise,
submitting a memorial to express his gratitude.
Emperor Gāozǔ read the memorial and praised him,
distributing it among his close officials for viewing.
Soon after, he was granted the title Xiāoyáo Xiānshēng,
and retired as Jiànyì Dàfū,
receiving a monthly stipend.
Yúnsǒu loved wine,
and once composed a poem about wine of twelve hundred characters.
Those who sought fame throughout the land copied it onto silk and paper,
using it as a gift.
Furthermore, there were those who traveled over a thousand li,
sending painters to secretly depict his likeness and arrange it on screens.
Such was the esteem he commanded at the time.
At the end of the Tiānfú era,
he died of old age,
at seventy-four years old.
He had a collection of writings in twenty volumes circulated in the world.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 18881.)
The historian says: Since ancient times, those who clung to the dragon’s scales,
attached themselves to the phoenix’s wings,
and thus reached the cloud-paved road,
were they only the gentlemen from Fēngpèi?
If one truly possessed talent and ability,
and met with a rising dynasty,
one could also achieve nobility for a time,
such as Lú Zhì and the several gentlemen below him.
As for Guózhēn’s forthrightness,
Rényuàn’s friendliness and brotherliness,
and the two gentlemen Zhào and Lǐ who died for the state,
all brought no shame to the scholarly community.
However, the integrity and reclusion of Yùyǔ,
and the profound reclusion of Yúnsǒu,
are sufficient to curb the trend of eager competition
and inspire a spirit of noble integrity.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 18881.) Textual Notes
Book of Jìn, Twenty Biographies, Ninth
Cháng Cóngjiǎn,
was a man from Chénzhōu.
His family had made a living by slaughtering sheep for generations.
He was strong enough to fight several men,
and skilled in using a spear.
Initially, he served Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Later Táng as a junior officer.
Whenever there was a siege,
men were called to be ‘ladder-heads’
(ladder-head,
originally written as
‘yángtóu’
in the original text, now corrected according to Ōuyáng’s history.
(Photographic copy, pasted slip)), Cóngjiǎn often volunteered.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng, impressed by his bravery,
promoted him to lead the Imperial Guard in front of the tent and concurrently serve as Commander-in-Chief of the Infantry.
One day,
Emperor Zhuāngzōng led a large army to confront the Liáng army,
and sat atop a high hill.
An enemy holding a large banner was displaying his might.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng pointed to him and said to his attendants:
“He is a brave warrior.”
Cóngjiǎn said:
“Your servant will capture him for Your Majesty.”
Emperor Zhuāngzōng, fearing he would not succeed,
did not permit it.
Cóngjiǎn withdrew,
then secretly led a dozen riders and rushed forward alone,
seized the banner, and returned.
The multitude cheered,
and Emperor Zhuāngzōng was impressed by his courage,
bestowing upon him generous rewards.
He also once suffered an arrow wound where the arrowhead penetrated the bone.
He had a physician remove it,
who had to chisel the bone with a blade.
Fearing the pain,
the physician hesitated for a long time, unable to move it.
Cóngjiǎn glared and said:
“Why don’t you chisel deeper?”
When it was removed,
everyone around him felt a pang of sympathy,
but Cóngjiǎn’s expression remained unchanged;
his bravery and fortitude were all of this kind.
In the first year of Tiānfú,
Gāozǔ raised an army and entered Luò.
He was promoted to Inspector-General of the Ministry of Punishments,
and awarded the title of Hùbì Zhōngxiào Gōngchén.
In the third year,
he followed Yáng Guāngyuǎn in pacifying Fàn Yánguāng at Yè,
and was appointed Du Yúhòu of the Fèngguó Army.
In the sixth year,
when Ān Cóngjìn of Xiāngzhōu rebelled,
he followed Gāo Xíngzhōu to suppress him,
but the city did not fall for over a year.
One day,
Qīng requested to lead the vanguard,
with the other armies following him.
There happened to be an internal respondent,
and thus the city was taken.
Qīng sustained severe injuries,
and an imperial edict praised and comforted him.
In the seventh year,
he was awarded the title of Tuīzhōng Bǎoyùn Gōngchén,
promoted to Gold-Purple Guanglù Dàfū,
and appointed Cìshǐ of Xīzhōu.
In the eighth year,
an imperial edict ordered him to station his troops at Yè.
In the spring of the ninth year,
the Qìdān moved south,
besieging the city.
Qīng and Zhāng Cóng'ēn defended it,
and the Young Emperor sent wax-sealed edicts of encouragement and exhortation,
and bestowed upon them mansions.
When the Qìdān retreated,
due to his merit in defending the city,
he was successively promoted in military ranks.
In the third month of spring, the second year of Kāiyùn,
he followed Dù Chóngwēi on a northern expedition,
and relieved the siege of Yángchéng.
He was promoted to Inspector-General Sītú.
In the seventh month of autumn that year,
an imperial edict ordered him and Huángfǔ Yù to deliver provisions to Yìzhōu.
In the eleventh month,
he followed Dù Chóngwēi to recover Yíngzhōu.
Hearing that a large Qìdān army was approaching,
Chóngwēi led his armies west along the Hūshuǐ River,
intending to secure Chángshān.
When they reached the Zhōngdù Bridge,
(Zhōngdù
was originally written as
"Píngdù",
now corrected according to the Liáo Shǐ.
(Photocopy edition sticky note)) the Qìdān had already camped on the north bank.
From the twenty-seventh day of that month to the fifth day of the twelfth month,
the army could not advance.
At that time, the Rong King arrived,
leaving his elite cavalry to resist us,
and dividing his weaker forces.
From the ancient Língdū City, they skirted the base of the mountains,
crossed the shallow parts of the Huòtuó River,
and led their forces south.
Reaching Zhàojùn,
a distance of over a hundred lǐ,
they cut off our supply lines
and blocked our return route.
Qīng, understanding the situation,
said to Chóngwēi:
"Our army is five lǐ from Chángshān.
If we stay here like waiting for a hare,
our camp will be isolated and our food exhausted. What will we do?
I request to lead two thousand infantry as a vanguard,
to seize the bridge and open the road.
You can then lead the other armies to follow.
If we enter Chángshān as planned,
we will surely succeed."
Chóngwēi agreed,
and dispatched Sòng Yànjūn to go with him.
Qīng captured the bridge with a single strike,
and the Qìdān retreated slightly.
Chóngwēi, however, hesitated and did not advance,
having secretly become disloyal to the state.
Yànjūn retreated and fled.
Qīng arrayed his troops on the north bank,
and strictly admonished his subordinates.
At dusk,
the fierce battle did not cease.
The Qìdān continuously brought in fresh troops,
while we had no reinforcements to add.
Qīng and his subordinates perished there.
(According to the Tōngjiàn: Qīng said to his troops:
"The commander-in-chief is holding back his troops,
idly watching us in distress without coming to our rescue.
He must have other intentions.
We should repay the nation with our lives!"
The troops were moved by his words,
and none retreated.
By dusk,
the battle did not cease.
The Qìdān reinforced with fresh troops,
and Qīng and all his soldiers died.
From this, all the armies lost morale.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) He was fifty-three years old at the time.
The Qìdān soon built a Jīngguān at the battle site.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he ordered men to level it,
and posthumously awarded Qīng the title of Tàifù.
That year,
Qīng's son, Shǒujūn, performed a soul-summoning ritual and buried him at his ancestral estate, Yìhuà Biéyè.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 6351.)
Liáng Hànzhāng,
courtesy name Guóbǎo,
was a native of Yìngzhōu.
In his youth, he served Táng Míngzōng with his bravery and strength,
and successively held the positions of Tuqí and Fèngdé Commander.
In the second year of Gāozǔ's reign,
he was remotely appointed Cìshǐ of Qīnzhōu.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Inspector-General Sīkōng,
and appointed Hùshèng Du Zhīhuīshǐ.
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Inspector-General Sītú,
and remotely appointed Tuánliànshǐ of Lángzhōu.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Fángyùshǐ of Chénzhōu.
After returning from Chánzhōu with the Young Emperor,
he was appointed Inspector-General Tàibǎo and Fángyùshǐ of Zhèngzhōu,
and served as Shìwèi Mǎjūn Du Zhīhuīshǐ.
Soon after, he was appointed Bīngmǎ Liúhòu of Yǒngqīng Army,
and shortly thereafter formally received the title of Jiézhì.
That year,
an imperial edict ordered him to lead a thousand cavalry to garrison Jìzhōu.
Soon after, due to Dù Chóngwēi's northern expedition,
an imperial edict appointed Hànzhāng as Běimiàn Mǎjūn Du Páizhènshǐ,
and sent him to recover Yūkǒu Pass.
He encountered five thousand Qìdān cavalry north of Fúyáng,
and fought bitterly all day.
Due to the disparity in numbers,
he was struck by a stray arrow,
and perished on the battlefield.
(According to the biography of Gāo Móhàn in the Liáo Shǐ: "Jìn sent Dù Chóngwēi, the Jiédùshǐ of Wèifǔ, with an army of 300,000 to resist.
Móhàn, with 300 men under his command, met them in battle,
killed their vanguard Liáng Hànzhāng,
and the remaining troops fled."
This differs from Xuē Shǐ.
The Tōngjiàn states: "Dù Chóngwēi and others arrived at Yíngzhōu,
and heard that the Qìdān general Gāo Móhàn had already led his troops out stealthily.
Chóngwēi sent Liáng Hànzhāng with two thousand cavalry to pursue him.
They encountered the Qìdān at Nányángwù,
and Hànzhāng was defeated and died."
Perhaps Hànzhāng, with two thousand cavalry against five thousand enemy cavalry,
faced a disparity in numbers,
leading to his defeat.
The Liáo Shǐ might not be reliable.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) This was in the eleventh month of that year,
and he was forty-nine years old at the time.
Hànzhāng was skilled in military affairs
and had accumulated many military merits.
However, when he served as a regional governor,
he was fond of accumulating wealth wherever he went,
and no good governance could be recorded.
When he garrisoned Gānlíng,
he had a strong ambition to pacify the Qìdān,
but because he led a partial army
and suddenly encountered a powerful enemy,
he suffered this defeat.
That month,
his son Hǎiróng presented Hànzhāng's personal riding whip, horse, and weapons.
The Emperor grieved for him
and posthumously awarded him the title of Tàiwèi.
Hànzhāng had a younger brother, Hàn táng,
who was also famous at the time for his skill in using a spear.
During the Tiānchéng period,
as commander of the Xiàojié Army in Wèifǔ,
he attacked Wáng Dū in Dìngzhōu.
Hàntáng led his contingent as the first to enter the city,
capturing Wáng Dū and several prized horses from the foreign general Tūněi.
At that time, Fàn Yánguāng, who was garrisoned in Chángshān,
desired the finest of these horses,
but Hàntáng did not agree.
Later, when Hàntáng was stationed in Zhàojùn,
he was killed due to a memorial,
and people at the time felt he was wronged.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 6614.)
Tàizǔ Shèngshén Gōngsù Wénwǔ Xiàohuángdì,
whose surname was Guō,
personal name Wēi,
courtesy name Wénzhòng,
was a native of Yáoshān in Xíngzhōu.
Some say he was originally the son of the Cháng family,
and when he was young, his mother married into the Guō family,
so he adopted their surname.
(According to the Wǔdài Huìyào: A descendant of Guóshū of Zhōu.)
His great-great-grandfather's personal name was Jǐng.
In the first year of Guǎngshùn,
he was posthumously honored as Ruìhé Huángdì,
with the temple name Xìnzǔ,
and his mausoleum was called Wēnlíng.
His great-great-grandmother, Lady Zhāng,
was posthumously enfeoffed as Ruìgōng Huánghòu.
His great-grandfather's personal name was Chén.
During the Hàn, he was granted the title Tàibǎo,
and was posthumously honored as Míngxiàn Huángdì,
with the temple name Xīzǔ,
and his mausoleum was called Qílíng.
His great-grandmother, Madame Shēn of Zhèngguó,
was posthumously enfeoffed as Míngxiào Huánghòu.
His grandfather's personal name was Yùn.
During the Hàn, he was granted the title Tàifù,
and was posthumously honored as Yìshùn Huángdì,
with the temple name Yìzǔ,
and his mausoleum was called Jiélíng.
(According to the Wǔdài Huìyào: Wēnlíng, Qílíng, and Jiélíng had no actual mausoleums,
and were worshipped from afar.)
His grandmother, Madame Hán of Chénguó,
was posthumously enfeoffed as Yìjìng Huánghòu.
His imperial father's personal name was Jiǎn.
During the Hàn, he was granted the title Tàishī,
and was posthumously honored as Zhāngsù Huángdì,
with the temple name Qìngzǔ,
and his mausoleum was called Qīnlíng.
His imperial mother, Madame Wáng of Yānguó,
was posthumously enfeoffed as Zhāngdé Huánghòu.
The Empress gave birth to the Emperor in the first *jiǎzǐ* year of Tiānyòu of the Táng dynasty, on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month,
at their old residence in Yáoshān.
On the night of his birth,
a red light illuminated the room,
and there was a sound like charcoal cracking in a furnace,
with sparks flying in all directions.
When the Emperor was three years old,
his family moved to Tàiyuán.
Not long after,
his imperial father was captured by the Yān army
and died in service to the state.
Before the Emperor reached childhood,
Empress Dowager Zhāngdé passed away prematurely.
His maternal aunt, Madame Hán of Chǔguó, took him in and raised him.
When he grew up,
he was robust in body and spirit,
with extraordinary and unyielding aspirations.
He loved military matters and delighted in bravery,
and did not bother with land and property.
At the end of Tiānyòu,
Lǐ Sìzhāo, the Jiedushi of Lùzhōu, died in battle at Chángshān.
His son, Jìtāo, proclaimed himself acting Military Governor,
formed alliances with the Liáng court to the south,
and occupied the city, defying orders.
He then distributed gold to recruit heroes.
The Emperor, then eighteen years old,
avoiding officials at Húguān,
stayed with his old friend, Mr. Cháng,
and then went to answer the call for recruits.
The Emperor was strong-willed and resolute,
fond of fighting and powerful.
Jìtāo admired him for this.
Even if he violated laws and prohibitions,
Jìtāo often pardoned him.
Once, he was strolling in the market of Shàngdǎng.
There was a sturdy butcher in the market,
feared by many.
The Emperor, with his intimidating spirit, challenged him,
and while drunk, ordered the butcher to cut meat.
Slightly displeased,
he yelled at him.
The butcher, enraged,
exposed his belly and said to the Emperor,
"Do you dare stab me?"
The Emperor immediately stabbed him in the belly.
The market people seized him and handed him over to officials,
but Jìtāo, regretting it, let him escape.
In that year,
Zhuāngzōng pacified Liáng,
and Jìtāo was executed.
His subordinate personal guards were assigned to the imperial cavalry.
The Emperor was among them,
then twenty-one years old.
The Emperor was intelligent and quick-witted,
and enjoyed writing.
When he joined the army,
he read many official documents and records,
and deeply understood the essentials of military history and governance.
Everyone admired his quickness.
He once visited Lǐ Qióng of Zhāoyì.
Qióng was reading the Kǔnwài Chūnqiū.
The Emperor immediately took it to look at it,
and said:
"This is about military strategy.
Brother, please teach me."
Qióng then taught him,
and he deeply understood its principles.
(According to Lǐ Qióng's biography in the Sòng Shǐ:
Táng Zhuāngzōng recruited brave warriors,
and he immediately responded.
He and Zhōuzǔ and ten others swore to be brothers.
One day, during a gathering,
Qióng looked closely at Zhōuzǔ,
knowing he was no ordinary man.
He then raised his cup and vowed:
"We ten individuals,
like dragons and snakes mixed together,
when we achieve wealth and status in the future,
must not forget each other.
Should anyone violate this oath,
may the gods inflict punishment."
They all pricked their arms and bled to swear.
Zhōuzǔ and Qióng had a particularly close relationship.
Zhōuzǔ once visited Qióng
and saw him sitting upright reading.
He then asked what book he was reading.
Qióng said:
"This is the Kǔnwài Chūnqiū.
It discusses how to govern a nation with righteousness
and employ military strategy with ingenuity,
comparing survival and demise, order and chaos,
and recording the success and failure of the wise and foolish –
it's all in here."
Zhōuzǔ asked him to read it,
and said to Qióng:
"Brother, you must teach me."
From then on, whenever Zhōuzǔ went out,
he always kept it in his sleeve.
Whenever he had free time, he would read it,
and whenever he had questions,
he referred to Qióng as his teacher.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
On the *xīnmǎo* day of the sixth month,
the Emperor did not hold court,
because the coffin of Hàn Yǐndì was still lying in state.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
all officials presented a memorial
requesting that the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month, the Emperor's birthday, be designated the Yǒngshòu Festival.
This was granted.
Xíngzhōu experienced heavy and continuous rain.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Liú Yuè, Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, proposed the posthumous title Yǐnhuángdì for the young Emperor of Hàn,
and the mausoleum name Yǐnglíng.
This was granted.
On the *xīnhài* day,
Wáng Jùn, Commissioner of Military Affairs, was appointed Minister of the Left and Minister of the Secretariat, acting as Grand Councilor,
and Supervisor of National History,
and continued to serve as Commissioner of Military Affairs;
Fàn Zhì, Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs and Minister of War, was appointed Minister of the Central Secretariat, acting as Grand Councilor,
and served as Grand Academician of the Jíxián Academy;
Lǐ Gǔ, Vice Minister of Revenue and Administrator of the Three Departments, was appointed Minister of the Central Secretariat, acting as Grand Councilor,
and Administrator of the Three Departments.
Dòu Zhēnggù, Minister of Works and Grand Master, and Supervisor of National History,
and Sū Yǔguī, Minister of Education and Minister of the Central Secretariat, acting as Grand Councilor, and Grand Academician of the Jíxián Academy,
were both dismissed from their premierships and retained their original offices.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
the Emperor visited Xīzhuāng.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
an imperial edict ordered Grand Councilor Fàn Zhì to participate in the affairs of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
Yèdū, Míng, Cāng, Bèi, and other prefectures experienced heavy and continuous rain.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
a report from Xījīng stated that
Guō Língtú, the newly appointed Grand Minister of the Imperial Clan, had died.
On the *dīngsì* day,
Yán Kàn, Assistant Minister of the Left, was appointed Minister of War,
and served as Academician of the Duānmíng Hall;
Zhái Guāngyè, Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of Palace Affairs, was concurrently appointed Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
On the *xīnyǒu* day, the first day of the seventh month of autumn,
the Emperor wore the imperial robe and crown,
and presided over the Chóngyuán Hall,
presenting the precious scrolls for the four ancestral temples to Fēng Dào, Minister of the Central Secretariat, and others,
who were to proceed to Xījīng to perform the rites.
On the *guǐhài* day,
Tián Mǐn, Assistant Minister of the Left, was concurrently appointed Administrator of the Guózǐjiān.
On the *wùchén* day,
Yú Décchén, Censor-in-Chief, was appointed Assistant Minister of the Right,
and Biān Guāngfàn, Director of the Imperial Library, was appointed Guest of the Crown Prince.
Zhāng Zhāo, Minister of Revenue, was appointed Guest of the Crown Prince.
His son, Bǐng, was appointed Clerk of Yángzhái,
but committed a crime and was found guilty.
Zhāo went to the imperial court to await punishment,
but an imperial edict released him.
He was then demoted to this office.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Historian Jiǎ Wěi and others presented the thirty volumes of the Veritable Records of Jìn Gāozǔ and the twenty volumes of the Veritable Records of the Young Emperor that they had compiled.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
the Emperor visited the residence of Grand Councilor Wáng Jùn.
(Note: Ōuyáng's history records *wùyín* as
the day the Emperor visited Wáng Jùn's residence.
(Verification of discrepancies in the Old History of the Five Dynasties))
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
a report from Zhènzhōu stated that
they had defeated the Hédōng bandit army west of Píngshān County,
beheading five hundred.
On the same day,
Biān Wèi, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, presented a memorial
proposing to change the names of the ceremonial dances for the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples,
the details of which are in the treatise on music.
On the *xīnmǎo* day of the eighth month,
the coffin of Hàn Yǐndì was moved. The Emperor went to Tàipíng Gōng to offer sacrifices and libations,
and ordered all officials to perform the farewell ceremony at the western suburbs.
In this year,
Yōuzhōu suffered a famine,
and refugees scattered into Cāngzhōu territory.
An imperial edict provided that refugees arriving
be given one *dǒu* of grain per person,
and also be given ownerless land,
allowing them to plant as they wished,
and exempting them from taxes and levies.
On the *guǐsì* day,
a tiger entered the Xīxíng Temple in Xījīng and injured people;
the citizens killed it.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
the Emperor visited Bānjīng Guǎn.
On the *rén'yín* day,
the Khitan sent Cáo Jìyún, a general from Yōuzhōu, to return the remains of Zhào Yíng, former Minister of the Central Secretariat of the Later Jìn.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Grand Tutor,
and also bestowed five hundred bolts of silk upon his son
to cover funeral expenses,
for burial in his hometown of Huáyīn.
On the *yǐsì* day,
the Emperor visited Xīzhuāng.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Wáng Yàn of Jìnzhōu was transferred to Xúzhōu,
Wáng Jǐng of Cāngzhōu was transferred to Hézhōng,
Sūn Fāngjiǎn of Dìngzhōu was transferred to Huázhōu,
Guō Cóngyì of Yǒngxīng was transferred to Xǔzhōu,
Wáng Jìhóng of Bèizhōu was transferred to Héyáng,
Lǐ Huī was transferred to Cāngzhōu.
Wǔ Xíngdé, Military Governor of Xǔzhōu, was appointed Defender of Xījīng.
Zhē Cóngrǔan of Huázhōu was transferred to Shǎnzhōu,
Hù Yànkē of Hézhōng was transferred to Huázhōu,
Lǐ Hóngxìn of Shǎnzhōu was transferred to Yǒngxīng,
Wáng Ráo of Huázhōu was transferred to Bèizhōu,
Wáng Yànchāo of Xúzhōu was transferred to Jìnzhōu.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
eight palace officials, including Consort Lǐ of the Imperial Kitchen, were all enfeoffed as Xiànjūn,
six, including Consort Liú of the Palace Scribes, were all enfeoffed as Jùnfūrén,
and three, including Consort Huángfǔ of the Palace Administration, were all enfeoffed as Guófūrén.
Under the Táng system, there were inner officials and palace officials,
each with their specific duties,
and no additional titles of *jùn* or *guó* were added.
In recent times, these have been added,
which is not in accordance with the old regulations.
Sūn Xíngyǒu, Prefect of Yìzhōu, was appointed Acting Military Governor of Dìngzhōu.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
the late Lady Chái was posthumously elevated to Empress,
and the relevant department was instructed to determine her posthumous title,
and prepare the rites for her investiture.
On the *gēngshēn* day, the first day of the ninth month,
the Emperor visited Tàipíng Gōng to pay respects to the Hàn Empress Dowager.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
the late Lady Yáng was posthumously granted the title Shūfēi,
and the relevant department was instructed to select a day and prepare the rites for her investiture.
The late Emperor's fifth daughter was posthumously enfeoffed as Princess Yǒngníng.
On the *guǐhài* day,
a report from Dìngzhōu stated that
Wùyù, Prince Yǒngkāng of the Khitan, had been killed by his subordinates.
(Note: The History of Liáo states that Shìzōng was assassinated on the *guǐhài* day of the ninth month.
It is unlikely that Dìngzhōu could have reported this on the very *guǐhài* day.
The original text is suspected to contain an error.)
On the *jiǎzǐ* day (10th),
Wǔ Tínghàn, former Commander of the Tuánliàn militia of Yàozhōu, retired as Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,

Qián Chǔ, Grand Marshal of all armies, Military Governor of Liǎngzhè, concurrently Grand Tutor, Minister of the Right, Minister of the Central Secretariat, and King of Wúyuè, was appointed Grand Marshal of all armies in the realm.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Liú Tāo, Drafter of the Central Secretariat, was demoted to Junior Supervisor of the Lesser Treasury,
to serve in Xījīng,
due to sending his son Xù to draft imperial edicts on his behalf.
Liú Xù, Censor Investigator, was demoted to Magistrate of Fùzhōu,
due to drafting imperial edicts on behalf of his father.
Yáng Zhāojiǎn, Drafter of the Central Secretariat, was dismissed from office and allowed to return to private life,
because he frequently took leave,
and did not attend to his duties.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 8980.)
Collation Note
Zhōu Shū, Volume 3, Biography of Tàizǔ.
In the eighth month, on the day *jǐyǒu*,
the Emperor visited Nánzhuāng.
On the day *bǐngchén*,
Qí Zàngzhēn, an envoy of the Palace Wardrobe, was dismissed
and exiled to Shāmén Dǎo.
Zàngzhēn had been commanded by imperial edict to repair a river,
but instead of staying in the work area under his jurisdiction,
he privately went to a nearby county to lodge.
When informed of the urgent danger to the dikes,
he remained peacefully asleep and did not move,
which consequently led to an overflow.
Hence, he received this punishment.
On the day *gēngshēn*,
Liú Cí, the Jìedùshǐ of Xíngzhōu, was transferred to command Hényáng.
On the day *xīnyǒu*,
Tián Jǐngxián, the Dūzhīhuīshǐ of the Left Wing of Lóngjié and the Fángyùshǐ of Lángzhōu, was appointed Liúhòu of Xíngzhōu.
(Jǐngxián
was originally written
as "Jǐngchéng";
Xíngzhōu
was originally written
as "Xíngzhōu";
both are now corrected according to the Tōngjiàn.
(Adhesive note in the scanned edition)) On the day *dīngmǎo*,
the river burst its banks at Héyīn,
and incessant heavy rain fell in the capital.
Firewood and fodder were differentially granted to the officers and soldiers of various armies.
On the day *guǐyǒu*,
Wáng Pǔ, a Hànlín Xuéshì and Hùbù Shìláng, was appointed Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì.
On the day *jiǎxū*,
Wáng Kuí of Tánzhōu reported:
"Liú Yán of Lángzhōu is colluding with the Huái River bandits,
and dispatched Commander Zhèng Jiào to lead troops,
intending to seize control of this region.
Zhèng Jiào was captured by the army,
and fled into Wǔlíng.
Liú Yán was soon deposed by various armies,
and I have already reached Lángzhōu to pacify the situation."
An imperial edict ordered Liú Yán to retire to his private residence,
and entrusted Wáng Kuí with his convenient placement.
This month, various prefectures and commanderies reported
continuous heavy rain,
which submerged crops
and damaged city walls and houses.
In the ninth month, on the day *jǐmǎo*,
Lú Sǔn, the Tàizǐ Shàobǎo, passed away.
On the day *dīngyǒu*,
Shēnzhōu reported:
"Dù Yánxī, the Bīngmǎ Dūjiān of Lèshòu County, was killed by garrison soldiers."
Previously,
soldiers from Bǎoníng Commandery in Qízhōu were stationed in Lèshòu.
The Dūtóu Liú Yànzhāng and others killed Yánxī and caused a rebellion.
At that time, Zhāng Wànyǒu, the Kāidào Zhīhuīshǐ of Zhèngzhōu, was also stationed in Lèshòu,
but he did not join them.
The court urgently dispatched the Gòngfèngguān Mǎ È to investigate the matter.
(Mǎ È
was originally written
as "Mǎ È";
now corrected according to the Tōngjiàn.
(Adhesive note in the scanned edition)) È then, with Wànyǒu, captured Liú Yànzhāng and thirteen others and executed them.
The remaining rebels fled to Qízhōu.
This month was mostly overcast and gloomy,
and trees blossomed a second time.
In winter, the tenth month, on the first day, *wùshēn*,
an imperial edict declared that on the first day of the first month of the coming year, there would be rites at the Southern Suburb,
and that no prefectures or commanderies of any circuit were to levy contributions
under the pretext of presenting offerings for the Southern Suburb.
On the day *jǐyǒu*,
Zhāng Yánchéng, the Yòujīnwú Shàngjiāngjūn, passed away.
On the day *gēngxū*,
Xuē Huáiràng, formerly the Jìedùshǐ of Tóngzhōu, was appointed Zuǒtúnyù Shàngjiāngjūn;
Tián Mǐn, the Shàngshū Zuǒchéng and concurrent Pàn Guózǐjiān, was given the provisional title of Quán Tàicháng Qīng;
Wáng Yì, the Lǐbù Shàngshū, was given the provisional title of Quán Bīngbù Shàngshū.
The Tàicháng reported that
the systems for the altars and positions at the suburban and ancestral temples and the altars of the gods of soil and grain
should be submitted to the relevant department for repair and upkeep.
This was approved.
Féng Dào, the Zhōngshū Lìng, was appointed Nánjiāo Dàlǐ Shǐ;
Róng, Prince of Jìn and Kāifēng Yǐn, was appointed Dùndì Shǐ;
Wáng Yì, the Quán Bīngbù Shàngshū, was appointed Lǔbù Shǐ;
Zhāng Xù, the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, was appointed Yízhàng Shǐ;
Tián Mǐn, the Quán Pàn Tàicháng Qīng, was appointed Lǐyí Shǐ.
Guō Qióng, formerly the Fángyùshǐ of Yǐngzhōu, was appointed Quán Zōngzhèng Qīng.
On the day *jiǎyín*,
Dīng Zhījùn, formerly the Guānglù Qīng, was reinstated as Guānglù Qīng.
On the day *bǐngchén*,
the Emperor visited Nánzhuāng and Xīzhuāng.
On the day *jǐwèi*,
Zhāng Jiànwǔ, formerly the Cìshǐ of Níngzhōu, was demoted to Yòusīyù Fùshuài,
due to the failure of the "Wild Pheasant Tribe" (yějī zú) military operation.
Yú Chóngliàng, formerly a Hànlín Xuéshì and Gōngbù Shìláng, was appointed Lǐbù Shìláng
and concurrently Hànlín Xuéshì.
At that time, Chóngliàng had resigned his post in Shǎnzhōu to care for his parents;
now he was re-appointed to a palace position,
and an imperial edict was issued to summon him,
ordering his home prefecture to provide travel equipment and horses,
so he could return to court with his parents.
Zhāng Zhāo, the Tàizǐ Bīnkè, was appointed Hùbù Shàngshū;
Lǐ Tāo, the Tàizǐ Bīnkè, was appointed Xíngbù Shàngshū.
An imperial edict commanded Féng Dào, the Zhōngshū Lìng, to go to the Western Capital to welcome and escort the spirit tablets of the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the day *jiǎzǐ*,
Féng Dào, the Zhōngshū Lìng, led all officials in presenting the honorific title "Shèngmíng Wǔwén Réndé Huángdì" (Sagely and Enlightened, Martial and Cultured, Benevolent and Virtuous Emperor).
The Emperor declined in his imperial reply.
After three petitions,
he finally assented,
but stipulated that it would be put into effect after the suburban rites were completed.
On the day *rénshēn*,
Yèdū, Xíng, Míng, and other prefectures all reported earthquakes,
with Yèdū being particularly severe.
In the eleventh month, on the day *xīnsì*,
the Gòngchéng rice fields administration was abolished,
allowing people to rent and cultivate them.
On the day *yǐyǒu*,
it was the winter solstice,
and the Emperor did not receive court greetings.
On the day *gēngyín*,
Hé Fújìn, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènzhōu, thrice petitioned to request an audience,
and it was granted.
An imperial edict appointed Cáo Yīng, the Shìwèi Bùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ, to provisionally manage military and administrative affairs in Zhènzhōu.
On the day *guǐsì*,
Lǐ Qióng, the Jiàngzuò Jiān, was appointed Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu.
On the day *rényín*,
an imperial edict stated:
"The counties and cities of the realm shall be reclassified.
Excluding the Gī Jì,
counties with 3,000 households or more shall be 'Wàngxiàn' (prestige counties);
2,000 households or more shall be 'Jǐnxiàn' (important counties);
1,000 households or more shall be 'Shàngxiàn' (superior counties);
500 households or more shall be 'Zhōngxiàn' (medium counties);
and fewer than 500 households shall be 'Zhōngxiàxiàn' (medium-lower counties)."
In the twelfth month, on the day *wùshēn*,
there was freezing rain.
On this day,
the spirit tablets of the four ancestral temples arrived at the Western Suburb.
The Emperor went to the suburbs to welcome them, offered sacrifices,
escorted the spirit tablets into the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
set up offerings, placated the spirits, and then retired.
On the day *rénzǐ*,
Zhào Fèng, formerly the Cìshǐ of Shànzhōu, was granted death.
(Shànzhōu
was originally written
as "Shànzhōu";
now corrected according to Zhào Fèng's biography.
(Adhesive note in the scanned edition))
This was because he was impeached by the people.
On the day *jiǎyín*,
an imperial edict stated that for households within the cities of all circuits, prefectures, counties, and garrisons,
the old practice of demanding payment for silkworm salt
was to be abolished from now on.
On the day *jiǎzǐ*,
Hé Fújìn, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènzhōu, came to court.
On the day *yǐchǒu*,
Wáng Yīn, the Liúshǒu of Yèdū, came to court.
On the day *bǐngyín*,
the Lǐyí Shǐ reported:
"For the Emperor's rituals at the suburban and ancestral temples,
we request that Róng, Prince of Jìn, be appointed secondary offerer (yàxiàn),
and concurrently preside over the final offering (zhōngxiàn) ritual."
This was approved.
On the day *jǐsì*,
Wáng Shēn, the Zuǒ Bǔquē, was suspended from his post,
because during a land inspection in Bózhōu,
he falsely relied on manipulated cadastral records.
On the day *xīnwèi*,
Wáng Yīn, the Liúshǒu of Yèdū and Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ, was stripped of his official titles and ranks,
exiled to Dēngzhōu,
and soon granted death in the Northern Suburb.
His family members
were not prosecuted.
On the day *guǐyǒu*,
the Emperor stayed in abstinence at Chóngyuán Diàn,
for he was personally to offer sacrifices at the Southern Suburb on the first day of the first month of the coming year.
At this time, the Emperor was already unwell.
On the day *jiǎxū*,
he stayed overnight at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
At dawn on the day *yǐhài*,
the Emperor personally offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
From the fasting palace, he traveled by palanquin to the temple courtyard,
donned his imperial robe and crown,
and ordered his close officials to assist him in ascending the steps.
(Shēngjiē
was originally written
as "Lùjiē";
now corrected according to the Tōngjiàn and Qìdān Guózhì.
(Adhesive note in the scanned edition))
He only performed the ritual in one chamber,
then bowed his head and retired,
ordering Prince of Jìn to lead the officials to complete the rest of the ceremony.
On this day, the imperial carriage proceeded to the suburban palace.
Shìzōng Ruìwǔ Xiàowén Huángdì,
whose given name was Róng,
was Tàizǔ’s adopted son,
and indeed the nephew of Shèngmù Huánghòu.
His original surname was Chái,
and his father, Shǒulǐ,
was Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo who retired from office.
(According to Lóngpíngjí: The Elder Chái
once lived alone in a room,
and people thought he was involved in dealings with the underworld.
One day,
he laughed uncontrollably.
His wife asked the reason,
but he did not answer.
The elder was fond of wine,
so his wife plied him with wine,
and then he said:
"The Heavenly Emperor has decreed
that Guō Láng shall be the Son of Heaven."
It is considered that the Elder Chái was the father of Shǒulǐ,
whose name is omitted in history.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎo Yì)) The Emperor was born in the eighteenth year of Tiānyòu of Táng,
in the Xīnsì year,
on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, a Bǐngwǔ day,
at a villa in Xíngzhōu.
(Xíngzhōu,
originally written as
"Luòzhōu",
is now corrected according to Wǔdài Huìyào.
(Yǐngkùběn Zhānqiān)) Before reaching adulthood,
he served Shèngmù Huánghòu
at Tàizǔ’s side.
At that time, Tàizǔ had no sons,
and the family fortunes were in decline.
However, because the Emperor was diligent and upright,
Tàizǔ entrusted him with miscellaneous affairs.
The Emperor managed everything with meticulous care,
and the family's resources were saved,
so Tàizǔ loved him dearly
and adopted him as his own son.
At the beginning of Hàn,
Tàizǔ, for his meritorious assistance in establishing the dynasty, became Púmì Fùshǐ,
