and the Emperor was first appointed Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Jiāngjūn.
(According to Guólǎo Tányuàn: Zhōu Shìzōng, when he was a Zhūwèi Jiāngjūn in Hàn,
once traveled to the capital region
and paid a visit to a xiànlìng,
whose name he forgot.
The xiànlìng was then gathering local guests to play dice,
and refused to see him.
Shìzōng held a grudge about this.
When he ascended the throne,
the xiànlìng was implicated in a corruption case involving several hundred bolts of silk while organizing corvée labor.
The prime minister Fán Zhì submitted the completed judicial report.
Shìzōng said:
"An official who governs the people, with such rampant corruption,
should by law be put to death."
Fán Zhì memorialized:
"Accepting property from those under one's jurisdiction is a crime,
but even if the corruption is severe,
the law does not prescribe death."
Shìzōng was angry,
and sternly said:
"Laws have been established by emperors since ancient times,
originally to prevent wrongdoing.
My law to execute corrupt officials
is not cruel punishment."
Zhì replied:
"Your Majesty may execute him,
but if he is handed over to the authorities,
I dare not sign the edict."
So his life was spared.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎo Yì)) In the second year,
Tàizǔ was stationed in Yè,
and the Emperor was appointed Tiānxióng Jūn Yánèi Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
concurrently Guìzhōu Cìshǐ, and Jiǎnjiào Yòu Púshè.
In the winter of the third year,
Tàizǔ marched in to quell internal strife,
leaving the Emperor to guard Yèchéng.
In the first month of Guǎngshùn first year,
Tàizǔ ascended the throne.
The Emperor earnestly requested to come for an audience,
but suddenly dreamed of reaching a river that he could not cross.
Soon after, he was appointed Chánzhōu Jiédùshǐ, Jiǎnjiào Tàibǎo,
and enfeoffed as Tàiyuán Jùnhóu.
While in office,
the Emperor governed with clarity and strictness,
and bandits did not cross the border.
Previously,
the streets and alleys of Chán were narrow and dilapidated,
and public offices were crumbling.
The Emperor immediately widened the streets
and enlarged the government buildings,
which benefited the officials and common people.
(According to Sòng Shǐ Wáng Zàn Zhuàn: Zhōu Shìzōng was stationed in Chányuān,
and every ten days he would preside over criminal cases.
Zàn cited the laws and regulations,
analyzing them with sound reason.
When asked,
it was discovered that he had previously studied extensively,
and he was immediately appointed to a high-ranking position.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎo Yì)) In the first month of the second year,
Mùróng Yànchāo of Yǎnzhōu rebelled.
The Emperor repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to lead an expedition,
and Tàizǔ commended him.
When Cáo Yīng and others marched east,
they achieved nothing for several months.
Tàizǔ wished to lead the campaign himself
and summoned his ministers to discuss the matter.
Prime Minister Féng Dào memorialized that it was the height of summer,
and the imperial carriage should not venture out.
Tàizǔ said:
"The rebels must not be underestimated.
If I cannot go,
I should send the son from Chánzhōu to attack the bandits;
only then will my affairs be settled."
At that time, Púmì Wáng Jùn did not want the Emperor to lead the troops,
so Tàizǔ led the campaign himself.
In the sixth month,
Yǎnzhōu was pacified.
In the twelfth month,
he was promoted to Jiǎnjiào Tàifù and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
In the first month of the third year,
the Emperor came for an audience.
In the third month,
he was appointed Kāifēng Yǐn concurrently Gōngdé Shǐ,
and enfeoffed as Jìn Wáng.
On the Gēngchén day of the first month of Xiǎndé first year,
he was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
(Kāifǔ,
originally written as
"Kāifēng",
is now corrected according to the text.
(Yǐngkùběn Zhānqiān)) Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi, concurrently Shìzhōng,
and remained Kāifēng Yǐn concurrently Gōngdé Shǐ,
presiding over internal and external military affairs.
At that time, Tàizǔ was gravely ill and lingering,
and the gentry and common people were anxious and dejected.
Upon hearing that the Emperor controlled all military power,
they were all pleased.
(According to Lóngpíngjí: Cáo Hàn was subordinate to Shìzōng's staff.
When Shìzōng was stationed in Chányuān,
he made him Yáxiào.
When he became Yǐn of Kāifēng,
Hàn was still in Chányuān.
Upon hearing that Zhōuzǔ was gravely ill,
he came to see Shìzōng without waiting for a summons,
and secretly said:
"As the heir apparent,
if you do not attend to his medical needs,
how will you live up to the expectations of the realm?"
Shìzōng understood,
and entered to attend in the forbidden palace,
entrusting Hàn to manage all matters of the prefecture.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎo Yì)) On the Rénchén day,
Tàizǔ passed away,
and the mourning was kept secret.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
Tàizǔ's dying imperial edict was issued from within the palace:
"Jìn Wáng Róng may ascend the throne before the coffin."
The ministers supported the Emperor in ascending the imperial throne.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Prime Minister Féng Dào led the hundreds of officials to submit a memorial requesting him to attend to state affairs,
which was submitted three times.
On the Rén Yín day,
the Emperor met his ministers under the east wing of the gate of the Wànsuì Diàn.
In the second year of Dàshùn,
Yáng Fùgōng, the Grand Director of the Palace Armies, fell out of favor
and fled to Shānnán.
He occupied Xīngyuán with Yáng Shǒuliàng and rebelled.
Mào Zhēn and Wáng Xíngyú jointly suppressed them.
An imperial edict ordered Chancellor Xú Yànruò to garrison Xīngyuán.
Mào Zhēn defied the edict
and memorialized to have his adopted son Jìhuī appointed as acting military governor.
He adamantly requested the banners and axes of authority,
and Zhāozōng had no choice but to grant them.
From then on, Mào Zhēn, relying on his achievements, became arrogant and unruly,
monopolizing troops and observing for opportunities.
He frequently interfered in court affairs,
and thus began to harbor ambitions of seizing the throne.
Later, he expelled Zhāng Qiú,
the military governor of Jīngyuán,
(Zhāng Qiú,
originally written as
"Zhāng Zhāng",
is now corrected according to the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn. (Sticky note in photocopied edition)) Yáng Shǒuzhōng, the military governor of Yángzhōu, and Mǎn Cún, the prefect of Fèngzhōu,
all of whose territories he seized.
He then memorialized to have his sons and younger brothers appointed as local officials,
which the court was unable to prevent.
When ministers discussed and memorialized about his excesses,
Mào Zhēn would immediately submit a memorial arguing his case,
with language that was not deferential.
The treacherous and wicked then attached themselves to him,
forming a faction,
and court governance thereupon deteriorated.
Zhāozōng, being astute by nature,
would not tolerate his coercion
and wished to launch a punitive expedition.
In the early years of Qiánníng,
he ordered Chancellor Dù Ràngnéng to mobilize troops.
Before the army crossed the border,
it was defeated by Mào Zhēn.
Mào Zhēn, taking advantage of the victory, advanced and encamped at Sānqiáo.
The capital was greatly shaken,
and officials and commoners fled.
The emperor then executed the palace superintendents Xīmén Chóngsuì
and Lǐ Zhōutóng and others to appease him.
Mào Zhēn maintained strict military posture, not relenting,
and his forces were about to point towards the palace gate.
He adamantly declared Ràngnéng's guilt,
stating that only his execution would make him stop.
When Wéi Zhāodù and Lǐ Xī became chancellors,
Mào Zhēn listened to Cuī Zhāowěi's wicked counsel
and once again obstructed their affairs.
He memorialized that Zhāodù and others had no talent for governing,
and should not be placed in high office,
fearing they would bring chaos to the realm.
The imperial edict replied:
"As for military affairs,
I will deliberate with the vassal ministers.
The appointment of chancellors to the court
originates from my own will."
He further requested to appoint Wáng Gǒng as military governor of Hézhōng.
The imperial edict replied:
"Tàiyuán's memorial arrived first,
and Wáng Kē has already been promised the position.
It cannot be changed."
In the fifth month of the second year of Qiánníng,
Mào Zhēn, Wáng Xíngyú, and Hán Jiàn led troops to the capital for an audience.
The capital was terrified.
The Son of Heaven ascended the tower to receive them.
They presented an adamant memorial requesting the execution of Chancellors Wéi Zhāodù and Lǐ Xī to apologize to the world,
and the transfer of Wáng Gǒng to Hézhōng.
After their return,
he left his adopted son Jìpéng to guard the palace,
who was also Yán Guī.
At that time, Emperor Wǔ of Later Táng submitted a memorial
requesting to suppress the three garrisons to pacify Guānfǔ.
In the seventh month of that year,
the Tàiyuán army reached Hézhōng.
Jìpéng and Jìshèng, son of Palace Superintendent Jǐng Xuān, forced the imperial carriage to Fèngxiáng.
Zhāozōng said:
"The Tàiyuán army has not yet arrived,
and the imperial carriage should not be moved rashly.
I will hold the Dà Nèi (Great Inner Palace) with the princes,
while you all pacify the capital.
If Tàiyuán truly arrives,
I can control them with strategy."
Jìpéng, Jǐng Xuān, and Palace Superintendent Luò Quánguàn then set fire to the East Market,
causing a great commotion in the middle of the night.
Zhāozōng ascended the Chéngtiānmén Tower to avoid the chaos,
ordering the commander of the Běngrì Imperial Guards, Lǐ Yún (Note: The Xīn Tángshū and Zīzhì Tōngjiàn both write Lǐ Jūn,
and Hán Jiàn's biography in Xuē Shǐ also writes Lǐ Jūn,
only this biography writes Lǐ Yún.),
to guard the area below the tower.
Jìpéng led his followers to attack Yún.
Zhāozōng leaned on the balustrade to comfort and admonish them.
Jìpéng drew his bow and shouted loudly,
an arrow grazing the imperial robe
and hitting a beam of the tower.
Attendants helped Zhāozōng down the tower and back to the palace.
Jìpéng then set fire to attack the palace gate.
Zhāozōng summoned the princes to discuss their destination.
Lǐ Yún memorialized:
"The situation is urgent.
Please take refuge in my camp for now."
Yún then, with the commander of the Hùbì Imperial Guards, Lǐ Jūnqìng, escorted Zhāozōng out through the Qǐxià Mén
and stopped at Huáyán Sì.
In the late afternoon,
they fled to Shāchéng in Nánshān,
stopping at the Buddhist temple on Shímén Shān.
In that month,
Emperor Wǔ arrived north of the Wèi River.
He sent his deputy, Wáng Guī, to present a memorial to the imperial entourage.
Zhāozōng appointed Emperor Wǔ as the Grand Commander of the Field Army,
to advance and attack Bīn and Qí.
Mào Zhēn, fearful,
executed Jìpéng and Jìshèng,
and submitted a memorial awaiting punishment.
Zhāozōng pardoned him.
Emperor Wǔ said:
"If Mào Zhēn is not executed,
Guānfǔ will never be peaceful."
At that time, those who sided with Mào Zhēn memorialized:
"If Tàiyuán completely destroys Bīn and Qí,
they will surely enter Guānfǔ,
and the capital's worries will be endless."
Thereupon, an edict ordered Emperor Wǔ to make peace with Mào Zhēn.
Then Xíngyú was executed,
Emperor Wǔ returned his army,
and Mào Zhēn's resentment and arrogance remained as before.
In the fifth month of the following year,
an imperial decree appointed Mào Zhēn as military governor of Dōngchuān.
It also ordered Prince Tōng and Prince Tán (Prince Tán,
originally written as
"Prince Tán",
is now corrected according to the New and Old Books of Tang. (Sticky note in photocopied edition))
to lead the imperial guards at the palace gates.
If Mào Zhēn defied the edict,
he would be immediately suppressed.
Mào Zhēn, fearful,
was about to proceed to his post.
When the imperial army reached Xīngpíng,
they panicked and dispersed during the night.
Mào Zhēn seized the opportunity to attack them,
and the government army was utterly defeated.
The imperial carriage hastily fled to Huázhōu.
Mào Zhēn's forces then attacked the capital,
burning down the palaces,
and plundering the markets before departing.
From then on, Cháng'ān's Dà Nèi became utterly desolate.
In the fourth year,
Zhāozōng again ordered Chancellor Sūn Wò to lead an army to suppress him.
Hán Jiàn advised against it,
and had Mào Zhēn submit a memorial requesting exoneration.
During the Guānghuà era,
Mào Zhēn was granted the titles of Shàngshū Lìng and Prince of Qí,
and his son Jìyún was ordered to guard the palace with troops.
Mǎ Xīfàn
During the Tiānfú reign of the Jìn dynasty,
he was appointed Dūtǒng of all circuits south of the Jiāngnán.
He was further promoted to Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn.
Péng Shìchóu (Note: The original text mistakenly wrote
「士秋」 ,
corrected here based on Ouyáng’s historical records and the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) of the Dòngmán people in Xīzhōu, raided Chénzhōu and Lǐzhōu.
Mǎ Xīfàn suppressed them.
Péng Shìchóu offered five prefectures in exchange for an alliance,
which was then inscribed on a bronze pillar.
Mǎ Xīfàn claimed to be a descendant of Fúbō Jūn Yuán of the Hàn dynasty,
and thus cast the bronze pillar to continue his legacy.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 8221.
Note: This biography has missing text.
The complete biographies of Mǎ Xīguǎng and Mǎ Xī'è are lost.)
(Wǔdài Shǐ Bǔ): Gāo Yù was a strategist for Wǔmù Wáng.
Zhuāngzōng had long heard of his name.
When he gained the empire,
he wanted to sow discord between them.
Coincidentally, Wǔmù Wáng sent his son Mǎ Xīfàn to court.
Zhuāngzōng, knowing Mǎ Xīfàn was young and easily provoked,
and seeing his quick and articulate responses,
patted his back and said:
"Everyone says that the Mǎ family's domain will surely be taken by Gāo Yù.
Now with a son like you,
how could Gāo Yù possibly take it!"
Mǎ Xīfàn had always resented Gāo Yù.
Upon hearing Zhuāngzōng's words,
he deeply believed them.
When he returned,
he told Wǔmù Wáng and asked him to execute Gāo Yù.
Wǔmù Wáng laughed and said:
"The Emperor fought battles to gain the empire,
and he is skilled in stratagems.
He wants to use Gāo Yù to build our hegemonic enterprise,
and thus he wants to sow discord between us!
Just like the Liáng dynasty removed Wáng Yànzhāng's military authority.
If one falls for this scheme,
it will surely lead to ruin.
If you execute Gāo Yù now,
you will fall right into his trap.
Do not mention this again."
Mǎ Xīfàn, seeing Wǔmù Wáng's indecision,
feared imminent disaster.
So, he slandered Gāo Yù, accusing him of rebellion, and had his entire clan exterminated.
From then on, the military administration
often fell into disorder,
and those who understood the situation grieved over it.
Initially,
Gāo Yù and Wǔmù Wáng both rose from the ranks.
Gāo Yù was greedy and pretentious.
He often felt that the well at his residence was not clear enough,
and thought of ways to purify it.
So he used silver foil to line its four sides,
from the inside to the outside,
calling it
"Tuòyì."
His extravagance in upkeep
was all of this sort.
Therefore, Zhuāngzōng was able to use this as an instigation.
Later, Gāo Yù was seen in the gloom,
and eventually, he was troubled by it.
Mǎ Xīfàn,
Wǔmù Wáng's legitimate son,
was naturally extravagant.
Not long after inheriting the throne,
he requested to establish officials and subordinates for the Tiāncè Fǔ according to old customs.
Thus, he promoted capable and virtuous officials.

These included Dūtǒng Pànguān Lǐ Duó, Jìngjiāngfǔ Jiédù Pànguān Pān Yù, Wǔ'ān Jūn Jiédù Pànguān Tuòbá Tǎn, Dūtǒng Zhǎngshūjì Lǐ Gāo, Zhènnán Jiédù Pànguān Lǐ Zhuāng, Zhāoshùn Jūn Jiédù Pànguān Xú Shōu, Lǐzhōu Guānchá Pànguān Péng Jìyīng, Jiāngnán Guānchá Pànguān Liáo Tú, Zhāoshùn Jūn Guānchá Pànguān Xú Zhōngyǎ, Jìngjiāngfǔ Zhǎngshūjì Dèng Yìwén, Wǔpíng Jūn Jiédù Zhǎngshūjì Lǐ Sōngnián, Zhènnán Jūn Jiédù Zhǎngshūjì Wèi Yǎn, Zhāoshùn Jūn Guānchá Zhīshǐ Péng Jìxūn, Wǔpíng Jūn Jiédù Tuīguān Xiāo Zhū, Guìguǎn Guānchá Tuīguān Hé Zhòngjǔ, Wǔ'ān Jūn Jiédù Xúnguān Mèng Xuánhuī, Róngguǎn Jiédù Tuīguān Liú Zhāoyǔ, and eighteen others,
all appointed as Xuéshì.
Other military officers,
from Yuán Yǒugōng to Zhāng Shàodí, were all appointed in sequence.
They extensively engaged in construction,
building grand palaces and halls.
The most magnificent among them were the Jiǔlóng and Jīnhuá Halls.
When the halls were completed,
cinnabar was used to paint their walls,
consuming hundreds of thousands of catties of the stone.
Whenever officials came for an audience,
and were about to ascend the hall,
they would feel the pervasive scent of cinnabar
assailing them.
All their expenses were of this kind.
Initially,
after the edict was issued,
the officials in charge looked at each other with worry, as cinnabar was not something that could be obtained quickly.
Not long after,
a mountain collapsed in the eastern territory,
and cinnabar gushed out,
piling up like hills.
Thus, it was collected and used.
When the Qìdān invaded the south,
they heard of this event,
and considered Mǎ Xīfàn an extraordinary person,
hastily sending an envoy to formally invest him as Shàng Wén.
Mǎ Xīfàn received the imperial mandate,
believing that the Qìdān were honoring him,
and joyfully accepted it.
Dīng Sījǐn, who had always possessed talent and strategy,
was a cavalry general for the Mǎ family.
He was deeply ashamed that Mǎ Xīfàn accepted the Qìdān's imperial mandate,
and thus said to Mǎ Xīfàn:
"Now that the court has fallen,
it is the time for loyal ministers and righteous warriors to rise up.
We should send manifestos to all directions,
lead our army directly to the capital,
drive out the Qìdān,
restore the Son of Heaven to his rightful place,
and then return victoriously.
If we do this,
then Qí Huán and Jìn Wén will not be worth mentioning.
The opportunity must not be lost.
I beg Your Royal Highness to plan this urgently."
Mǎ Xīfàn originally lacked long-term strategy,
and moreover, the construction of his official residence was not yet complete,
so he could not bear to abandon it.
He consequently dismissed Dīng Sījǐn's plan.
Dīng Sījǐn was overcome with indignation
and said to his confidants:
"The ancients lamented that their names were not recognized after death.
Now, facing such turmoil,
I cannot achieve great deeds for the empire.
Instead, I am concerned about a few houses!
This is truly lamentable."
From then on, Dīng Sījǐn was often dejected.
Wénzhāo Wáng's wife, Lady Péng,
was enfeoffed as Qínguó Fūrén.
She often went to the Bàobēnsì temple north of the city to burn incense.
At that time, a leading monk, referred to as the Elder,
asked her:
"Whose family's woman is the Lady?"
Lady Péng was greatly angered.
She snatched her sedan chair and rushed back home.
Wénzhāo Wáng was surprised and asked:
"Why have you returned so quickly?"
The Lady said:
"Today was truly unlucky.
I was asked by an old bald villain, 'whose family's woman is this concubine?'
This is generally an impolite way to address a woman,
how could he say that to me!"
Wénzhāo Wáng laughed and said:
"This is what is called a 'Zen opportunity.'
Lady, you should have replied, 'this disciple is a daughter of the Péng family,
and a wife of the Mǎ family.'
Then you would have understood its meaning.
Why be angry?"
The Lady, who had always been intelligent,
was ashamed that she couldn't answer.
So she said:
"In that case, this concubine truly has no insight into her nature."
She then felt ashamed and embarrassed for several days.
Shí Wéndé
was from Liánzhōu.
He was short and ugly,
but fond of learning,
and particularly skilled in poetry.
During the reign of the Hegemonic Kingdom,
he repeatedly presented poems seeking employment.
Wénzhāo Wáng, considering his humble appearance,
never treated him with respect.
Consequently, Shí Wéndé remained in poverty.
There was a prince, Nánzhái Wángzǐ,
who always valued scholars
and invited him to his retinue.
Later, Wénzhāo Wáng learned of this,
and also became angry at Nánzhái Wángzǐ,
intending to publicly humiliate Shí Wéndé and banish him.
Not long after,
Qínguó Fūrén Lady Péng passed away.
Wénzhāo Wáng was deeply saddened,
and ordered all scholars to compose eulogies.
Shí Wéndé also submitted more than ten pieces.
One couplet read:
"The moon sets over the cold Xiāngpǔ,
flowers wither in the autumn of the Hàn palace."
Wénzhāo Wáng was greatly astonished when he read it,
and exclaimed:
"Shí Wéndé has such literary talent!
I merely slighted him for his humble appearance.
I am not as discerning as that boy Nángōng, who recognized his worth!"
Thereupon, he finally summoned Shí Wéndé and apologized to him with shame.
Not long after,
he was appointed Yuánwàiláng of the Ministry of Public Works
and made Governor of Róngzhōu.
Shí Wéndé was particularly fond of writing in his later years,
and he compiled the Dàtáng Xīnzǎnn, thirteen volumes.
It contained many anecdotes of famous people.
Although the writing was not exquisite,
the events were often worth noting.
At the time, he was praised for his extensive knowledge.
Hé Zhòngjǔ
was from Yíngdào.
He had a beautiful appearance,
and at thirteen,
he was exceptionally outstanding.
At that time, his family was poor,
and he failed to pay taxes by the deadline.
Lǐ Gāo was the Magistrate of Yíngdào,
angrily,
he was then collared and jailed,
about to be flogged.
Someone then spoke to Lǐ Gāo, saying:
"Although this fellow is young,
he can compose poetry,
often completing it on the spot.
I hope the Illustrious Prefect will take a look at him."
Lǐ Gāo heard this,
and immediately summoned him, asking:
"I know you are literate,
and also quick-witted.
Regarding today's matter,
if you can write a piece without revision,
a self-description,
I will pardon you."
Zhòngjǔ took up his brush and finished it,
saying:
"Like jade, I came to prison,
leaving home to don the cangue.
Pitiable are these two pieces of wood,
clamping a single flower."
Lǐ Gāo was greatly astonished,
and personally freed him from the cangue,
inviting him to the main hall to treat him with equal courtesy.
From then on, Zhòngjǔ began to earnestly devote himself to study.
During the Tiānchéng reign,
he entered Luòyáng.
At that time, Qín Wáng was the Prefect of Hénán,
and especially esteemed scholars.
Zhòngjǔ, along with Zhāng Háng and Jiāng Wénwèi, all frequented his gate.
When he was recommended to the east,
hundreds of people were publicly nominated,
but only Zhòngjǔ was considered to have excelled.
Zhòngjǔ then presented a poem, saying:
"As verses of emerald clouds leave my hand,
immortals of the Purple Palace all nod in approval."
Qín Wáng was greatly pleased,
praising him without end,
and thus he passed the examination on the first attempt.
Upon his return,
he met Wénzhāo Mǎ Shì who was acting as regent.
Following the precedent of Táng Tàizōng,
eighteen scholars were appointed to the Tiāncè Fǔ.
He was made the head of the scholars,
and also held the reins of government.
However, Zhòngjǔ, considering himself to be a protégé of Lǐ Gāo,
even after gaining official recognition in the central court,
never slackened in his service to Lǐ Gāo.
Lǐ Gāo was moved and pleased,
and thus further promoted him.
Before long,
he was ranked alongside Lǐ Gāo.
When he was sent out,
he also served as Prefect of Quán and Héng prefectures.
Previously,
Húnán was particularly rich in poets.
The most prominent among them were Shěn Bīn, Liáo Níng, Liú Zhāoyǔ, Shàng Yán, Qí Jǐ, and Xū Zhōng,
but Zhòngjǔ was considered particularly shallow among these gentlemen.
Only Lǐ Gāo alone highly praised him,
often reciting his poem "Autumn Day's Evening View" to the public, saying:
"Trees greet high birds returning to the deep wilderness,
clouds accompany the setting sun past distant mountains."
He would tap the ground with his foot,
and sigh, saying:
"Hé Zhòngjǔ is truly a transcendent and elegant poet!
When officials judge acceptance or rejection,
the rest are mere servants,
only occasional talents."
Therefore, Zhòngjǔ was grateful for Lǐ Gāo's recognition,
and was finally able to exert himself,
maintaining his reputation and integrity,
unblemished from beginning to end.
Critics regarded Lǐ Gāo as having the discerning eye to recognize talent.
Ōuyáng Bīn was
a native of Héngshān.
His family had been county clerks for generations,
but Ōuyáng Bīn was particularly fond of learning,
and skilled in prose and poetry.
When the Mǎ family established their rule in Húnán,
Ōuyáng Bīn intended to seek their employment,
so he carried his writings to the yamen
to request an audience.
It was necessary to first submit a calling card.
There was a clerk in charge of guests,
whom everyone called Fán Zhīkè.
He loved bribes,
and secretly sent someone to tell Ōuyáng Bīn:
"Your arrival
is not without purpose;
you truly wish to distinguish your family and make a career for yourself.
If you do not offer anything as a gift,
how can this be?"
Ōuyáng Bīn was ashamed to advance through bribery,
and ultimately gave nothing.
Afterward, Fán Shì became angry,
and threw the calling card to the ground, saying:
"How can the son of a petty official wish to seek an audience with princes and marquises!"
Ōuyáng Bīn deeply resented this,
and thereupon retired to compose a poem, saying:
"No money to beg Fán Zhīkè,
my calling card sprouted hair, unannounced."
Consequently, he became down-and-out in the streets,
cavorting with singing girls and drunkards
without restraint.
There was a singer named Ruìqīng,
who admired his talent,
and so invited him to her home.
Ruìqīng was a skilled singer,
and every year on Wǔmù Wáng's birthday,
she would sing at the banquet.
At that time, Húnán, in addition to its original seven prefectures,
had added Wǔlíng and Yuèyáng,
making it nine prefectures.
Ōuyáng Bīn composed the "Song of the Nine Prefectures" and gave it to Ruìqīng,
telling her to sing it at the appointed time,
hoping to move Wǔmù Wáng.
However, he was ultimately not recognized,
and Ōuyáng Bīn sighed, saying:
"At a time when the world is fragmented,
even common laborers can exert themselves.
Am I poor to this extent!"
Having no other recourse,
he thought of fleeing to a neighboring region,
but had nowhere in mind yet.
Not long after,
he heard that a convoy to Xīshǔ was about to depart,
so Ōuyáng Bīn decided to plan his journey to Shǔ,
and privately said to Ruìqīng:
"I have been living in your home because my attempts to gain an audience failed,
and you have never shown weariness.
How can I lightly abandon you!
However, a scholar lives for fame and achievement,
and if I do not pursue it now,
I fear I will regret it later.
Now that I am going elsewhere,
I hope to achieve something.
Do not worry about it."
Ruìqīng said:
"You cannot be said to be without affection for me,
but if you suddenly do not allow me to hold you back,
and leave out of love,
is it not that fame and fortune are about to arrive!
I am truly surprised by this.
My family wealth is about several strings of cash;
although not abundant,
I wish to divide it in half
to assist with your journey."
Ōuyáng Bīn did not decline,
and used all that Ruìqīng had given him to bribe the convoy officials,
requesting to be a boatman.
The convoy officials agreed.
When he arrived in Shǔ,
he presented his "Rhapsody on a Lone Carp Facing Heaven,"
and the Lord of Shǔ was greatly pleased,
promoting him to an important position.
Later, he rose to the position of Minister of the Left,
and was then sent out as Military Governor of Kuízhōu.
After taking charge of Kuízhōu,
Wǔmù Wáng had already passed away,
and his son Xīfàn succeeded him.
He then sent a letter to Xīfàn,
recounting the reasons for his journey to Shǔ in the past,
and entrusting him with the care of his relatives in Héngshān.
Xīfàn felt great shame upon receiving the letter,
and all of Ōuyáng Bīn's relatives and friends were exempted from taxes and labor service.
An order was issued to seek out talented individuals in the wilderness,
whereupon all scholars, whether virtuous or not,
were welcomed and treated as guests,
all due to Ōuyáng Bīn.
Ōuyáng Bīn had an elegant demeanor,
and his prose was accessible and his reasoning true.
Even those who were unlettered, upon hearing it,
would readily understand,
and it was through this that he achieved success.
Dài Yǎn was
a native of Jīnlíng.
He could compose poetry,
and was particularly fond of admonishing through satire.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, caught in turmoil,
he traveled to Xiāngzhōng.
It was during the Mǎ family's reign,
and Wénzhāo Wáng came to power as a prince,
being particularly fond of extravagance.
He built the Tiāncè Fǔ,
constructing the Jiǔlóng, Jīnhuá, and other palaces.
The work of carpentry and masonry,
the sounds of axes and chisels,
continued day and night without ceasing.
Dài Yǎn disapproved of this,
calling himself Xuánhuángzǐ,
and composed a hundred "Fisherman's Poems" which he presented,
intending to satirize him.
Thus, some of his lines were:
"Just swallowed the world down their throat,
it is due to extravagance that danger and ruin come."
He also said:
"If you must discard it, then discard it,
do not wait until the wind is high and the water is deep."
Mǎ Xī’è (馬希萼) was greatly pleased,
and so, combining with Kě Qióng's (可瓊) forces, he drove straight in.
Mǎ Xīguǎng (馬希廣) had always revered the Buddha.
When he heard of this,
he could think of no solution.
So he donned a monk's robe and led a group of monks to recite
"Bǎoshèng Rúlái" (寶勝如來),
calling it a prayer to ward off disaster.
A moment later,
fire broke out in the prefectural office,
and people suddenly fell into chaos,
yet the sound of their chanting did not cease.
Such was his foolishness.
Shǎo Díyōu (少敵憂) worried about him,
and there was good reason for it.
Before this,
the streets within the city still had locust trees planted,
with hardly one or two willow trees.
By this time, inside and out, everything had changed, and only willow trees were planted,
with no more locust trees.
Moreover, residents were fond of weaving straw sandals at night,
making a sound like beating straw,
which could be heard in the suburbs.
Soon there was a children's rhyme that went:
"The city of Húnán (湖南) has good long streets,
planted entirely with willows, not locusts.
The common people flee with nothing to do,
just beating straw and weaving straw sandals."
Everyone, young and old, recited it.
Not long after, the country fell into chaos,
the common people fled,
and eight or nine out of ten died in ditches.
It was only then that commentators began to understand.
For "long streets" (長街) meant
roads connecting the inside and outside;
"locust" (槐)
was a homophone for "懷" (huái), meaning "cherish" or "fraternal affection"
not planting locusts
meant that brothers were not harmonious,
leading to the downfall of the state
and the loss of fraternal affection.
"Straw sandals" (草鞋)
were used for long journeys,
symbolizing the common people traveling far and fleeing.
After Mǎ Xī’è (馬希萼) ascended the throne,
he did not attend to state affairs,
often indulging in drinking with his officials.
There was a minor official named Xiè Tíngzé (謝廷擇),
originally a stableboy under his tent.
He had a good appearance,
and Xī’è (希萼) had always favored him
At every banquet,
Tíngzé (廷擇) was ordered to sit at the table,
while many officials were placed below him.
Consequently, the衆眾were enraged,
often whispering among themselves:
"According to the old rules for these people,
at banquets,
they were only used as soldiers to guard the gates
to prevent other troubles.
Now they are ranked alongside us,
what an extreme humiliation!"
His younger brother, Mǎ Xīchóng (馬希崇), taking advantage of the general anger and resentment,
secretly launched a coup with his faction,
captured Xī’è (希萼) and imprisoned him in Héngyáng (衡陽),
and then crowned himself.
Before many days passed,
Jiāngnán (江南) sent Yuánzhōu (袁州) prefect Biān Hào (邊鎬) to lead troops to attack amidst the chaos.
Xīchóng (希崇) judged that he could not resist
and consequently surrendered.
Before this,
a children's rhyme in Chángshā (長沙) went:
"Whip the horse,
no time to flee."
Not long after,
it was indeed destroyed by Biān Hào (邊鎬).
Initially,
Hào (鎬) had once been a monk,
to spy on Húnán (湖南).
He was particularly skilled at playing cymbals.
Every morning, he would play cymbals and beg for alms,
and whenever he encountered a city, he would often toss the cymbals up to gauge the height of the gates.
When he came to Húnán (湖南),
many gentry and commoners recognized him.
The Liáo (廖) clan were
people from Gànxiàn (贛縣) in Qiánzhōu (虔州).
They had three sons:
the eldest was Tǔ (圖),
the second was Yǎn (偃),
and the youngest was Níng (凝).
Tǔ (圖) and Níng (凝) both had reputations for poetry,
while Yǎn (偃) was exceptionally brave and strong,
and thus arrogant and unruly,
feared by his鄉里.
Jiāngnán (江南) appointed the meritorious minister Zhōng Zhāng (鐘章) as Qiánzhōu (虔州) prefect
He deeply resented them,
so Tǔ (圖) and Níng (凝) and others discussed, saying:
"Looking at Zhāng's (章) actions,
he only wants to exterminate our clan.
If we cling to this land and do not leave,
disaster will soon befall us."
So they led their clan and their subordinates, over three thousand people,
fully armed and with proper commands, and then departed.
Zhāng (章) dared not pursue them,
so they fled to Húnán (湖南)
At that time, King Wǔmù (武穆王) was on the throne.
Seeing their large numbers,
he feared they would be difficult to control
and wanted to execute them all.
Someone said:
"Your Majesty's surname is Mǎ (馬),
and Liáo (廖) has come to surrender.
Liáo (廖) sounds like 'liào' (料), meaning 'fodder'.
A horse that gets fodder will surely grow fat.
This is truly a sign of the state's great prosperity.
How can they be killed?"
Wǔmù (武穆) was pleased
and treated them well.
He then issued an order appointing Níng (凝) as Yǒngzhōu (永州) prefect,
Tǔ (圖) as Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬),
and Yǎn (偃) as a commander in the Tiāncè Fǔ (天策府)
They were also granted estates in Héngshān (衡山),
where Yǎn (偃) called himself an "eremite."
Yǎn (偃) was able to stand upright on horseback,
take off a wet garment, shake it out, and put it on,
to demonstrate his agility.
Gāo Jìxīng's (高季興) second son from Jīngnán (荊南),
whose name is forgotten,
commanded the imperial guard regiment Yúnměng Dū (雲猛都),
and was called
"Yúnměng Lángjūn" (雲猛郎君).
Hearing of Yǎn's (偃) reputation,
and as the two territories were engaged in warfare,
he requested to fight Yǎn (偃).
Yǎn (偃) eagerly went.
Yúnměng (雲猛) was skilled with a spear.
Seeing Yǎn (偃) was thin and small,
he underestimated him.
He galloped his horse and thrust at Yǎn (偃).
Just as it was about to reach him,
Yǎn (偃) feigned falling from his horse.
Yúnměng (雲猛) had no time to stop his momentum.
Yǎn (偃) from behind struck him with a ge (戈) and knocked him to the ground,
and thus captured him alive.
From then on, Yǎn's (偃) reputation grew even greater.
Therefore, King Wǔmù (武穆王) was never underestimated by neighboring states throughout his life,
thanks to Yǎn's (偃) strength.
When his son, Mǎ Xīfàn (馬希範), succeeded to the throne,
the Barbarians of Jiǔxī (九溪蠻) rebelled.
Yǎn (偃) was ordered to lead troops to suppress them,
but he was wounded by a stray arrow
and died among the Barbarians.
When the grim news arrived,
Xīfàn (希範) sent someone to inform Yǎn's (偃) mother, Zhāng (張)氏.
Zhāng (張)氏 did not weep,
but said to the messenger:
"Please thank His Majesty for me, your concubine.
Our whole family of over three hundred mouths
has received the king's bounty of food and clothing.
Even if we all died, it would not be enough to repay him,
how much less one son!
I hope His Majesty will not dwell on it."
Xīfàn (希範) heard this and sighed, saying:
"The Liáo (廖) clan has such a mother;
how could they not prosper!"
Thus, he generously cared for them
and then sent an envoy to summon Níng (凝),
appointing him as an aide.
When Xīfàn (希範) died,
the state fell into chaos
and was destroyed by Jiāngnán (江南).
Níng (凝) was then moved to Jīnlíng (金陵).
The Southern Táng (唐) ruler appointed him as the Assistant Director of the Bureau of Waterways (Shuǐbù Yuánwàiláng 水部員外郎)
and Prefect of Liánchāng County (連昌縣令) in Hóngzhōu (洪州).
Not long after,
he was again transferred to be Commander of the Militia (Tuánliàn Shǐ 團練使) in Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Níng (凝) was uninhibited and
fond of humor.
He once read Péi Yuè's (裴說) poem "On Dù Gōngbù's (杜工部) Tomb," which said:
"I intend to break open this lonely tomb,
and let the great master be reborn."
He then said:
"If so,
Péi Yuè (裴說) is a grave robber!"
Those who heard him laughed.
While in Jiāngzhōu (江州),
during the height of summer,
he often suffered from dry skin.
So he would fill a large tub with cold water
and sit in it,
sometimes for the entire day.
Even when guests or friends visited,
he would stick out his head and chat and laugh with them.
Such was his casualness.
Before this,
Níng (凝) had once dreamed that someone bestowed an official seal upon him.
As he bowed to receive it,
one corner of the seal was missing.
Níng (凝) could not interpret it.
When he received the appointment to Jiāngzhōu (江州),
Qián Liú died on the twenty-eighth day of the third month of the third year of Chángxīng,
aged eighty-one.
An imperial edict stated:
"The late Commander-in-Chief of all military forces under Heaven, Shàngfù, King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú,
was a veteran elder of several dynasties,
a meritorious and virtuous figure of his time.
His position had reached the pinnacle for a subject,
and his name was always held high in historical records.
Since there are no higher titles or ranks to bestow in a posthumous honorific ceremony,
it is fitting to demonstrate exceptional reverence through a change of name.
The relevant office should be ordered to determine his posthumous title,
bury him with royal rites,
and also grant a spirit-way stele."
His posthumous title was Wǔsù.
When Qián Liú first served Dǒng Chāng,
he was then just in the prime of his manhood,
and his nature was still stern and fiery.
At that time, a scholar came to visit the chief commander,
and having already presented his card,
he saw Qián Liú appear somewhat lax.
Qián Liú grew angry,
and threw him into the Luóchà Jiāng.
When the usher was about to announce him,
Qián Liú falsely said:
"The guest has already brushed his clothes and left."
Later, when he became a commander,
someone presented a poem that read:
"A river flows before the railing."
Qián Liú was displeased,
believing it to be a satire of himself,
and soon had him killed.
It was not until his later years
that he began to love people and treat scholars with respect,
focusing his mind on the Way.
For several decades,
he was highly praised.
Qián Liú especially relied on his grandeur and prosperity,
dividing the two Zhè regions into several garrisons,
whose administration and control he would sign off on before reporting.
His immediate circle and those around him were all his sons, grandsons, nephews, and grandnephews.
The decorations of his palace and his attire
rivaled those of a king.
The common folk of the two Zhè regions
all called him "Hǎilóng Wáng" (Dragon King of the Sea).
During the Kāipíng era of the Liáng dynasty,
the people of Zhè appealed,
requesting to erect a shrine for Qián Liú while he was still alive.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng granted this,
ordering Hanlín scholar Lǐ Qí (Lǐ Qí,
originally written as
"Lǐ Qí,"
now corrected according to the Tōngjiàn.
(Photocopy notes)) to compose the stele for the living shrine, which was bestowed upon him.
To this day, the common people offer sacrifices to him,
and his descendants preserve it.
He was indeed a renowned king of recent times.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 18125.)
Qián Yuánguàn was
Qián Liú's fifth son.
He started his career as an inspector for salt and iron transport and distribution,
and was officially appointed Minister of the Treasury, Langzhong,
and granted the Jinzi (purple robe with gold ornaments).
In the Tiānfù era,
the local subordinate officers Xǔ Zàisī and others revolted,
colluding with Tián Yūn, the Military Governor of Xuānzhōu.
Tián Yūn led his troops and arrived suddenly.
Qián Liú defeated Xǔ Zàisī
and made peace with Tián Yūn.
Tián Yūn sought an alliance with Qián Liú.
Qián Liú summoned all his sons and asked them:
"Who among you can become a son-in-law to the Tián clan for me?"
They all showed reluctance.
At that time, Yuánguàn was sixteen years old,
and stepped forward, saying:
"Only by Your Majesty's command."
Thus, he went to Xuānzhōu to marry.
In the early Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty,
he was successively promoted by imperial order to Acting Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs, and Commander of the Inner Palace Guard.
Within a few years,
he fought against rebels and resisted invaders,
achieving great merits and achievements.
In the summer of the fourth year of Zhēnmíng of the Liáng dynasty,
Qián Liú launched a major campaign against Wú,
appointing Yuánguàn as Commander-in-Chief of all naval forces.
When the war fleet reached Dōngzhōu,
the Wú people resisted with their navy.
Yuánguàn used fire rafts and, with the wind, spread ash to envelop them,
making it appear like mist in broad daylight.
The Wú forces lost their way
and were defeated.
They captured Commander Péng Yànzhāng (Péng Yànzhāng,
the original text omitted the character
"zhāng,"
now added according to the Jiǔguó Zhì.
(Photocopy notes)) and over seventy military officers,
and obtained four hundred warships.
The Wú people, knowing they could not contend,
made peace with Qián Liú.
For his achievements, Yuánguàn was appointed Deputy Military Governor of Zhènhǎi Command and Acting Sītú.
At the end of the Liáng dynasty,
he was promoted to Military Governor of Qīnghǎi Command, Acting Tàifù, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
In the early Tóngguāng era of the Later Táng dynasty,

he was additionally appointed Acting Tàishī, concurrently Minister of the Department of State Affairs, and Commissioner of Military Governor of Zhèndōng and other commands, and Surveillance and Disposition.
At that time, Qián Liú was himself the Commander-in-Chief of all military forces under Heaven, Shàngfù, Keeper of the Minister of the Department of State Affairs, and King of Wúyuè.
When Qián Liú retired as Tàishī,
Yuánguàn repeatedly submitted memorials
requesting the restoration of his old titles.
Emperor Míngzōng of Táng granted this.
As Qián Liú was advanced in age,
he wished to establish an heir.
He summoned his sons, asking each to state his merits,
and requested them to yield to Yuánguàn.
When Qián Liú was gravely ill,
he summoned his generals and officials and said to them:
"My illness will not allow me to recover.
My sons are all foolish and weak,
and I fear they cannot be your commander.
I am parting with you all.
You must choose your commander yourselves."
The generals and officials wept, saying:
"Your Excellency has military merits,
is virtuous and filial,
and already governs two garrisons.
Why does Your Majesty say such things?"
Qián Liú asked:
"Is this one truly capable or not?"
They replied:
"We all wish to serve the virtuous commander."
Immediately, several baskets of seals and keys were brought out before them,
and Qián Liú said to Yuánguàn:
"The three armies say you are worthy to be served.
Take these."
After Qián Liú died,
Yuánguàn consequently succeeded to his father's position.
In the fourth year of Chángxīng of the Táng dynasty,
the Director of the Department of Works, Lǐ Lín (The original text omitted the two characters
"Lǐ Lín,"
now added according to the Tōngjiàn.
(Photocopy notes)), was sent to reinstate Yuánguàn's official titles and ranks.
He also ordered Minister of Revenue Zhāng Wénbǎo to bestow upon him the concurrent title of Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
In the early Qīngtài era,
he was enfeoffed as King of Wú.
In the second year,
he was enfeoffed as King of Yuè.
In the first year of Tiānfú,
he was granted a gold seal.
In the third year,
he was enfeoffed as King of Wúyuè.
In the fifth year,
he was given the additional title of Commander-in-Chief of all military forces under Heaven.
In the sixth year,
he was granted the title of Commander-in-Chief of all military forces under Heaven.
In the summer of that year, he fell ill.
In autumn, his official residence suffered a fire,
burning completely to ashes.
He then moved to another place,
but the flames followed and erupted there as well.
Yuánguàn, due to shock and fright, went mad,
and died on the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month of that year,
aged fifty-five.
His posthumous title was Wénmù.
Yuánguàn was intelligent and sensitive as a child,
and adept at governance and management as an adult.
He commanded armies for fifteen years,
making decisions with divine speed,
and was supported by the military and civilians.
However, his extravagance and construction projects
surpassed those of his father,
hence the disaster of fire.
Yuánguàn had a thousand poems,
and the most excellent three hundred were compiled
and named the Jǐnlóu Jí (Collection from the Brocade Tower).
Scholars in the Zhè region all circulated it.
His son, Zuǒ, succeeded him.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 4692.)
Qián Zuǒ,
courtesy name Xuán-yòu.
When Yuán-guàn passed away,
he succeeded to his position.
At the end of the Tiān-fú era of the Jìn dynasty,
an imperial edict appointed him Grand Preceptor of Inspection, concurrent Chancellor, King of Wúyuè.
He was also bestowed with a jade tablet engraved for the appointment.
Among the jade tablets of previous dynasties,
there was one for enfeoffing King Yí.
During the period of the false Liáng, wanting to treat Qián Liú generously,
they first set this as a precedent,
so it was adopted without change.
Soon after, he was appointed Grand Master of the Palace with Ceremonial Privileges, and Acting Grand Commandant.
At that time, Jiàn'ān was attacked by the Huái bandits,
so he was appointed Grand Marshal of the Armies of the Southeast.
Qián Zuǒ immediately dispatched a naval force to suppress them.
The Huái people were greatly defeated,
and for this achievement, he was promoted to Acting Grand Preceptor.
When Emperor Gāo of Hàn entered Biàn,
Qián Zuǒ was the first to offer tribute and gifts,
leading the way for the eastern regions.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn commended him,
appointing him Grand Marshal of the Armies of all Circuits.
Qián Zuǒ governed his territory for seven years.
The region was prosperous.
Three generations of his ancestors had all been marshals,
which was considered an honor at the time.
In the early Hàn dynasty,
he died in office due to illness.
His posthumous title was Zhōng-xiàn.
Qián Zuǒ loved books from a young age,
and was gentle and respectful by nature.
He was skilled at composing five- or seven-character poems.
Whenever his officials encountered beautiful scenes of snow or moonlight,
he would always host a banquet for them to enjoy together.
Because of this, scholars were devoted to him.
His officials also had registered titles below Chancellor,
but their salaries were very meager,
making it difficult for them to support themselves.
Whenever an official from the imperial court arrived,
they would abolish their false titles.
If they met for an assembly, the ducal residence would provide them with servants and horses.
Their handling of affairs was often petty
and similar to these examples.
However, the income from sea trade,
contributed millions annually.
When an imperial envoy arrived,
the gifts bestowed were extensive.
Therefore, the imperial court favored him,
making him the foremost among all the regional rulers.
Qián Zuǒ had a son, Yù,
who was five years old
and not yet capable of handling state affairs.
So his younger brother, Zōng, succeeded to the throne.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 4692.)
Qián
Zōng was
intelligent, astute, and resolute by nature.
Before he came to power,
he often felt that because Qián Zuǒ was lenient and benevolent,
those in charge of military power would be difficult to control.
When he replaced Qián Zuǒ as marshal,
he disciplined his subordinates with strict etiquette and laws,
and did not show excessive courtesy
to veteran generals or old meritorious officials.
General Hú Jìn-sī was quite displeased with him,
and secretly plotted with the imperial guards to remove Zōng.
In the twelfth month
of the year Emperor Gāo of Hàn entered Biàn,
Jìn-sī led three hundred armored soldiers, making a great clamor,
and burst into the government office.
Zōng closed the door to resist them.
His attendants fought them,
but were all killed by Jìn-sī.
Zōng was then moved to a separate residence,
escorted by armored guards,
and confined in Jǐn-jūn.
(Jǐn-jūn
should probably be
"Yì-jǐn-jūn".
Examination of the Cèfǔ Yuánguī citing Xuē-shǐ also has "Jǐn-jūn",
so we retain the original here.
(Photocopy notes))
Jìn-sī then installed Zōng's half-brother, Chǔ, as marshal.
In the fourth month of the summer of that year,
Jìn-sī died from a carbuncle on his back.
The Yuè people rejoiced,
believing it to be a punishment from the spirits for his treachery.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 4692.)
Qián
Chǔ was
the son of Yuán-guàn and
Zōng's half-brother.
After Zōng was confined by the military officers,
Chǔ was at the time the Prefect of Wēn-zhōu.
The people, being without a marshal,
welcomed and installed him.
This was on the fifteenth day of the first month of the first year of Qián-yòu of the Hàn dynasty.
In the eighth month of that year,
he was first appointed Grand Preceptor of Inspection, concurrent Chancellor,
and concurrently Commissioner of the Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng Armies, and Grand Marshal of the Armies of the Southeast.
In the Guǎngshùn era of the Zhōu dynasty,
he was successively promoted to Acting Grand Minister of Education, Chancellor, and King of Wúyuè.
In the early Jiànlóng era of the Imperial Dynasty,
he was again granted the title of Grand Marshal of the Armies of All Under Heaven.
His later affairs are detailed in the Imperial Dynasty's Daily Records.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 4692.)
(Wǔdài Shǐ Bǔ: After Qián Liú was enfeoffed as King of Wúyuè,
he extensively built government offices.
The sound of construction and axes
was incessant day and night.
The soldiers grumbled and complained.
Some would secretly write in white chalk on the gate in the middle of the night:
"No end in sight,
rise early,
return late."
When Liú saw it, he was delighted,
and immediately ordered a scribe to also write a few characters in white chalk beside it:
"No end in sight,
no sooner are spring clothes finished than winter clothes appear."
People at the time considered it divine assistance,
and from then on, the complaints ceased.
Monk Zhāo,
who was skilled in divination,
resided in the Two Zhè regions
and was greatly honored by Qián Liú of Qiántáng,
who called him the State Preceptor.
One day, when he visited Liú,
a small palace child was playing nearby,
and dropped dozens of coins.
Liú saw this
and said to the child:
"Quickly pick them up, lest someone steps on and breaks your coins."
Master Zhāo smiled and said:
"For your coins to be broken by stepping on them,
it would require an ox."
Liú was pleased,
interpreting it as a symbol of the stability of his state.
Later, by the time of his great-grandson, Chǔ,
the entire clan submitted to the court,
and thus the kingdom was abolished.
Chǔ's birth year belonged to the ox zodiac,
so it could be said that an ox broke the coins.
In his later years, Qián Liú suffered from problems with both eyes.
A physician, whose origin was unknown,
claimed to be from a family that had for generations treated internal and external eye diseases.
His technique was particularly skilled with needles,
and always effective.
Liú heard of this,
summoned him, and had him examine his eyes.
The physician said:
"It can be treated.
However, Your Majesty is no ordinary person;
this ailment is probably given by Heaven.
If I treat it,
it would go against the natural order
and might not benefit your lifespan.
Please consider this carefully."
Liú said:
"I rose from the ranks of soldiers,
and have occupied this region.
My wealth and status are sufficient.
As long as I can see with both eyes,
wouldn't it still be enjoyable to be a ghost!"
Immediately, he commenced the treatment,
and all were instantly and completely effective.
Liú was delighted,
and the rewards he bestowed were in the tens of thousands.
The physicians all declined to accept them.
The following year,
Liú died.
Monk Qì-yíng,
a native of Mǐn-zhōng,
was well-versed in both internal and external studies,
and especially sharp and quick-witted.
In the early Guǎngshùn era,
he was traveling in Qiántáng.
One day,
he accompanied the King of Wúyuè on an outing to the Bìlàng Pavilion.
At that time, the tide had just come in,
and boats converged,
their bow and stern unseen from afar.
The King happily said:
"Wúyuè is over three thousand *lǐ* from the capital,
yet who knew the benefit of a single waterway could be so great!"
Qì-yíng replied:
"It can be described as 'a single waterway three thousand *lǐ* away,
with two tides in twelve hours.'"
People at the time considered it an excellent couplet.
At that time, Jiāngnán was not yet accessible,
so tribute from the Two Zhè regions reached Qīng-zhōu by sea,
hence the mention of three thousand *lǐ*.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day of the sixth month,
Wáng Jǐng (王景), Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng, was appointed Military Commissioner of Qínzhōu,
concurrently serving as Commander-in-Chief of the Western Frontier Patrol.
Xiàng Xùn (向訓), Director of the Southern Bureau of the Privy Council and Military Commissioner of Chénzhōu, was appointed Military Commissioner of Huáinán,
retaining his former post as Director of the Southern Bureau of the Privy Council,
and promoted to concurrently hold the title of acting Grand Commandant (*Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi*).
Hán Tōng (韓通), Military Commissioner of Cáozhōu, was appointed Military Commissioner of Xǔzhōu,
and promoted to concurrently hold the title of acting Grand Commandant.
Wáng Quánbīn (王全斌), Defense Commissioner of Bózhōu, was appointed Defense Commissioner of Lǒngzhōu,
remotely holding the posts of Provisional Administrator of Lìzhōu and Zhāowǔ Army.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Wáng Yànchāo (王彥超) of Xǔzhōu was transferred to command the Yǒngxīng Army,
and Tián Jǐngxián (田景咸) of Dèngzhōu was transferred to command Fūzhōu.
Yáng Zhāojiǎn (楊昭儉), Palace Censor-in-Chief; Zhào Lì (趙礪), Investigating Censor-in-Chief; and Zhāng Jiū (張糺), Investigating Censor, were all dismissed from their posts,
due to their failure to ascertain the facts in a judicial inquiry.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Táo Gǔ (陶穀), Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, was appointed Vice Minister of the Ministry of War,
and made Chief Academician of the Hanlin Academy.
Hù Zài (扈載), Director of the Bureau of Waterways and Draftsman for Imperial Edicts, and Wáng Zhù (王著), Director of the Bureau of Finance,
(Wáng Zhù,
originally written as
"Wáng Shǔ" (王署),
is now corrected according to the *Sòng Shǐ*.
(Adhesive note in facsimile edition)) were both appointed Hanlin Academicians, retaining their current official ranks.
Gāo Fáng (高防), Palace Counselor, was appointed Right Remonstrance Official (*Yòu Sànqí Chángshì*).
Xuē Jūzhèng (薛居正), former Director of the Bureau of Judicial Affairs and Draftsman for Imperial Edicts, was appointed Left Grand Master of Remonstrance (*Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū*),
and made Academician of the Zhāowén Hall,
supervising its affairs.
On the *rénshēn* day,
a partial pardon was granted to all prisoners in the various prefectures of the Huáinán Circuit.
From the eleventh day of the sixth month of this year onwards,
all transgressions,
regardless of their severity,
were not to be further investigated.
It was also announced that during the time when the region belonged to Jiāngnán,
any unreasonable taxes and corvée,
and levies without names,
were all to be abolished.
On the *wùyín* day,
Hù Yànkē (扈彥珂), Grand General of the Right Palace Guard, retired with the title of Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince.
On the *gēngchén* day,
Wáng Yàn (王晏), Grand Administrator of Xījīng, was appointed Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
the Zhànguó Army was elevated to Bīnzhōu.
Lǐ Chóngjìn (李重進), Commander of the Huáinán Expeditionary Force, reported
that the enemy army in Shòuzhōu attacked the southern redoubt,
and the imperial army suffered a setback.
Previously,
an imperial edict ordered Lǐ Jìxūn (李繼勳), Commander-in-Chief of the Infantry, to encamp south of Shòuzhōu
and attack the enemy stronghold.
On this day,
the enemy troops sallied from the city to attack our army,
breaking through the palisade and entering.
All the siege equipment was burned by the enemy,
and hundreds of officers and soldiers died.
Lǐ Chóngjìn, who was in the eastern redoubt,
was also unable to provide aid.
At that time, the city was strong and had not yet fallen,
and the army was exhausted outside its walls.
Moreover, the summer heat was deadly,
and food supplies were intermittent.
After the loss of Lǐ Jìxūn,
the army lost its morale,
and the generals discussed retreating.
Fortunately, the present emperor, having personally led troops from Liùhé back to the capital,
passed by the city and
stayed there for ten days,
whereupon the imperial army was revitalized.
On the *xīnmǎo* day, the first day of the seventh month of autumn,
Zhōu Xíngféng (周行逢), Military Commissioner of Wǔqīng Army and Administrator of Tánzhōu, was appointed Grand Commander of Lǎngzhōu,
concurrently Military Commissioner of Wǔpíng Army,
and promoted to concurrently hold the titles of acting Grand Commandant and Serving Attendant (*Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi* and *Jiān Shìzhōng*).
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Lú Jià (盧價), Guest of the Crown Prince, retired with the title of Minister of Rites.
Lǐ Míng (李明), Palace Counselor, was appointed Grand Judge.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Liú Chóngjìn (劉重進), Commander-in-Chief of the Lúzhōu Field Army, reported,
that he had defeated over a thousand Huáinán rebels within the prefectural boundary.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Wǔ Xíngdé (武行德), Commander-in-Chief of the Háozhōu Field Army, reported,
that he had defeated two thousand Huáinán rebels within the prefectural boundary.
On the *gēngxū* day,
Wáng Rényù (王仁裕), Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, passed away.
On the *xīnhài* day,
Empress Fú (符氏) passed away.
Xiàng Xùn, Military Commissioner of Huáinán, withdrew his forces from Yángzhōu
and garrisoned them in Shòuchūn.
At that time, the imperial army had been besieging Shòuchūn
for a year without success,
and the Jiāng and Huái regions were swarming with bandits.
The prefectures of Shū, Qí, Hé, Tàl, etc., were again occupied by the Wú people.
Therefore, Yángzhōu was abandoned to concentrate forces on Shòuchūn.
(According to Mǎ Líng's (馬令) *Nán Táng Shū*: Xiàng Xùn requested to abandon Yángzhōu
and concentrate forces to attack Shòuchūn.
He then sealed the treasuries and handed them over to the responsible officials,
and dispatched former generals of Huáinán to patrol the city.
They left without taking even a thread or a needle.
The Huái people were greatly pleased
and carried provisions to send off the Zhōu army.
(*Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*))
On the *rénxū* day of the eighth month,
Bái Chóngzàn (白重贊) of Héyáng was transferred to command Jīngzhōu,
and Zhāng Zé (張澤) was transferred to command Hézhōng.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Hóu Zhāng (侯章), former Military Commissioner of Dèngzhōu, was reinstated as Military Commissioner of Dèngzhōu.
Lǐ Jìxūn, Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard Infantry and Military Commissioner of Zhāngxìn Army, was appointed Military Commissioner of Héyáng.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Jù Kějiǔ (劇可久), Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud, was dismissed,
due to being implicated in the recommendation of an official.
On the *wùchén* day,
Wáng Pǔ (王朴), Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, completed and presented a new calendar,
named Xiǎndé Qīn Tiān Lì (顯德欽天曆).
The Emperor personally wrote a preface for it,
and it was then handed over to the Directorate of Astronomy to be put into use.
Zhāng Yǒngdé (張永德), Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard, reported,
that he had defeated Huáinán rebels at Xiàcài.
Previously,
Lǐ Jǐng (李景) of Jiāngnán, knowing that the imperial army was still in Shòuzhōu,
sent his generals Lín Rénzhào (林仁肇) and Guō Tíngwèi (郭廷謂) with land and naval forces to Xiàcài,
intending to seize the pontoon bridge.
They filled boats with firewood and straw
and set them on fire, carried by the wind.
Yǒngdé repelled them.
After a moment,
the wind direction reversed,
and the rebel forces gradually retreated,
whereupon they were defeated by the imperial army.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Wáng Mǐn (王敏), Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works, was dismissed,
due to recommending his son-in-law Chén Nánjīn (陳南金) as records officer for Héyáng.
(Nánjīn,
originally written as
"Nánqiān" (南僉),
is now corrected according to the biography of Wáng Mǐn.
(Adhesive note in facsimile edition))
On the *bǐngwǔ* day of the ninth month,

Wáng Pǔ, Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, Right Remonstrance Official, and acting Administrator of Kāifēng Prefecture, was appointed Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (*Shàngshū Hùbù Shìláng*),
and made Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Jiāo Jìxūn (焦繼勳), Commander-in-Chief of the Right Yǔlín Guard, was appointed Grand General of the Left Túnwèi Guard.
Yáng Chéngxìn (楊承信), Grand General of the Left Palace Guard, was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Right Yǔlín Guard.
Sòng Yánwò (宋延渥), Grand General of the Left Jiānmén Guard, was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Right Shénwǔ Guard.
On the *rén yín* day,
the emperor again visited Yángzhōu.
The military title of Lúzhōu was changed to Bǎoxìn Jūn.
On the *jiǎ chén* day,
Zhào Zàn, Commander of the Right Dragon Imperial Guard, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Lúzhōu.
Mùróng Yánzhāo, Supervisor of the Palace Guards, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán and concurrently Deputy Commander of the Palace Guards.
(Yánzhāo was
originally written as
"Tíngjiàn,"
now corrected according to *Dōngdū Shìlüè*.
(Photocopy sticky note)) Shēntú È, Supervisor of Yánchéng, was dispatched to *Jiāngnán* Lǐ Jǐng with a letter and ten imperial horses,
fully adorned with gold and silver bridles,
forty loose horses,
and a thousand sheep.
È had previously been captured by the imperial army,
hence he was sent.
On the *bǐng wǔ* day,
Lǐ Jǐng of *Jiāngnán* sent his appointed Chancellor, Féng Yánsí, to offer 100,000 *liǎng* of silver for army provisions,
100,000 bolts of silk,
100,000 strings of cash,
500,000 *jīn* of tea,
and 200,000 *dàn* of rice and wheat.
On the *gēng xū* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Yáng Xíngmì, the late Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán, and Xú Wēn, the late Jìedùshǐ of Shēngfǔ,
shall each be granted tomb-guarding households.
All officials and gentry of *Jiāngnán* whose ancestral tombs are located north of the *Jiāng* [River]
shall have local chief officials dispatch personnel to inspect them."
On the *xīn hài* day,
Lǐ Jǐng sent his appointed Lord of Línrǔ Commandery, Xú Liáo, to present 2,000,000 cash for banquets,
and also sent fifty musicians to come with Liáo to present a toast for longevity.
In the fourth month of summer, on the *guǐ chǒu* day,
a banquet was held for accompanying ministers and the *Jiāngnán* envoy Féng Yánsí and others at the temporary palace.
Xú Liáo presented the longevity toast on behalf of Lǐ Jǐng,
and offered gold wine vessels, imperial robes, rhinoceros belts, gold and silver, brocade and damask, saddles and horses, etc.
On the *yǐ mǎo* day,
the imperial carriage departed from Yángzhōu to return to the capital.
On the *bǐng chén* day,
Zhào Lì, Academian of the Grand Astrologer and Acting Prefect of Xùzhōu, was dismissed,
for being slow in investigation and impeachment.
Earlier,
Mǎ Dàoxuán, a Hanlin imperial physician, had submitted a petition,
complaining that his son was killed by bandits in Shòuzhōu,
that the main bandit had been captured
and was currently in Xùzhōu,
but the prefecture had not investigated and decided the case.
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
and dispatched Dòu Yí, Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, by express post to investigate.
When the case was concluded,
twenty-four people were condemned to death with their families.
On the day Yí took his leave,
the Emperor's command was very severe,
hence Yí's use of punishment was excessively harsh.
On the *wù wǔ* day,
Lǐ Yànxūn, former Commander of Yánzhōu, was appointed Commander of Cāngzhōu.
On the *gēng shēn* day,
the new Imperial Ancestral Temple was completed,
and the spirit tablets of the five temples were moved into its chambers.
On the *rén shēn* day,
the emperor returned from Huáinán.
On the *guǐ yǒu* day,
Zǎn Jūyùn, Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of the Xuānhuī, was ordered to govern Kāifēng Prefecture.
On the *jiǎ xū* day,
Zhāng Yǒngdé, Jìedùshǐ of Chénzhōu, proceeded to the northern border according to imperial edict,
because the Qìdān had encroached upon the frontier.
(According to *Liáo Shǐ*: In the fourth month of the eighth year of Yìnglì,
Xiāo Sīwēn, Commander of Nánjīng, captured border prefectures and counties.
In the fifth month,
Zhōu captured Shùchéng County.
*Dōngdū Shìlüè*'s biography of Guō Chóng states: Shìzōng campaigned in Huáidiàn,
and 10,000 Qìdān cavalry plundered the border.
Chóng led his army to defeat them at Shùlù,
beheading several hundred and
capturing over 30,000 people, cattle, and sheep.
Xuē Shǐ only mentions the encroachment,
without elaborating,
and Ouyáng Shǐ omits it.
(Kǒng edition)) On the *dīng chǒu* day,
Liǎngzhè reported that
on the nineteenth day of the fourth month, a fire in Hángzhōu
burned down nearly all residential houses and government offices.
On the *xīn sì* day, the first day of the fifth month,
the Emperor presided over court in Chóngyuán Hall,
with guards and attendants in proper order.
An imperial edict stated:
"All imperial guards and officers and soldiers of various circuits
shall be granted excellent rewards according to their ranks.
For those officers and soldiers who died in imperial service during the campaign,
posthumous official titles shall be granted,
and their direct descendants
shall be recruited according to their talents.
Those wounded or disabled
shall be given separate relief.
For the prefectures of Huáinán and Xú, Sù, Sòng, Bó, Chén, Yǐng, Xǔ, Cài, etc.,
the outstanding autumn and summer taxes from last year
shall all be remitted."
On the *bǐng xū* day,
Dòu Yí, Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, was ordered to govern Hénán Prefecture and concurrently serve as Commander of Xījīng.
On the *xīn mǎo* day,
Ān Shěnqí, Jìedùshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Qīngzhōu;
Hán Tōng, Jìedùshǐ of Xǔzhōu, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Sòngzhōu,
retaining his previous concurrent position as Supervisor of the Imperial Cavalry and Infantry;
Xiàng Xùn, Jìedùshǐ of Sòngzhōu, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Xiāngzhōu;
and the current Emperor was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ Jūn,
retaining his previous position as Commander of the Palace Guards.
In the Huáinán campaign,
the current Emperor's contribution was the greatest.
When this decree was issued,
although it was said to be a reward for his achievements,
it was only a relocation of command,
and the reward was too light,
which public opinion deemed unfair.
On the *guǐ sì* day,
Wǔ Xíngdé, Supreme General of the Left Imperial Guard, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Fùzhōu;
Sòng Yánwò, Commander of the Right Divine Imperial Guard, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Huázhōu.
(According to the *Xiǎochù Jí* inscription for Sòng Yánwò, it says: In the fifth month,
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Yìchéng Jūn.
The decree broadly stated:
"The army that advanced quickly down the river
was like crossing uninhabited land.
You have established extraordinary merit in eliminating evil and overcoming difficulties;
I shall not forget the generous reward for your oath by the mountains and rivers.
The old state of Nányàn
is near the northern palace.
As a bulwark by the riverbank,
you oversee from afar the ford of Báimǎ;
commanding troops below Ráng,
you now guard the land of Wòlóng."
(*Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*)) Wáng Huī, former Commander of Tóngzhōu, was appointed Commander of Xiāngzhōu.
On the *yǐ wèi* day,
names were established for the gates of the Luóchéng of the Eastern Capital:
the two eastern gates were Yínbīn and Yánchūn;
the three southern gates were Zhūmíng, Jǐngfēng, and Wèijǐng;
(Wèijǐng
was originally written as
"Sījǐng."
*Wǔdài Huìyào* writes Wèijǐng.
According to the northern gate Àijǐng in the text below,
Wèijǐng for the southern gate should be correct,
now corrected.
(Photocopy sticky note)) the two western gates were Yíngqiū and Sùzhèng;
the three northern gates were Yuándé, Chángjǐng, and Àijǐng.
On the *xīn chǒu* day,
the emperor visited Huáixìn post station.
On the *yǐ sì* day,
an imperial edict instructed all civil officials at court to again recommend one person suitable for secretarial or magisterial positions.
On the *wù shēn* day,
Xiàng Xùn, Jìedùshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, was appointed concurrently Commander of Water and Land Transport and Pacification for the Southwest Frontier.
On the *jǐ yǒu* day,
Féng Yánlǔ, Minister of the Imperial Treasury, was appointed Imperial Envoy to the State of *Jiāngnán*,
with Zhōng Mó, Junior Minister of the Imperial Guard, as his deputy.
Lǐ Jǐng was bestowed with imperial robes,
a jade belt,
100,000 bolts of brocade, damask, silk gauze, and plain silk combined,
1,000 *liǎng* of gold vessels,
10,000 *liǎng* of silver vessels,
five imperial horses,
fully equipped with gold and jade saddles and bridles,
one hundred loose horses,
and three hundred sheep.
Lǐ Hóngjì, the Crown Prince of *Jiāngnán*, was bestowed with vessels, silks, saddles, and horses, etc.
A separate letter was given to Lǐ Jǐng, which read:
"The Emperor respectfully inquires of the Lord of *Jiāngnán*.
The benefits of the sea
are on your coast.
When the territories were first divided,
there was concern about a shortage of provisions.
The various commanderies east of the *Jiāng* [River]
have long been known for their abundance.
However, among the rivers and marshes,
there were previously no salt lands.
Having received your previous sincere intention,
it has always been kept in mind.
I wish to share the surplus of accumulated goods
to assist in military expenditures.
It has already been ordered to the Three Departments
to annually allocate 300,000 *dàn* of military salt provisions."
Also, a scroll of this year's calendar was bestowed upon Lǐ Jǐng.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
the imperial carriage halted at Cāngzhōu.
Xuē Jūzhèng, formerly the Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left, was appointed Vice Minister of Punishments.
On this day,
the Emperor led all the armies on a northern expedition.
On the day Rénchén,
they reached Qiánníngjūn.
Wáng Hóng, the self-proclaimed Regional Inspector of Níngzhōu, surrendered the city.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
the Emperor boarded a dragon boat,
leading the naval fleet northwards with the current,
stretching for dozens of *lǐ* from end to end.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
they arrived at Yìjīn Guān.
(According to *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*: Upon arriving at Yìjīn Guān,
Qìdān commander Zhōng Tínghuī surrendered the city.
(*Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*)) From this point westward,
the waterway gradually narrowed,
making it difficult for the naval fleet to advance.
So, they abandoned the boats and disembarked.
On the day Rényín,
they camped in the wilderness.
At this time, the Emperor had arrived ahead of schedule,
and the main army had not yet assembled.
The retinue accompanying the imperial carriage
was less than one *lǚ* (500 men).
It was thanks to the present Emperor (i.e., Zhào Kuàngyìn, who would later found the Sòng Dynasty) who led the skilled officers and cavalry to guard the imperial carriage.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
the present Emperor arrived first at Wǎqiáo Guān.
Yáo Nèibīn, the self-proclaimed commander, surrendered the city.
(According to *Lóngpíng Jí*: Yáo Nèibīn
was a native of Píngzhōu.
When Shìzōng went on the northern expedition,
he led troops to Wǎqiáo Guān.
Nèibīn, being the pass commissioner,
opened the gate and offered surrender.
Shìzōng appointed him Regional Inspector of Rǔzhōu.
(*Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*)) On the day Jiǎchén,
Liú Chǔxìn, the Regional Inspector of Mòzhōu, surrendered his prefecture.
(Note: Regarding the surrender of Mòzhōu,
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* follows Xuē Shǐ (Xue Juzheng's *Old History of the Five Dynasties*) in dating it to the fourth month,
while *Liáo Shǐ* dates it to the fifth month,
which is probably an error.
In the fifth month, on the first day Ěsì,
the Emperor stopped at Wǎqiáo Guān.
Lǐ Chóngjìn, the Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Army, and other generals arrived successively at the traveling court.
Gāo Yànhuī, the Regional Inspector of Yíngzhōu, returned his city to allegiance.
The region south of the pass was pacified,
gaining three prefectures,
seventeen counties,
and eighteen thousand three hundred sixty households.
In this campaign,
the imperial army, numbering tens of thousands,
did not lose a single arrow,
and all border cities and towns submitted at the mere mention of their approach.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Emperor discussed with his generals the attack on Yōuzhōu.
All the generals considered it not yet feasible,
but the Emperor did not listen.
That night,
the Emperor fell ill,
and so the plan was halted.
On the day Wùshēn,
Sūn Xíngyǒu, the Military Commissioner of Dìngzhōu, reported
the capture of Yìzhōu,
and presented the self-proclaimed Regional Inspector Lǐ Zàiqīn, who was then captured,
and executed in the military market.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Wǎqiáo Guān was established as Xióngzhōu.
(According to the biography of Chén Sīràng in *Sòng Shǐ*: Wǎqiáo Guān was gained and made Xióngzhōu,
and Sīràng was appointed Commander-in-Chief
to lead troops to garrison it.
(*Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*)) Yìjīn Guān was established as Bàzhōu.
(According to the biography of Hán Lìngkūn in *Sòng Shǐ*: He was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Bàzhōu,
leading his troops to garrison it.
(*Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*)) On this day,
Zhāng Zàngyīng, the Commander-in-Chief of the Vanguard, defeated several hundred Qìdān cavalry north of Wǎqiáo Guān,
and captured Gù'ān County.
An edict was issued to conscript male laborers from Bīn and Dì Prefectures to build the city of Bàzhōu.
On the day Gēngxū,
Lǐ Chóngjìn, the Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Army, was dispatched to lead troops out through Tǔmén,
entering the Hédōng territory.
On the day Rénzǐ,
the imperial carriage departed from Xióngzhōu,
(Note: *Liáo Shǐ* states that the Zhōu army retreated on the day Xīnwèi of the fifth month,
which differs from Xuē Shǐ.
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* follows Xuē Shǐ in dating it to Rénzǐ.
) and
returned to the capital.
Liú Cóngxiào, the Military Commissioner of Quánzhōu, dispatched Assistant Prefect Wáng Yǔxī to present tribute at the traveling court.
The Emperor considered Quánzhōu to be subservient to Jiāngnán,
and Lǐ Jǐng had just submitted to the state,
so he did not wish to seize its allegiance.
He merely bestowed an edict of praise.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
the Western Capital reported
that Sītú Xǔ, the Grand Master of Ceremonies (retired), had died.
On the day Jǐsì,
Lǐ Chóngjìn, the Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Army, reported
defeating the Hédōng bandit army at Bǎijǐng,
beheading two thousand men.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the Emperor arrived from Xióngzhōu.
(According to *Què Sǎo Biān*: After Zhōu Shìzōng had pacified the three passes,
he fell ill and retreated.
He delayed at Chányuān, refusing to proceed.
Even the prime ministers and close officials who inquired about his illness were not allowed to see him,
causing fear both inside and outside the court.
At that time, Zhāng Yǒngdé was the Military Commissioner of Chányuān.
Yǒngdé was married to the daughter of Zhōu Tàizǔ,
and due to this kinship,
he alone was allowed into the imperial bedchamber.
Thus, the officials persuaded Yǒngdé, saying:
"The realm is not yet settled,
the foundation is empty,
and the regional lords in all four directions only hope for unrest in the capital.
Now, Chányuān and Biànpíng are very close.
If Your Majesty does not return quickly to reassure the people,
but instead fears the toil of a day or night,
and lingers here,
should anything unfortunate happen,
what would become of the imperial ancestral temple!"
Yǒngdé agreed with them.
He seized an opportunity to convey the officials' message to Shìzōng.
Shìzōng asked:
"Who made you say this?"
Yǒngdé replied that all the officials wished for this,
and Shìzōng pondered for a long time,
then sighed:
"I knew you must have been taught by someone,
but do you not understand my intentions!
However, seeing your dire straits,
how could you bear this!"
That very day, he hastened his carriage back to the capital.
(*Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*))
However, this person can ultimately not be placed in the Zhōngshū.”
Not long after,
Táo also died.
Táo was a person who did not adhere to rites and laws.
Although he and his younger brother, Huǎn, were very harmonious,
during their conversations,
indecorous words
often interspersed.
Huǎn married the daughter of Dòu Nínggù, the Lǐbù Shàngshū.
She was slightly older.
On the night of their wedding,
Madame Dòu came out to pay respects.
Táo immediately bowed down in front of her.
Huǎn was surprised and said,
“Elder brother, are you mad?
The new bride pays respects to her uncle,
how can there be a return of the courtesy?”
Táo replied,
“I am not mad;
I just thought it was my in-law (the bride’s mother).”
Huǎn was both ashamed and angry.
After sitting down,
Madame Dòu bowed again.
Táo again clasped his hands in front of his chest,
and spoke a xiēhòuyǔ, saying,
“Ashamed that there is no Dòu Jiàn,
mistakenly acting as Liángshān,
yes, yes, yes!”
At that time, all who heard it collapsed in laughter.
Thus, Táo’s disregard for rites and laws within the household
was like this.
Shìzōng considered him to lack the demeanor of a great minister,
and did not employ him again.
This was fitting!
Shìzōng’s ambition was for the four directions.
He often feared that the imperial fortune would be short-lived and his achievements unfulfilled.
Knowing that Wáng Pú was skilled in divination,
he once casually asked him,
“How many years will I live?”
He replied,
“Your Majesty, with your heart
devoted to the welfare of the common people,
Heaven is high but hears the humble,
and you will naturally be blessed.
I am ignorant and unrefined,
but based on my learning,
I cannot predict beyond thirty years.”
Shìzōng joyfully said,
“If it is as you say,
then I will spend ten years expanding the empire,
ten years nurturing the common people,
and ten years achieving great peace—that will be enough.”
Thereafter, he turned back his army from Wǎqiáo Guān.
He died before reaching the pass.
Counting his reign, it was only five years and six months.
Five and six are indeed thirty.
This was probably Pú speaking euphemistically.
In Shìzōng’s later years,
he launched a major campaign to take Yōuzhōu.
When the Qìdān heard of his personal expedition,
the ruler and ministers were terrified.
All the cities and fortresses along the border surrendered at the mere sight of his approach.
All the barbarian tribes in Yōuzhōu
also fled overnight.
When the imperial carriage arrived at Wǎqiáo Guān,
the reconnaissance was true,
and he was very pleased,
believing that great achievements would surely be accomplished.
He ascended a high mound
to observe his grand army.
Shortly after,
over a hundred elders came bearing oxen and wine as offerings.
Shìzōng asked,
“What is this place called?”
They replied,
“Through generations,
it has been called Bìnglóng Tái.”
He remained silent,
and immediately mounted his horse and galloped away.
That night,
the emperor’s health was not well.
The next day, his illness became critical.
An edict was issued to turn back the army,
but he died before reaching the pass.
Before this,
when Shìzōng was still a commoner,
he often dreamt of a divine person presenting him with a large umbrella,
the color of turmeric,
and a scroll of Daoist scriptures.
Thereafter, he gained the empire.
When he fell ill at Wǎqiáo,
he again dreamt that the same divine person came to demand the umbrella and the scriptures.
He returned them in the dream and awoke with a start.
He told his close attendants,
“My dream is inauspicious.
