Is it not that Heaven’s mandate is about to depart?”
Thereupon, he summoned his great ministers
and instructed them on his posthumous affairs.
Initially,
when Yōuzhōu heard that the imperial carriage was approaching,
some elders secretly discussed, saying,
“This is not a cause for worry.
Moreover, the Son of Heaven’s surname is Chái,
and Yōuzhōu is the land of Yān.
Yān also refers to smoke and fire.
This firewood entering fire is an unfavorable omen;
how can success be achieved?”
It ultimately turned out as they said.
The historian says: Shìzōng, when he was in obscurity,
was particularly adept at concealing his talents.
When Heaven’s mandate was bestowed upon him,
and he inherited the grand enterprise,
he quickly broke the formation at Gāopíng,
and within a year recovered the fiefs of Qín and Fèng.
Jiāngběi and Yānnán
were taken as easily as picking up mustard seeds.
His divine martial prowess and heroic strategy
made him an eminent ruler of his generation.
Furthermore, he paid close attention to governmental affairs,
working tirelessly day and night.
He exposed hidden faults and distinguished between the righteous and the treacherous,
often arriving at correct judgments.
When his subordinates made mistakes,
he would certainly rebuke them face-to-face.
He often said that Tàizǔ had nurtured the evils of the two kings,
leading to the eventual breakdown of the relationship between ruler and minister.
Therefore, the emperor managed heroes
by clearly stating their faults if they erred,
and generously rewarding them for their merits.
He employed both civil and military officials,
and none failed to be convinced by his wisdom and touched by his kindness.
Thus, on the day he passed away,
those near and far mourned him deeply.
However, his nature was marred by excessive scrutiny,
and his use of punishment was excessively severe.
After implementing measures,
he often expressed self-reproach.
Towards his later years,
he gradually adopted lenient policies,
realizing the frequency of military campaigns
and empathizing with the toil of the common people.
He indeed had the intention of bringing peace and prosperity.
However, his lifespan was not long,
and his noble aspirations were not fulfilled.
Alas!
(From Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 8984.)

Zhōushū, Volume 11, Gōngdì Jì

on the fourth day of the eighth month,

sixth year of Xiǎndé,

with an allocated revenue of three thousand households,

Shìzōng passed away.

the assembled officials supported the emperor in ascending the throne and then retired.

Hán Lìngkūn, the Běimiàn Bīngmǎ Dūbùshǔ, reported

In this month,
sixteen prefectures and commanderies reported continuous heavy rain for ten days without stopping.
Empress Shèngmù Chái of Tàizǔ was
a native of Lónggǎng, Xíngzhōu.
(Commentary: The Lóngchuān Biézhì records her as a native of Chéng'ān, Wèi.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) Her family was wealthy and powerful.
When Tàizǔ was still humble,
he heard in Luòyáng of the empress's virtue and wisdom,
and so he sought her hand in marriage.
(Commentary: The Zhāng Yǒngdé biography in the Dōngdū Shìlüè states: Empress Chái of Zhōu Tàizǔ
was originally a concubine of Táng Zhuāngzōng.
When Zhuāngzōng died,
Míngzōng sent her back to her family.
As she traveled to the river,
her parents came to meet her.
It happened that there was a great storm,
and they stayed at an inn for several days.
A man ran past their door,
his clothes ragged and unable to protect himself.
The empress saw him
and exclaimed in surprise:
"Who is that?"
The innkeeper said:
"That is Guō Què'ér, a commander of the cavalry and infantry."
The empress found him extraordinary
and wished to marry him,
so she asked her parents.
Her parents angrily said:
"You were in the presence of the Emperor;
when you return, you should marry a Jiédùshǐ.
Why do you wish to marry this man?"
The empress said:
"This is a nobleman;
he must not be lost.
I will divide the money in my bag, giving half to my parents,
and I will take the other half."
Her parents knew they could not dissuade her,
and so the marriage took place at the inn.
The so-called Guō Què'ér
was none other than Zhōu Tàizǔ.
This matter is not recorded in Xuē Shǐ,
probably because it was suppressed at the time.)
In his prime, Tàizǔ
loved to drink and gamble,
and enjoyed being a knight-errant,
not adhering to minor conduct.
The empress admonished him for his excesses,
and often provided him with inner assistance.
Emperor Shìzōng was the empress's nephew;
he was careful and compliant from a young age,
and the empress greatly doted on him,
so Tàizǔ adopted him as his own son.
Tàizǔ once slept,
and the empress saw a small five-colored snake enter between his cheekbones and nose.
She found this extraordinary
and knew he would surely become noble,
so she served him with even greater reverence.
She passed away before he achieved nobility.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he issued a decree saying:
"Among deep bonds, none precedes that of marriage;
among weighty rites, none is greater than posthumous veneration.
As I rule, I often reflect
and cherish the past.
The virtuous conduct by the river bank
still transmits the poem of the water mallow;
the great renown of Guīruì
does not match the nobility of the jade pendants.
Let the grand ceremony of the hairpins be performed
to express the sentiment of seeking the sword.
Therefore, the late lady, Chái,
her family records transmit her fragrance,
and the Xiang spirits gather blessings.
Her gentle demeanor displayed the adorned pheasant robe,
her fragrance like pepper and orchid;
she upheld her chastity to be chosen as a palace official,
her renown shining in records and histories.
Her admirable example remains in the women's quarters,
her wise words aiding in admonition and guidance.

originally written as

it should refer to Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's 'observing the vital energy' at Héjiān.

(Yǐngkùběn niánqiān)) and lament the swiftness of 'hiding the boat.'
Just as the imperial destiny was about to open,
she suddenly departed from the jade terrace.
It is fitting to formally entitle her in the imperial palace
and let her radiance shine in the female principle.
She is to be posthumously named Empress.
The relevant authorities are commanded to determine her posthumous title
and prepare the ceremonial investiture."
Subsequently, the officials submitted the posthumous title Shèngmù.
In the first year of Xiǎndé,
Tàizǔ's spirit tablet was enshrined in the temple,
and the empress was enskrined alongside him in his chamber.

Consort Shū Yáng
was a native of Zhēndìng, Zhènzhōu.
Her father, Hóngyù,
was the Zhēndìng Shàoyǐn.
(Commentary: The Yáng Tíngzhāng biography in the Dōngdū Shìlüè states: Her father Hóngyù
once fished at Diāoqí Pō.
Someone gave him two stone geese,
one with a wing covering its left side,
the other covering its right,
saying:
"I am an envoy from the Northern Marchmount."
After speaking, he disappeared.
That year, Zhōu's Consort Shū was born,
and the following year, Tíngzhāng was born.
) During the heyday of Héshuò,
its territories
were governed by defending commanders,
so beautiful young women
were all selected for the royal palace.
The consort was chosen from a good family when she was young,
and served Prince Zhào, Wáng Róng.
During Zhāng Wénlǐ's rebellion,
the consort was displaced.
When Táng Míngzōng was in his fief,
he sought out those who had been overlooked.
Ān Chónghuì protected the consort's family
and helped them advance in their careers.
Her parents then married the consort to a local man, Shí Guāngfǔ.
She became a widow within a few years.
When Tàizǔ first assisted the Hàn dynasty,
Consort Shèngmù had passed away.
Hearing of the consort's virtues,
he formally sought her hand in marriage.
(Commentary: The Yáng Tíngzhāng biography in the Sòng Shǐ states: He had an elder sister who was a widow in the capital.
When Zhōu Zǔ was still humble, he wished to marry her,
but the sister refused.
He had a matchmaker convey that he might resort to force,
and the sister informed Tíngzhāng.
Tíngzhāng went to see Zhōu Zǔ
and returned to tell his sister:
"This man has an extraordinary appearance;
he cannot be refused."
The sister then consented.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
The consort was harmonious with her relatives and cared for orphans,
providing great assistance to the family.
At the end of Tiānfú of Jìn,
she died in Tàiyuán
and was subsequently buried in the outskirts of Jìn.
In the ninth month of the first year of Guǎngshùn,
she was posthumously enfeoffed as Consort Shū.
Tàizǔ had one empress and three consorts in total.
When Sōnglíng was to be interred,
it was proposed that they all be interred with him.
At that time, since the consort's coffin was in enemy territory
and could not be moved,
Shìzōng ordered the authorities to prepare an empty tomb
beside Sōnglíng,
intending to arrange the funeral once the rebels were pacified.
In the summer of the first year of Xiǎndé,
Shìzōng campaigned in Hédōng
and indeed fulfilled his long-cherished wish.
The consort's elder brother, Tíngzhāng,
(Commentary: The Dōngdū Shìlüè states: Tíngzhāng was Consort Shū's younger brother.
The Xù Tōngjiàn Chángbiān also states: Tíngzhāng had an elder sister who was a consort of Zhōu Tàizǔ.
Both differ from Xuē Shǐ.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) served Tàizǔ early on.
Upon Tàizǔ's ascension, he successively held internal positions
before being sent out as the Jiédùshǐ of Jìnzhōu.
When the Imperial Dynasty took over,
he was transferred to Xíngzhōu,
then again to Fūzhōu.
After his tenure, he returned to the capital
and died in his private residence.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Vol. 1266.
Empress Dowager Zhāng,
was a native of Zhēndìng, Héngzhōu.
Her grandfather, Zhāng Jì,
was the Jiéduó Pànguān of the Chéngdé Army and the Jiǎnjiào Bīngbù Shàngshū.
Her father, Zhāng Tóngzhī,
was the Zīchéngguān of his native prefecture and the Jiǎnjiào Gōngbù Shàngshū.
He served Wáng Róng, the King of Zhào,
and held important positions throughout his career.
(The positions of Zīchéngguān and Zhōngyào
are not found in the Zhíguān Zhì (Register of Officials).
It is suspected that they were private offices established by the regional governors (fānzhèn) at that time.
As they cannot be further investigated now,
they are noted here.
(Adhesive note in the Yingku bản)) Towards the end of Tiānyòu,
Zhāng Wénlǐ, a general of Zhào, killed Wáng Róng,
and surrendered Zhènzhōu to the Liáng dynasty.
Zhuāngzōng ordered the general Fú Cúnshěn to suppress and pacify him.
At that time, the Consort was still young.
There was a general from Yōuzhōu named Wǔ Cóngjiàn,
who was stationed at her family's home.
Seeing her beauty and youth,
he betrothed her to his son.
The Wǔ family lived in Tàiyuán.
When Tàizǔ (later Shìzǔ) followed the Emperor of Hàn (Liú Zhīyuǎn) to garrison Bìngmén,
Lady Yáng (his first wife) passed away from illness.
Not long after, Wǔ's son also died.
Tàizǔ had long heard of the Consort's virtues,
and so took her as his second wife.
When Tàizǔ rose to prominence,
she was successively enfeoffed as the Lady of Wú.
At the end of the reign of Emperor Yǐn of Hàn,
a rebellion broke out within the palace,
and many high-ranking officials were massacred.
Tàizǔ was slandered while in Yèzhōu,
and the Consort and other imperial relatives were killed on the same day in the old residence in Dōngjīng.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
she was posthumously enfeoffed as Guìfēi,
and a period of mourning was declared.
Thus, Shìzōng later issued an order for her re-interment.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
he converted Tàizǔ's old residence, which was the place where the Consort met her tragic end,
into a Buddhist monastery,
named Huángjiàn.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 8989.)
Consort Dé Dǒng,
was a native of Língshòu, Chángshān.
Her grandfather, Dǒng Wénguǎng,
was the Lùshì Cānjūn of Shēnzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Her father, Dǒng Guāngsì,
was the Zhāoqìng Wèi of Zhàozhōu.
As a child, the Consort was intelligent.
From the moment she could speak and listen,
she could distinguish sounds by pressing on stringed and wind instruments.
At the age of seven,
she encountered the Zhènzhōu uprising,
her relatives scattered,
and she became separated from her family.
A general from the Lùzhōu army division found her,
and hid her in his home.
His wife, whose own daughter had not survived,
doted on the Consort,
more than her own child.
Her governess taught her etiquette and precepts,
and she became skilled in accomplishments and demeanor.
The Consort's family mourned her loss.
Her elder brother, Dǒng Yǔ, searched for her everywhere
for six or seven years.
Later, the Lùzhōu general entered official service at court.
Some of the Consort's hometown acquaintances knew about her.
When Dǒng Yǔ met the Lùzhōu general,
he joyfully reunited with her.
At that time, she was thirteen.
About a year after the Consort returned home,
she married Liú Jìnchāo, a local man.
Liú Jìnchāo held an internal official position.
In the year the Khitans conquered Jìn,
he was captured by the barbarians and died.
The Consort lived as a widow in Luòyáng.
Empress Yáng Shūfēi, Tàizǔ's consort, was from the same hometown as the Consort.
She often spoke of the Consort's virtue and wisdom.
When Tàizǔ accompanied the Emperor of Hàn (Liú Zhīyuǎn) to Luòyáng,
he remembered Shūfēi's words,
and soon took her in with proper rites.
At the beginning of the new dynasty,
Empress Zhāng Guìfēi met her tragic end,
leaving the position of Empress vacant.
So, she was enfeoffed as Dékfēi.
Since Empress Shèngmù's early demise,
Tàizǔ had repeatedly lost virtuous women of noble families.
Among his inner court assistants,
only the Consort remained.
Moreover, she always set an excellent example, even in the smallest details like fastening her sash and removing her hairpin.
In the summer of Guǎngshùn three (953 AD),
she fell ill.
During her medical treatment,
Tàizǔ was on a campaign in Yǎn-Hǎi.
(Yǎn-Hǎi,
originally written as
"Gǔnhǎi" in the original text,
is now corrected according to Ōuyáng Xiū's history.
(Adhesive note in the Yingku bản)) As the imperial carriage was about to depart,
the Consort reported:
"It is now the height of summer's heat,
and it is a great effort for Your Majesty to inspect the region.
Setting out at dawn and traveling at night
requires attendants.
All the officials from the Sībo and below, who are in charge of duties,
have already been arranged to accompany you."
Tàizǔ replied:
"Your illness has not yet subsided.
You need frequent examinations and treatment.
This journey is short,
so there is no need for palace women."
However, when Tàizǔ was stationed in Lǔzhōng,
the Consort insisted on having palace women sent to attend him,
sending eunuchs back and forth to convey her message.
Tàizǔ personally issued an edict to Zhèng Rénhuì, saying:
"I am very concerned that Dékfēi, knowing I am at the military encampment in Yǎnzhōu,
will insist on sending palace women to attend me.
Since the armies are in the field,
it is not appropriate for them to be present.
I order Zhèng Rénhuì to pay close attention to this matter.
If Dékfēi insists on sending palace women eastward,
you must report it to me and stop them.
If they request saddles and horses,
do not provide them.
If her intention is firm,
then show her this imperial edict."
After Yǎnzhōu was pacified,
and the imperial carriage returned to the capital,
the Consort's illness showed no improvement.
She soon passed away in the Great Palace,
at the age of thirty-nine.
Court was suspended for three days.
The Consort's eldest brother, Dǒng Yǔ,
retired as a Zuǒ Zànshàn Dàfū.
Her second brother, Dǒng Xuánzhī,
and youngest brother, Dǒng Zìmíng,
all served successively as郡shǒus (prefects).
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 8989.)
Empress Zhēnhuì Liú of Shìzōng,
was the daughter of a military family.
She married Shìzōng in her youth.
During the Qiányòu era of Hàn,
Shìzōng was in the western ranks,
and the Empress was first enfeoffed as the Xiànjūn of Péngchéng.
When Shìzōng accompanied Tàizǔ to Yè,
the Empress remained in their residence.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, when Lǐ Yè and others rebelled,
the Empress, Empress Dowager Zhāng, and other imperial relatives all met with disaster on the same day.
At the beginning of the (Later Zhōu) dynasty,
she was posthumously enfeoffed as the Jùnfūrén of Péngchéng.
In the fourth month of summer, Xiǎndé four (957 AD),
she was posthumously enfeoffed as Empress,
with the posthumous title Zhēnhuì.
Her tomb was named Huìlíng.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 8989.)
Xuānyì Huánghòu Fú Shì [Fú Shì],
her ancestor was Fú Cúnshěn [Fú Cúnshěn].
He served Emperor Wǔ [Wǔ Huáng] and Emperor Zhuāng [Zhuāng Zōng] of the Later Táng [Hòu Táng],
achieving the highest positions as general and chancellor.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Qín Wáng [Qín Wáng].
Her father, Fú Yànqīng [Fú Yànqīng],
was the Jiedushi [Jiédùshǐ] of Tiānxíongjūn [Tiānxíongjūn]
and was enfeoffed as Wèi Wáng [Wèi Wáng].
The Empress was first married to Lǐ Chóngxùn [Lǐ Chóngxùn], the son of Lǐ Shǒuzhēn [Lǐ Shǒuzhēn].
(Chóngxùn [Chóngxùn]
was originally written
"Chóngchóu" [Chóngchóu]
but is now corrected according to the Tōngjiàn [Tōngjiàn].
(Note on a sticky slip in the facsimile edition.)) During the Qiányòu [Qiányòu] era of the Hàn [Hàn] dynasty,
Shǒuzhēn [Shǒuzhēn] rebelled in Hézhōng [Hézhōng].
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] attacked him with troops.
When the city fell,
Chóngxùn [Chóngxùn] killed his younger siblings with his sword.
He was about to strike the Empress when
she hid behind a screen.
She concealed herself with curtains and blinds.
Chóngxùn [Chóngxùn], in a panic, searched for the Empress but could not find her,
and so he committed suicide by cutting his own throat.
The Empress thus escaped death.
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] entered Hézhōng [Hézhōng],
and ordered someone to find her, which they did.
He immediately sent a female attendant to escort her to her father.
From then on, the Empress always felt Tàizǔ's [Tàizǔ] great kindness,
and she recognized Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] as her adoptive father.
When Shìzōng [Shìzōng] was garrisoned at Chányuān [Chányuān],
Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ] arranged her marriage to Shìzōng [Shìzōng].
The Empress was gentle and benevolent by nature
and was adept at discerning Shìzōng's [Shìzōng] wishes.
If Shìzōng [Shìzōng] became violently angry with his subordinates,
the Empress would always calmly intercede and resolve the situation.
Shìzōng [Shìzōng] greatly esteemed her.
Upon his accession,
she was granted the title of Empress.
When Shìzōng [Shìzōng] was about to embark on a southern expedition,
the Empress often advised him against it.
Her words were very direct and earnest,
and Shìzōng [Shìzōng] was moved by them.
When the imperial carriage was stationed in Huáidiàn [Huáidiàn],
having endured the scorching heat for a long time,
the Empress fell ill due to worry and distress.
On the twenty-first day of the seventh month of the second year of Xiǎndé [Xiǎndé],
she passed away in Zīdé Diàn [Zīdé Diàn],
at the age of twenty-six.
Shìzōng [Shìzōng] mourned her deeply.
Afterward, the officials submitted the posthumous title Xuānyì [Xuānyì].
She was buried in Xīnzhèng [Xīnzhèng],
and her tomb was named Yìlíng [Yìlíng].
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn [Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn], scroll 8989.
Note: The later Empress Fú [Fú Hòu] of Shìzōng [Shìzōng]
was the younger sister of Xuānyì [Xuānyì].
Xuē Shǐ [Xuē Shǐ] did not provide a biography for her,
which is an omission.
Wǔdài Shǐ Bǔ [Wǔdài Shǐ Bǔ] states: Empress Fú [Fú Shì] of Shìzōng [Shìzōng]
was the daughter of Wèi Wáng [Wèi Wáng] Yànqīng [Yànqīng].
At that time, a physiognomist saw her and was greatly astonished,
secretly telling Wèi Wáng [Wèi Wáng]:
"This girl's nobility is beyond words."
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn [Lǐ Shǒuzhēn] had long harbored rebellious ambitions,
and therefore married her to his son Chóngxùn [Chóngxùn].
After the ceremony,
Shǒuzhēn [Shǒuzhēn] was very pleased.
Later, he rebelled, occupying Hézhōng [Hézhōng].
Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ] was the Púmìshǐ [Púmìshǐ]
and was ordered to lead an expedition.
The Empress knew that Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ] had old ties with her father.
When the city was breached,
she sat by the hall entrance
and shouted at the various armies:
"I am the daughter of Fú Wèi Wáng [Fú Wèi Wáng]!
Wèi Wáng [Wèi Wáng] and Púmì Tàiwèi [Púmì Tàiwèi]
are like brothers, or even closer.
You must not be disrespectful!"
Thereupon, the various armies were startled and withdrew.
Shortly thereafter,
Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ] arrived
and said joyfully:
"This woman was preserved amidst a flurry of blades.
She can truly be called an extraordinary person!"
He then sent her back to Wèi Wáng [Wèi Wáng].
Upon Shìzōng's [Shìzōng] accession,
she was taken as Empress.
After escaping the calamity in Hézhōng [Hézhōng],
her mother wished for her to become a nun
to accumulate blessings and longevity.
The Empress was displeased and said:
"Life and death are fated.
Who can shave their head and go barefoot to seek a temporary survival!"
Her mother realized she could not be forced,
and so she stopped.
Shìzōng [Shìzōng] had always considered the Empress virtuous,
and upon hearing that she did not consider becoming a nun,
he esteemed her even more,
which is why she became the mother of the empire.
The imperial historian commented: There were six empresses and consorts in the Zhōu [Zhōu] imperial house,
and four of them were posthumously honored.
Therefore, the internal regulations of the inner palace
are rarely heard of.
Only the virtuous examples of Dǒng Fēi [Dǒng Fēi] and Empress Fú [Fú Hòu]
are truly worthy of the historian's brush.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn [Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn], scroll 8989.
Another note: Xuē Shǐ [Xuē Shǐ] has no biographies of imperial relatives by marriage.
An examination of Wǔdài Huìyào [Wǔdài Huìyào] states: The third daughter of Zhōu Tàizǔ [Zhōu Tàizǔ], Princess Lè'ān [Lè'ān Gōngzhǔ],
was harmed by the Hàn [Hàn] imperial house.
She was posthumously enfeoffed in the second month of the first year of Guǎngshùn [Guǎngshùn],
and in the fourth month of the fourth year of Xiǎndé [Xiǎndé],
she was again posthumously enfeoffed as Princess Commander of Jǔguó [Jǔguó Zhǎnggōngzhǔ].
The fourth daughter, Princess Shòu'ān [Shòu'ān Gōngzhǔ],
was married to Zhāng Yǒngdé [Zhāng Yǒngdé].
She was enfeoffed in the fourth month of the first year of Guǎngshùn [Guǎngshùn],
and in the first year of Xiǎndé [Xiǎndé],
she was enfeoffed as Princess Commander of Jìnguó [Jìnguó Zhǎnggōngzhǔ].
The fifth daughter, Princess Yǒngníng [Yǒngníng Gōngzhǔ],
was posthumously enfeoffed in the ninth month of the first year of Guǎngshùn [Guǎngshùn],
and in the fourth month of the fourth year of Xiǎndé [Xiǎndé],
she was again posthumously enfeoffed as Princess Commander of Liángguó [Liángguó Zhǎnggōngzhǔ].
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì [Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì])) Collation Notes:
Zhōu Shū [Zhōu Shū] scroll 13, Zōngshì Lièzhuàn [Zōngshì Lièzhuàn] 2.
Yǎn Wáng Dòng [Yǎn Wáng Dòng],
son of Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ].
His original name was Qīnggē [Qīnggē].
He was killed at the end of the Hàn [Hàn] dynasty.
Upon Tàizǔ's [Tàizǔ] accession,
an edict posthumously granted him the title of Tàiwèi [Tàiwèi]
and bestowed the name Dòng [Dòng].
He was posthumously enfeoffed in the fourth year of Xiǎndé [Xiǎndé].
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn [Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn], scroll 1266.
Shí Wáng Xìn [Shí Wáng Xìn],
son of Tàizǔ [Tàizǔ].
His original name was Yìgē [Yìgē].
He was killed at the end of the Hàn [Hàn] dynasty.
Upon Tàizǔ's [Tàizǔ] accession,
an edict posthumously granted him the title of Sīkōng [Sīkōng]
and bestowed the name Xìn [Xìn].
He was posthumously enfeoffed in the fourth year of Xiǎndé [Xiǎndé].
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn [Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn], scroll 1266.
Note: Tàizǔ's [Tàizǔ] sons were killed at a young age,
and originally had no deeds recorded.
The record in Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn [Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn] from Xuē Shǐ [Xuē Shǐ] is too brief,
presumably abridged,
and cannot be verified now.
According to Ōuyáng Shǐ's [Ōuyáng Shǐ] Jiārén Chuán [Jiārén Chuán]: Initially,
when the Emperor raised an army in Wèi [Wèi],
the Hàn [Hàn] dynasty besieged the Emperor's residence with troops.
At that time, Consort Zhāng [Zhāng Guìfēi] and her sons Qīnggē [Qīnggē] and Yìgē [Yìgē],
and nephews Shǒuyún [Shǒuyún], Fèngchāo [Fèngchāo], and Dìnggē [Dìnggē] were all executed.
Qīnggē [Qīnggē] and Yìgē [Yìgē] did not know who their mother was.
Upon Tàizǔ's [Tàizǔ] accession,
an edict posthumously granted his late second son Qīnggē [Qīnggē] the title of Tàiwèi [Tàiwèi]
and bestowed the name Dòng [Dòng];
and his third son Yìgē [Yìgē] the title of Sīkōng [Sīkōng]
and bestowed the name Xìn [Xìn].
His imperial nephew Shǒuyún [Shǒuyún] was posthumously granted the title of Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Wèi Jiāngjūn [Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Wèi Jiāngjūn].
As
"yún" [yún]
sounds similar to
"róng" [róng],
to avoid Shìzōng's [Shìzōng] given name,
he was renamed Shǒuyuàn [Shǒuyuàn].
Fèngchāo [Fèngchāo] was posthumously granted the title of Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Jiāngjūn [Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Jiāngjūn].
Dìnggē [Dìnggē] was posthumously granted the title of Zuǒ Qiānnú Wèi Jiāngjūn [Zuǒ Qiānnú Wèi Jiāngjūn]
and bestowed the name Xùn [Xùn].
On the Guǐwèi [Guǐwèi] day of the fourth month of summer in the fourth year of Xiǎndé [Xiǎndé] of Shìzōng's [Shìzōng] reign,
an edict stated:
"Rites are based on emotion,
and grace on mourning the past.
How much more so for those in the ranks of brothers,
where feelings of sorrow are especially intense.
The late imperial younger brothers, posthumously granted Tàiǎo [Tàiǎo] Dòng [Dòng] and Sīkōng [Sīkōng] Xìn [Xìn],
whose glorious destiny had just begun but whose natural lifespan was not reached,
leaving Us without them in the end,
this truly grieves Our heart.
Dòng [Dòng] can be posthumously granted Tàiǎo [Tàiǎo] and enfeoffed as Tán Wáng [Tán Wáng];
Xìn [Xìn] can be granted Sītú [Sītú]
and enfeoffed as Qǐ Wáng [Qǐ Wáng]."
Another edict stated:

"The late imperial cousins, posthumously granted Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Wèi Jiāngjūn [Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Wèi Jiāngjūn] Shǒuyuàn [Shǒuyuàn], posthumously granted Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Jiāngjūn [Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Jiāngjūn] Fèngchāo [Fèngchāo],
and posthumously granted Zuǒ Qiānnú Wèi Jiāngjūn [Zuǒ Qiānnú Wèi Jiāngjūn] Xùn [Xùn], etc.,
due to the recent chaotic era,
did not enjoy long lives.
Every time We recall their unjust deaths,
the sorrow cannot be forgotten.
Shǒuyuàn [Shǒuyuàn] can be posthumously granted Zuǒ Wèi Dàjiāngjūn [Zuǒ Wèi Dàjiāngjūn];
Fèngchāo [Fèngchāo] Rǒuwèi Dàjiāngjūn [Rǒuwèi Dàjiāngjūn];
Xùn [Xùn] Yǒuwǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn [Yǒuwǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn]."
Note: The edict recorded in Ōuyáng Shǐ [Ōuyáng Shǐ]
is already found in the basic annals of Xuē Shǐ [Xuē Shǐ],
but is appended here
for reference.
Yuè Wáng Zōngyì,
Shìzōng's son,
was murdered at the end of the Hàn dynasty.
In Xiǎndé 4th year, he was posthumously enfeoffed.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Juàn 16628.)
Cáo Wáng Zōngràng,
Shìzōng's son,
was enfeoffed in Xiǎndé 6th year.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Juàn 16628.)
Jì Wáng Xījíng,
Shìzōng's son,
was enfeoffed in Xiǎndé 6th year,
and died in Qiándé 2nd year of the imperial dynasty.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Juàn 16628.)
Qí Wáng Xīhuì,
Shìzōng's son,
was enfeoffed in Xiǎndé 6th year.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Juàn 16628.
Ouyáng Shǐ's family biography states: Shìzōng had seven sons.
The eldest was named Yígē,
the next two were unnamed,
then Gōng Huángdì,
then Xīràng,
then Xījíng,
then Xīhuì.
The identity of their mothers is unknown.
Yígē and the two others were executed by the Hàn.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he issued an edict to bestow names upon the imperial grandsons:
Yì was posthumously granted Zuǒ Xiāowèi Dàjiàngjūn,
Chéng Zuǒ Wǔwèi Dàjiàngjūn,
and Xián Zuǒ Túnwèi Dàjiàngjūn.
In Xiǎndé 3rd year,
the assembled officials requested the enfeoffment of the imperial clan.
Shìzōng said that the nation had been established for too short a time,
and his favor and trust had not yet reached the people.
It was necessary for his merits and virtues to be fully accomplished,
and his blessings to flow through the generations,
before this matter could be discussed.
In the 4th month of summer of the following year, on the Guǐwèi day,
Tàizǔ's sons were first enfeoffed.
An edict also stated:
"The way of father and son
is not forgotten by the sages.
To reflect again on the circumstances of their premature deaths
only increases feelings of sorrow.
Therefore, the former imperial princes, Zuǒ Xiāowèi Dàjiàngjūn Yì, Zuǒ Wǔwèi Dàjiàngjūn Chéng, and Zuǒ Túnwèi Dàjiàngjūn Xián,
in recalling past events,
cause sufficient grief.
It is appropriate to increase their enfeoffment by one character,
and posthumously grant them the rank of Sāntái.
Yì is to be posthumously granted Tàiwèi
and posthumously enfeoffed as Yuè Wáng;
Chéng Tàifù,
Wú Wáng;
and Xián Tàibǎo,
Hán Wáng."
However, the imperial princes who were still alive were not enfeoffed.
In the 6th year,
after retaking the Sānguān to the north,
he fell ill and returned to the capital.
On the Guǐwèi day of the 6th month,
imperial prince Zōngxùn was promoted to Tèjìn Zuǒwèi Shàngjiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Liáng Wáng.
Zōngràng was also appointed Zuǒ Xiāowèi Shàngjiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Yān Guó Gōng.
Ten days later, Shìzōng died,
and Liáng Wáng ascended the throne,
who was Gōng Huángdì.
In the 8th month of that year,
Zōngràng changed his name to Xīràng
and was enfeoffed as Cáo Wáng.
Xījíng and Xīhuì had not previously been enfeoffed with titles.
So Xījíng was appointed Yòuwǔwèi Dàjiàngjūn
and enfeoffed as Jì Wáng;
Xīhuì Zuǒlǐngjūn Wèi Dàjiàngjūn
and enfeoffed as Qí Wáng.
In the 10th month of Qiándé 2nd year,
Xījíng died.
The fates of Xīràng and Xīhuì are unknown.
Note: Xuē Shǐ does not record Wú Wáng Chéng or Hán Wáng Xián,
suggesting missing text.)
COLLATED NOTES
Zhōu Shū, Juàn 14, Lièzhuàn 3
Gāo Xíngzhōu,
courtesy name Shàngzhì,
(Note: Tōngjiàn Kǎoyì cites Zhuāngzōng Shílù: Xíngzhōu is written
"Xíngwēn".
This book's Táng Jì still retains the old record.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) was from Yōuzhōu.
He was born in Diāokē Lǐ, Huáiróng Jūn, Guīzhōu.
His great-grandfather, Shùnlì,
was generationally stationed at Huáiróng.
His father, Sījì,
had three brothers,
all of whom were valiant and skilled in military affairs,
their fame spreading throughout Shuòfāng.
When Táng Wǔhuáng pacified Yōuzhōu,
he appointed Liú Rén'gōng as commander,
and also left troops to guard it.
He made Sījì's elder brother the Xiānfēng Dūjiāng and Guīzhōu Cìshǐ,
Sījì the Zhōngjūn Dūjiāng and Shùnzhōu Cìshǐ,
(Note: Ouyáng Shǐ says: Sījì was Lǐ Kuāngwēi's garrison commander,
first recruited by the Jìn Wáng,
later serving Rén'gōng.
This differs from Xuē Shǐ.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) and Sījì's younger brother the Hòujūn Dūjiāng.
The brothers jointly commanded the Yān army.
Their subordinate officers and soldiers
were all magnates from Shānběi.
Rén'gōng deeply feared them.
When Wǔhuáng was about to return,
he privately told Rén'gōng:
"The Gāo vanguard commander and his brothers
wield power that overshadows the prefecture.
The source of trouble for Yān
will surely be this clan.
You should plan carefully."
After a long time,
the Tàiyuán garrison troops became arrogant and oppressive.
Sījì's brothers controlled them with law,
killing many.
Tàizǔ was enraged
and scolded Rén'gōng,
who then complained about the Gāo brothers,
and so they were all killed.
Rén'gōng then made the vanguard commander's son, Xíngguī, a Yájiàng,
and all his sons were listed under his banner,
greatly appeasing them to comfort their hearts.
At that time, Xíngzhōu was a little over ten years old,
and was also appointed to a post,
remaining by Rén'gōng's side.
Xíngguī has a separate biography,
in the Táng Shū.
(Note: Tōngjiàn Kǎoyì cites Zhōu Tàizǔ Shílù: Xíngguī was in Wǔzhōu,
and running out of food,
he descended at night with his brother Xíngzhōu into the Jìn army to beg for troops.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
When Zhuāngzōng recaptured Yān,
he assigned Xíngzhōu to Míngzōng's command.
He often commanded the elite guard troops with the last emperor of the Táng.
When Míngzōng campaigned against Yān,
he led troops to follow.
A local, Zhào Déjūn, said to Míngzōng:
"Xíngzhōu is very cautious and benevolent;
he will surely attain high rank."
When the Liáng general Liú Xún occupied Xīn,
he confronted the Tàiyuán army,
engaging in battle day and night.
One day,
when the two armies were arrayed,
Yuán Xíngqīn was pursued by the enemy,
a sword struck his face,
and the bloody battle was not yet resolved.
Xíngzhōu, with his elite cavalry, broke through the enemy formation to rescue him,
and Xíngqīn escaped.
Zhuāngzōng, who favored Xíngqīn,
summoned Xíngzhōu, comforted and rewarded him,
and wished to place him under his own command.
However, he also remembered that he had already taken Xíngqīn from Míngzōng's command,
and feared that taking Xíngzhōu as well
might hurt Míngzōng's feelings.
So he secretly sent someone to tempt Xíngzhōu with wealth and position.
Xíngzhōu declined, saying:
"The Grand Commander employs people
also for the sake of the state;
serving the Grand Commander is like serving the King.
My brothers and I,
escaped disaster and were reborn,
having received the Grand Commander's profound kindness,
how could we betray him!"
(Note: Tōngjiàn Kǎoyì states: Míngzōng was then the Cìshǐ of Dàizhōu,
and only became Fùzǒngguǎn in Tiānyòu 18th year.
This is likely an error in Zhōu Tàizǔ Shílù,
which Xuē Shǐ failed to correct.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
When the two armies were encamped by the river,
scouts reported that the Liáng army had entered Yángcūn Zhài from Biàn.
Míngzōng arrived at Dòumén in the morning,
setting an ambush to intercept them,
but being outnumbered,
was instead caught.
At that time, spears and halberds were densely gathered,
and the situation was very perilous.
Xíngzhōu heard of it,
and led his cavalry to strike the Liáng army laterally,
thus enabling Míngzōng to escape.
When Míngzōng attacked Yùnzhōu,
Xíngzhōu was the vanguard.
It happened that at midnight, heavy rain fell,
and people had no desire to advance.
Xíngzhōu said:
"This is heaven's aid;
they must be unprepared."
That night,
he crossed the river and entered the East City,
Ān Shěnhuī,
courtesy name Míngyuǎn,
was the elder brother of Shěnqí.
He began his career as the Commander of the Zhǎngzhí Army,
then transferred to become the Commander of the Left Wing of the Outer Yá.
He followed Zhuāngzōng to pacify Yōu and Jì,
fought in Shāndōng,
and pacified Hénán;
he participated in all these achievements.
During the Tóngguāng reign,
he was appointed Prefect of Yùzhōu.
In the early Tiānchéng reign,
he was transferred to become Vice Defender of Rǔzhōu,
then successively served as Vice Military Governor of Fèngxiáng and Xúzhōu, and Campaign Manager of Hédōng.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne (lit. 'dragon soared'),
he was appointed Acting Garrison Commander of Zhènwǔ Military with the title of Senior Official of the Hegemon's Prefecture.
He was then promoted to Military Governor of Héyáng.
Less than a month later, he was transferred to command Fūzhōu.
He observed mourning for his parent,
then was reinstated to his duties.
In the fifth year,
Lǐ Jīnquán rebelled in Ānzhōu.
An imperial edict ordered Mǎ Quánjié to be the Grand Commander,
leading troops to suppress him.
(Quánjié
was originally written
as "Quánjī";
it is now corrected according to the *Tōngjiàn*.
(Adhesive note from the photocopy collection)) Shěnhuī was made his deputy.
After Ānlù was pacified,
he was transferred to command Dèngzhōu,
and promoted to Provisional Grand Tutor.
In the winter of the sixth year,
Ān Cóngjìn rebelled in Xiāngzhōu,
leading the forces of Hànnán to attack Nányáng from the north.
Nányáng had no city walls,
only defending the Yá City.
When the rebels reached the city walls,
Shěnhuī ascended the battlements
and summoned the rebel leader to reprove him.
Cóngjìn was unable to overcome it and retreated.
After Xiāngzhōu was pacified,
he was additionally appointed Provisional Grand Preceptor.
When the Young Emperor succeeded to the throne,
he was further appointed Provisional Grand Master,
relieved of his command,
and appointed Commander of the Right Yǔlín Army.
After more than a year,
he was sent out to command Shàngdǎng.
When the Qìdān invaded,
he was appointed Military Governor of Xíngzhōu.
Not long after,
his eye disease suddenly flared up.
He submitted a memorial requesting a replacement,
and returned to the capital
to recuperate for several years.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he summoned Shěnhuī to the inner hall,
and consulted him at leisure.
He greatly admired and respected him.
He intended to appoint him to office with emoluments,
but Shěnhuī declined, citing his old age,
wishing to retire and enjoy his old age.
He was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ tàishī) and retired,
ennobled as Duke of Lǔ,
with a cumulative stipend of five thousand households,
and a true stipend of four hundred households.
He died in the spring of Guǎngshùn second year,
at the age of sixty-three.
The court was suspended for two days.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Grand Counselor (shìzhōng)
and the posthumous name Jìng.
His son, Shǒulín,
served the imperial dynasty as Grand Master of Zànshàn.
(From *Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn* scroll 18,144.)
Ān Shěnxìn,
courtesy name Xíngguāng,
was Shěnqí's paternal cousin.
His father, Jīnyòu,
was for generations a border general of the Shābù,
whose fame was known in the borderlands.
Shěnxìn was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
His paternal uncle, Jīnquán,
in the early Tiānchéng reign,
was Military Governor of Zhènwǔ,
and appointed him as a Staff General.
Soon after, his elder brother, Shěntōng, became Military Governor of Cāngzhōu,
and employed him as Commander of the Yá Inner Provost.
He successively served as Commander of the Horse and Foot Armies for the three prefectures of Tóng, Shǎn, and Xǔ.
When Jìnzǔ started his uprising in Tàiyuán,
the Last Emperor of Táng ordered Zhāng Jìngdá to attack him with troops.
(Jìngdá
was originally written
as "Jìngyuǎn";
it is now corrected according to Ōuyáng Shǐ.
(Adhesive note from the photocopy collection)) Shěnxìn, leading his subordinate troops, was the first to defect and enter Bìngzhōu.
Jìnzǔ, seeing him as an old friend,
was greatly pleased to have him.
His wife and two sons in the capital
were all executed by the Last Emperor of Táng,
only sparing his elderly mother.
After the Qìdān had surrendered the Jìn'ān Fortress,
Jìn Gāozǔ appointed Shěnxìn as Prefect of Fénzhōu, Provisional Grand Guardian,
and concurrent Deputy Commander of the Horse and Foot Armies.
When Jìnzǔ entered Luò,
he was appointed Military Governor of Hézhōng,
Provisional Grand Preceptor, and Co-administrator of Affairs with the Grand Imperial Secretariat.
Shěnxìn's nature was capricious
and often suspicious and jealous.
When he was in Púzhōng,
whenever an imperial envoy announced a decree,
if the retinue was slightly numerous,
he would secretly prepare defenses
to guard against any plot against himself.
He successively served as commander of Xǔ and Yǎn prefectures.
Wherever he went, he made gathering wealth his priority,
which greatly distressed the people.
When the court planned a major northern expedition,
all regional commanders were to participate as generals.
Shěnxìn was appointed Commander of the Right Wing of the Horse and Foot Armies.
Soon after, he was transferred to Military Governor of Huázhōu.
In the early Hàn dynasty,
he was transferred to command Tóngzhōu,
then entered the court as General-in-Chief of the Left Guard.
In the early Guó dynasty,
he was transferred to General-in-Chief of the Right Jīnwú.
In the fourth month of summer, the third year,
Tàizǔ entered the Guányuán Hall and the inner chambers.
Shěnxìn did not attend his assigned position,
and was impeached by the censor.
An imperial edict pardoned him.
At that time, Shěnxìn had been ill for a long time,
and his mind was confused.
Hearing the impeachment by the Censorate,
he declared:
"Being a little late for court
is not a major offense.
Why impeach me?
I will eventually offer twenty thousand *mín* [to the emperor]
and drive away all these beggars!"
Not long after,
he requested retirement due to illness,
and was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (tàizǐ tàishī) and retired.
He died in the autumn of that year,
at the age of sixty.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Counselor (shìzhōng)
and the posthumous name Chéngmù.
(From *Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn* scroll 18,144.)
Lǐ Cóngmǐn,
courtesy name Shúdá,
was the nephew of Táng Míngzōng.
He was profound and taciturn,
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and resourceful.
Initially,
Zhuāngzōng summoned him for an audience,
tested his archery and horsemanship,
and appointed him Commander of the Yá Inner Cavalry.
He followed to pacify Biàn and Luò,
and was appointed Commander of the Tent-Front.
He was promoted to Commander of the Běngshèng Guard.
When Míngzōng transferred his command to Zhēndìng,
he memorialized for Cóngmǐn to be Commander of the Chéngdé Army's Horse and Foot Armies.
Cóngmǐn followed Míngzōng into Luò,
and was appointed Imperial City Commissioner,
then left to become Military Governor of Shǎnfǔ.
When Wáng Dū rebelled in Dìngzhōu,
Wáng Yànqiú was ordered to be the Commander of the Expedition,
leading troops to suppress him.
Cóngmǐn was made his deputy,
and concurrently Military Governor of Cāngzhōu.
After Wáng Dū was pacified,
he was transferred and appointed to Dìngzhōu.
Soon after, he replaced Fàn Yánguāng as Military Governor of Chéngdé,
was additionally appointed Provisional Grand Preceptor,
and ennobled as Prince of Jīng.
(Jīng Wáng
was originally written
as "Wèi Wáng";
it is now corrected according to Ōuyáng Shǐ.
(Adhesive note from the photocopy collection))
Féng Huī,
a man from Wèizhōu.
Initially, he was a soldier of the Xiàojié Army.
He was strong and brave, skilled in cavalry and archery,
and feared by his comrades.
He first served Yáng Shīhòu as a company commander.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng entered Wèi,
he designated the Yínqiāng Xiàojié (Silver Spear Valiant Warriors) as his imperial guards.
When facing the Liáng forces across the river,
Huī, feeling that his provisions were meager,
absconded into the Southern Army.
The Liáng general Wáng Yànzhāng placed him under his command.
When Zhuāngzōng pacified Hénán,
Huī confessed his crimes
and was pardoned.
He followed Míngzōng in the campaign against Lùzhōu
and earned merit by executing Yáng Lì.
He also followed Wèi Wáng Jìjí in the campaign against Shǔ.
After Shǔ was pacified,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Kuízhōu.
At that time, Gāo Jìxīng of Jīngzhōu rebelled,
and with his troops attacked its city.
Huī resisted him,
repeatedly defeating the Jīng forces.
During the Chángxīng reign,
he became Cìshǐ of Xīngzhōu,
establishing his administrative seat in Gānqú.
When the two Chuān regions rebelled
and the Shǔ people invaded,
Huī, finding his forces vastly outnumbered,
fled back to Fèngxiáng.
The imperial court was angered by his loss of the city
and issued an edict for him to be stationed in a bureaucratic post in Tóngzhōu.
Not long after,
he followed Jìn Gāozǔ in the campaign against Shǔ.
The Shǔ people defended Jiànmén.
He led his subordinate troops to cross the treacherous terrain
and emerged from another path to the left of Jiànmén to launch a surprise attack,
slaughtering almost all of the defending soldiers.
When Jìnzǔ returned with his army,
the imperial court appointed Huī as Cìshǐ of Chánzhōu.
(Chánzhōu,
originally written as
"zhōu" (州),
is now corrected according to Ōuyáng Shǐ.
(From the slip in the photocopy edition)) In the early Tiānfú reign of Jìn,
Fàn Yánguāng rebelled and occupied Yè.
He appointed Huī as the Mǎbù Dūjiāng
and Sūn Ruì as the Jiānjūn.
From Liùmíngzhèn, they crossed the river,
intending to ambush Huátái.
They were soon defeated by the imperial army.
Huī retreated back to Yè
to defend the city for Yánguāng.
In the autumn of the following year,
Huī surrendered during a sortie,
and was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Huázhōu and Jiǎnxiào Tàifù.
After Yè was pacified,
he was transferred to command Língwǔ.
Previously,
Zhāng Xīchóng had been stationed in Língzhōu.
Having been in the Northern Frontier for a long time,
he was quite knowledgeable about border affairs.
Within several years,
invasions and banditry had ceased.
After Xīchóng died,
there was no commander-in-chief,
and the Fan tribes engaged in raids and plunder
without fear.
The imperial court, knowing Huī's reputation for strength and ferocity
was heard in distant lands,
therefore entrusted him with the post.
When Huī arrived at the commandery,
he held a grand banquet.
With abundant wine and delicacies,
the various barbarians became drunk
and competed to offer congratulations.
Huī rewarded them all with brocade and silk,
which greatly pleased the Fan tribes.
Tuòbá Yànzhāo of the Dǎngxiàng,
who was the leader of the largest tribe in the region,
came to visit Huī upon his arrival.
Huī treated him generously,
even building a residence for him
and providing him with lavish clothes and ornaments.
He then kept him, not allowing him to return to his tribe.
As a result, horses and sheep from Héxī
became easy to trade.
Within a year, Huī acquired five thousand horses,
and the Fan tribes submitted to him,
which caused concern in the imperial court.
(According to the biography of Yào Yuánfú in the Lóngpíngjí: The three tribes of Xīróng attacked Língzhōu,
and Yuánfú was ordered to assist Fèng Huī, the Jiédùshǐ of Shuòfāng, in suppressing them.
Shuòfāng was seven hundred *lǐ* from Wēizhōu.
The land had no water or grass
and was called
"Dry Sea."
When provisions arrived,
Huī ran out of food.
The next morning, they marched forty *lǐ*,
but tens of thousands of enemy cavalry blocked the key pass.
Huī was greatly afraid
and sent someone to offer bribes and seek a truce.
Though agreed,
by midday, it was still undecided.
Huī said:
"What should we do?"
Yuánfú said:
"They only want to exhaust us.
Observing their situation,
although the enemy is numerous,
those arrayed against the Western Mountain are
their elite troops.
I request to lead the elite forces to first strike the Western Mountain.
If they show a little fear,
we should raise a yellow banner as a signal."
Huī approved of his plan
and slaughtered almost all of them.
(Kǎoyì of the Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ))
In the early Kāiyùn reign of Jìn,
Sāng Wéihàn, who was assisting in governance,
wished to launch a major campaign
to control the Northern Rong.
He appointed fifteen generals and aides,
all of whom were regional commanders.
Only Huī was not among them.
He then submitted a memorial explaining his situation,
stating that he was not yet old and still capable of service,
yet had been omitted from the imperial decree.
The imperial edict replied:
"It is not that the imperial decree forgot,
but truly Shuòfāng is a critical location,
and the Fan tribes are watching the border.
Without your heroic reputation,
how could they be suppressed?
We had intended to transfer you to the interior,
but finding a replacement would also require an exceptional talent."
Huī was very pleased to receive the edict.
He then conveyed his feelings and requested a transfer to Bīnzhōu,
and was immediately granted the *jiéyuè* (credentials of a military governor).
Before he could reach Bīn,
he was appointed to Shǎanzhōu instead.
Huī offered a thousand horses and five hundred cattle.
Not long after being in Shǎan,
he was appointed Shìwèi Bùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
also concurrently governing Héyáng.
Wáng Lìngwēn was then appointed Jiédùshǐ of Língwǔ.
Since Huī was in charge of the imperial guards
and concurrently governed a nearby commandery,
being detained by the imperial court,
he somewhat regretted leaving Língwǔ.
When Féng Yù and Lǐ Yàntāo held power,
Huī served them well.
Not long after,
Huī was again appointed Jiédùshǐ of Shuòfāng,
and additionally granted Jiǎnxiào Tàishī.
When Hàn Gāozǔ founded the dynasty,
he was additionally granted Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
When Yǐndì ascended the throne,
he was additionally granted concurrent Shìzhōng.
In the early period of the state,
he was additionally granted Zhōngshūlìng
and enfeoffed as Chénliú Wáng.
In the summer of Guǎngshùn three,
he died of illness
at the age of sixty.
He was posthumously granted Wèi Wáng.
His son, Jìyè,
was Shuòfāng Yánèi Dūyúhòu.
After Huī's death,
the three armies requested that he be appointed to manage the military affairs of the prefecture.
He was then appointed Jiǎnxiào Tàibǎo
and served as the Shuòfāng Bīngmǎ Liúhòu.
During the Qiándé reign of the Imperial Dynasty,
he was transferred to the interior,
and is now the Jiédùshǐ of Tóngzhōu.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 18133.
His younger brother, Xíngyǒu (行友), subsequently became the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Dìngzhōu (定州).
During the Qiándé (乾德) reign of the Imperial Dynasty,
because of her heretical deceptions that misled the populace,
an imperial edict ordered the destruction of the Lángshān (狼山) Buddhist temple.
Her (the nun's) decayed bones were moved to the capital,
and sent to be cremated in the northern suburbs.
Xíngyǒu (行友) was made a Grand General of the Imperial Guards.
From then on, the heretics ceased.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn (永樂大典), Volume 3561.
According to Xù Tōngjiàn Chángbiān (續通鑑長編): In the eighth month of the second year of Jiànlóng (建隆),
Sūn Xíngyǒu (孫行友), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yìchéng (義成) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事),
had been in his post for over eight years,
and the influence of the demonic nun Shēnyì (深意) of Lángshān (狼山) grew even stronger.
When the emperor first ascended the throne,
Xíngyǒu (行友) felt uneasy,
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to resign and return to the mountains,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Xíngyǒu (行友) feared,
and thus began to repair his armor and weapons,
intending to abandon his treasury,
and return to occupy the mountain stronghold to rebel.
The Commander of Cavalry and Infantry, Lè Jìnèng (樂繼能), secretly reported the matter.
The emperor sent the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Insignia, Wǔ Huáijié (武懷節), to ride swiftly to gather troops from Zhèn (鎮) and Zhào (趙),
falsely claiming to patrol the border,
and directly entered Dìngzhōu (定州).
Xíngyǒu (行友) did not realize it.
Eventually, an edict was issued and shown to him,
ordering his entire clan to return to the imperial court.
Xíngyǒu (行友) hastily obeyed the command.
Upon his arrival,
the Imperial Censor Shìyùshǐ (侍御史), Lǐ Wéiyuè (李維岳), was ordered to immediately investigate and ascertain the facts.
On the day of Jǐyǒu (己酉),
an imperial decree stripped Xíngyǒu (行友) of his official titles and ranks,
and confined him to his private residence.
The corpse of the nun Shēnyì (深意) was taken
and burned in the northwestern corner of the capital city.
Xíngyǒu’s (行友) younger brother, Fāngjìn (方進), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yìzhōu (易州),
and his nephew, Quánhuī (全暉), the Commander of Bǎosài (保塞) Garrison,
both went to the imperial court to await punishment.
An imperial edict pardoned them.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì (舊五代史考異))
The Historian said: In the final years of the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
enemy cavalry rode unhindered,
and the Central Plains had no master.
Although Emperor Gāo (漢祖) thought of saving the drowning,
he had not yet succeeded in his southern campaign.
Zhào Huī (趙暉) first initiated change in the suburbs of Shǎn (陝),
jointly supporting the righteous cause.
In the rise of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
Huī (暉) was instrumental;
to appoint him as a vassal
was without shame.
Shǒuyēn (守恩) seized the opportunity to show loyalty,
though commendable,
his love of profit and cruelty to the people,
what was there to value?
Yǔnquán (允權) and Fāngjiàn (方諫),
during an era of upheaval,
usurped the power of a screen and bulwark.
How far they are
from the meritorious officials whose portraits were painted on the Yúntái (雲臺) Terrace!
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn (永樂大典), Volume 3561.)

Zhōu Shū (周書), Volume 17, Biographies No. 6
Féng Dào (馮道),
courtesy name Kědào (可道),
a native of Jǐngchéng (景城), Yíngzhōu (瀛州).
His ancestors were farmers and scholars,
not fixed in their profession.
Dào (道) was pure and gentle in his youth,
fond of learning and skilled in writing.
He was not ashamed of poor clothes and food.
Besides carrying rice to support his parents,
he solely devoted himself to reading, reciting, and chanting.
Even when heavy snow blocked the door,
and dust lay thick on the mat,
he remained serene.
During the Tiānyòu (天祐) reign,
Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) appointed him as a clerk in Yōuzhōu (幽州).
When Shǒuguāng (守光) led troops to attack Zhōngshān (中山),
he consulted his subordinates.
Dào (道) always advised him on the advantages and disadvantages.
Shǒuguāng (守āng) was enraged
and imprisoned him,
but he was soon rescued.
When Shǒuguāng (守āng) was defeated,
Dào (道) fled back to Tàiyuán (太原).
The Overseeing Army Envoy, Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業), appointed him as the Patrol Officer of his administration.
Chéngyè (承業) valued his literary accomplishments and conduct
and treated him very well.
At that time, there was a man named Zhōu Xuánbào (周玄豹),
who was skilled in judging character.
He did not get along with Dào (道)
and said to Chéngyè (承業):
"Féng Shēng (馮生) has no future;
you should not promote him excessively."
At that time, Lú Zhì (盧質), the Secretary of Hédōng (河東), heard this and said:
"I once saw a portrait of Sīkōng (司空) Dù Huángshāng (杜黃裳).
Dào’s (道) appearance is strikingly similar to his.
He will certainly be greatly employed in the future.
Xuánbào’s (玄豹) words are not to be trusted."
Chéngyè (承業) soon recommended Dào (道) as an Attendant Official of the Hegemon's Prefecture,
and shortly thereafter appointed him as the Chief Scribe of Tàiyuán (太原).
At that time, Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) had conquered Hébĕi (河北),
and official documents were very numerous;
he entrusted everything to Dào (道).
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) and the Liáng (梁) army were arrayed against each other across the river.
One day,
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) stated that the large number of accompanying officers at meals
made it impossible for the steward to manage,
and requested a reduction.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) angrily said:
"I am not even free to provide meals for those who serve me.
For the three prefectures of Hébĕi (河北),
let the three armies choose another person to be their commander.
I request to return to Tàiyuán (太原) to make way for the worthy."
He immediately ordered Dào (道) to draft the statement in his presence,
intending to show it to his troops.
Dào (道) held the brush for a long time.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) sternly urged him,
and Dào (道) slowly rose and replied:
"As the one in charge of brush and inkstone,
how dare I not perform my duty?
Currently, Your Majesty has repeatedly achieved great merits
and is about to pacify the southern rebels.
The advice from Chóngtāo (崇韜)
is not overly inappropriate.
It is acceptable to reject it,
but one should not use such words
to stir up public opinion.
If the enemy were to know,
they would say that there is discord between Your Majesty and your ministers.
I hope you will consider it carefully;
then the world will be most fortunate."
Shortly thereafter, Chóngtāo (崇韜) came in to apologize,
due to Dào’s (道) intervention.
People then began to respect his courage.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) ascended the throne in Yè (鄴) Palace,
Dào (道) was appointed as a minister of the imperial secretariat (Shěngláng, 省郎)
and Hanlin Academician (Hànlín Xuéshì, 翰林學士),
and was granted the purple robe from his green one.
When the Liáng (梁) dynasty was pacified,
he was promoted to Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén, 中書舍人) and Vice Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng, 戶部侍郎).
Upon his father's death,
he observed mourning in Jǐngchéng (景城).
(According to Tán Yuàn (談苑), it is said: When Dào (道) heard of his father's death,
he immediately walked until he saw stars,
and his family followed with his clothing bag, catching up with him.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì (舊五代史考異))) During a lean year,
he distributed all his surplus salary to his hometown.
Dào’s (道) dwelling
was only a thatched cottage.
(Péngcí (蓬茨),
originally written as
"Féngcì" (逢次),
now corrected according to Cèfǔ Yuánguī (冊府元龜).
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān (影庫本粘籤)))
He accepted no gifts from local officials,
not even a peck of grain or a bolt of silk.
At that time, the Qìdān (契丹) were powerful
and had heard of Dào’s (道) reputation.
They wanted to abduct him,
but coincidentally, the border people were prepared,
and he escaped capture.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn (永樂大典), Volume 403.)

Reflecting on the beginning and end,
blessings extend to the living and the dead,
all from the grace of the state,
all from family tradition,
following the principles of instruction and teaching,
touching the source of moral cultivation,
being filial at home,
being loyal to the state,
no unrighteous words spoken,
no ill-gotten gains entering the door.
My wish is not to deceive the earth below,
not to deceive people in the middle,
not to deceive
heaven above,
taking these three "not deceiving" as my principle.
When humble, so it was;
when noble, so it was;
when young, so it was;
when old, so it was.
In serving parents, serving the sovereign, serving elders, and dealing with others,
I was greatly
favored by Heaven's forgiveness,
repeatedly experiencing hardship yet gaining much fortune,
once trapped by barbarians yet returning to the Central Plains.
This was not by human planning,
but by Heaven's blessing.
Within the six directions, there are fortunate ones.
After a hundred years, there will be a resting place.
Do not place pearls or jade in the mouth,
but rather use everyday clothes for burial,
and use mats for the coffin,
and choose land where no food is grown for burial,
because I am not
equal to the ancients.
Sacrifice with a single sheep,
to caution against taking life.
Sacrifice with things that do not harm life.
Do not erect a spirit tablet,
because the tombs of the Three Dynasties did not
have tablets erected.
Do not request a posthumous title,
because I lack virtue.
I also reflect that from being a subordinate official to a chief minister and when leading a frontier region,
there might have been minor benefits to the state
or notable actions,
all recorded in public documents.
As for my writings and poems,
due to many events, some were lost,
but what was collected
is compiled in a family collection.
Within them, my aspirations can be seen.
(Within them, my aspirations can be seen;
the original text is suspected of being erroneous.
According to Xuē Shǐ cited in Cèfǔ Yuánguī,
