(Yǐngkùběn niánqiān)) Those who know me,
those who criticize
me,
I do not know how many there are.
I have estates, residences, and numerous books,
and two sons who can inherit my legacy.
On this day, I wash five times,
and examine myself thrice daily,
still
knowing daily what I lack,
and not forgetting monthly what I am capable of.
As a son, as a younger brother, as a minister, as a teacher, as a husband, as a father,
I have sons and nephews,
and grandchildren.
In terms of personal conduct, I have more than enough.
But for the times, it is not enough.
What is not enough?
I could not help the great sovereign achieve unification and pacify the four directions,
I am truly ashamed of
my successive offices and ranks.
How can I repay the beneficence of Heaven and Earth?
Sometimes opening a scroll,
sometimes drinking a cup,
tasting flavors, discerning sounds, clothed in colors,
will I rest peacefully in this generation?
Old
and self-content,
what joy is like this!
This preface was written by Zhū Míngyuè, Chánglèlǎo, in the third year of Qiányòu.
The two poems "[My] courtyard is like a tranquil Chan heart,"
etc.,
attributed to the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shǎoshī),
should also be genuine works from this year.
They have now been removed by people,
and the stone carvings no longer exist;
perhaps someone has obtained old copies.
There are also two letters of family inquiry to his nephew, the Imperial Censor (Shìyù),
posthumously inscribed as "in the first month of summer in the guǐchǒu year of Guǎngshùn."
The genuine works are in the home of a scholar in Luòyáng.
Furthermore, there is a judgment on a house contract of over fifty characters,
carved by someone in the home of the late Director of the Bureau of Personnel (Zhífāng Láng), Lǐ, in Luòyáng.
It has no year,
but only states "the sixteenth day of the seventh month,
Yáng Cǎomíng, Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shǎoshī)."
This should also be during the Guǎngshùn period.
The family genealogy also states: The Yáng clan, who practiced self-cultivation during the Táng dynasty,
originated from the family branch of the Duke of Yuè (Yuègōng).
Its root source was Xié (Jié), the Chancellor of Zhōngshān.
His second son, Jì, begot Huī, the Prefect of Luòzhōu.
Huī begot Ēn, the Administrator of Héjiān.
Ēn begot Jūn, Duke Gōng of Yuè (Yuègōng).
They moved to reside in Féngyì.
Down to Zàngqì, they moved to Xúnyáng.
Yízhēn, the father of Yáng Shōu, a Chancellor of Táng,
had four sons,
whose given names all contained the radical
"yòu" (又).
They were Fā, Jiǎ, Shōu, and Yán,
taking their meaning from the four seasons.
Therefore, all of Fā's sons' names contained the radical
Jiǎ's sons the radical
"huǒ" (火);
Shōu's sons the radical
"jīn" (金);
and Yán's sons the radical
"shuǐ" (水).
Yán begot Shè;
Shè begot Níngshì.
And Shōu was Zàngqì's elder brother and Shè's paternal uncle.
The "Biographies of the Six Ministers of Táng" in the Xīn Wǔdài Shǐ (New History of the Five Dynasties) mistakenly states that Shōu was Shè's grandfather
and Yán's father.
This is incorrect.
The biography also states: Yáng Níngshì,
courtesy name Jǐngdù,
was a descendant of Yáng Sù, Duke of Yuè (Yuègōng) of the Suí dynasty,
and the son of Yáng Shè, a Chancellor of Táng.
He was naturally intelligent and perceptive,
skilled in cursive and clerical scripts,
and adept at literary composition.
During the Zhaōzōng reign, he passed the jinshì examination
and became a Circuit Official of the Bureau of Finance (Dùzhī Xúnguān),
then successively promoted to Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Láng)
and Compiler in the Imperial Academy of History (Zhíshǐguǎn).
In the Kāipíng era of the Liáng dynasty,
he served as Palace Censor (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ) and Supernumerary Secretary of the Board of Rites (Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng).
He then left to be invited by Zhāng Quányì of the Western Capital
to serve as a Retainer of the Acting Commissioner (Liúshǒu Xúnguān).
Zhào Guāngyì, a Chancellor of Liáng, valued his talent
and nominated him to be a Bachelor of the Jíxián Academy (Jíxiándiàn Zhíxuélshì),
later changing to Supernumerary Secretary of the Board of Civil Office (Kǎogōng Yuánwàiláng).
In the early Tóngguāng era of Táng,
he became a Director of the Bureau of Judicial Administration (Bǐbù Lángzhōng) and then Drafter of Imperial Edicts (Zhī Zhìgào),
later changing to Supervising Secretary (Jǐshìzhōng) and Compiler and Editor of the Imperial Academy of History (Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn),
presiding over the affairs of the academy.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
During the Chángxīng era,
he successively served as Right Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary (Yòu Sànqí Chángshì) and Vice Minister of Works, Rites, and Revenue (Gōng, Lǐ, Hù Sān Shìláng).
Later, due to illness, he was relieved
and made Supervisor of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān).
In the early Qīngtài era,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng),
and again returned to Luòyáng due to illness.
During the Tiānfú era of Jìn,
he was promoted to Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Bīnkè),
and shortly thereafter was appointed Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) and retired.
During the Kāiyùn era,
Chancellor Sāng Wéihàn memorialized to reinstate him as Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo) with concurrent duties.
During the Qiányòu era of Hàn, he successively held the posts of Junior Tutor (Shǎofù) and Junior Mentor (Shǎoshī).
In the Guǎngshùn era of Zhōu,
he again requested retirement,
and was appointed Minister of the Right (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè) upon retirement.
In the early Xiǎndé era, he was changed to Minister of the Left (Zuǒ Púyè) and Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
In the winter of the first year
he died in Luòyáng
at the age of eighty-two,
and was posthumously granted Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
Initially,
Níngshì's father and grandfather
were prominent during the Táng dynasty.
When Shè served as Chancellor under Emperor Ài,
treacherous officials were arrogant and contemptuous,
the royal house was in ruins and turmoil,
and many virtuous people suffered misfortunes.
When Shè received the imperial decree,
he tearfully said to Níngshì:
"The world is at its extreme.
I am caught in a snare and cannot escape;
disaster will soon strike
and also implicate you."
When Zhū Quánzhōng usurped the Táng dynasty,
Shè was supposed to deliver the Imperial Seal.
Níngshì remonstrated, saying:
"Your Excellency, as Chancellor, has allowed the state to reach this point.
This is not without fault.
To then hand over the Son of Heaven's seals and ribbons to another,
even if you preserve your wealth and status,
what will the historical records say a thousand years from now!"
At that time, Quánzhōng feared that old Táng officials
would be disadvantageous to him.
He often secretly inquired about public opinion,
and many people who were suspected of disloyalty
consequently suffered disaster.
Shè often did not feel secure.
Suddenly hearing Níngshì's words,
he was greatly alarmed and said:
"You will destroy my clan!"
Níngshì, fearing the matter would be exposed,
then feigned madness.
And Shè, by exercising humility,
ultimately avoided the disaster of the Liáng dynasty.
All those who governed Luòyáng were princes and dukes of the time.
Níngshì sometimes acted haughtily and did not adhere to proper etiquette.
The governors also, considering his distinguished talent and mad honesty,
did not blame him.
Níngshì was originally from a renowned family.
Since he did not meet a favorable time,
yet at the juncture of Táng and Liáng,
he established himself through integrity and righteousness,
possessing a broad and magnanimous spirit.
He ultimately avoided the calamities of the Five Dynasties
and died at a venerable age.
There were many calligraphic works of his in the Buddhist temples of Luòyáng.
During the Xīngguó era of this dynasty,
the great temples and pagodas of the Three Rivers region
were mostly dilapidated,
with few brushworks remaining.
Now, a few murals still exist.
Scholars and high officials also cherished his calligraphic works,
all preserving them as refined objects of appreciation.
The world considered Níngshì's running script to be quite similar to Yán Lǔgōng's,
hence it was called Yán-Yáng.
(Kǒng Běn)
Xuē Rénqiān,
courtesy name Shǒuxùn,
resided in Hédōng for generations.
In recent times, his family moved to Biàn,
and he is now a native of Jùnyí.
His father, Yánlǔ,
served the Táng dynasty as Grand Administrator of Rǔzhōu (Rǔzhōu Chángshǐ),
and was posthumously honored as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
Rénqiān was cautious, honest, incorruptible, and strict,
deeply understanding worldly affairs.
Luó Shàowēi, the Prince of Yè (Yè Wáng) of Liáng, greatly esteemed him
and repeatedly appointed him to various official positions in his administration.
When Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng ascended the throne in Wèi,
he was appointed Palace Usher (Tōngshì Shèrén).
In the Kāipíng era of Liáng,
he was sent on a mission to Wú,
performing his diplomatic duties commendably.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of the Imperial Guards (Wèiwèi Shǎoqīng) and Deputy Envoy for Receiving Guests (Yǐnjìn Fùshǐ),
and was successively given the concurrent title of Minister of War (Jiǎnjiào Bīngbù Shàngshū).
During the Chángxīng era,
he was transferred to Commissioner of the Guest Department (Kèshěng Shǐ) and Vice Minister of the Court of Diplomatic Receptions (Hónglú Shǎoqīng).
He was sent out as Deputy Military Commissioner of Jiànxióng (Jiànxióngjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ),
advanced in rank to Grand Master of Imperial Splendor (Guānglù Dàfū) and concurrently Grand Minister of the Left (Jiǎnjiào Zuǒ Púyè),
and then changed to Vice Minister of Ceremonies (Guānglù Shǎoqīng).
In the early Tiānfú era of Jìn,
he was appointed concurrently Grand Minister of Works (Jiǎnjiào Sīkōng) and Deputy Military Commissioner of Hézhōng (Hézhōng Jiédù Fùshǐ).
Upon returning to court, he became Vice Minister of the Imperial Guards and Vice Minister of the Imperial Stud (Wèiwèi, Tàipú Èrqīng).
After mourning his stepmother,
and completing the mourning period,
he was appointed Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng).
In the Qiányòu era of Hàn,
he retired from his current office.
In the early Zhōu dynasty,
he was changed to Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Bīnkè) upon retirement,
and was further given the concurrent title of Grand Minister of Education (Jiǎnjiào Sītú),
and elevated to the rank of marquis.
In the winter of the third year of Xiǎndé,
he died of illness
at the age of seventy-eight.
He was posthumously granted Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū).
Initially,
when Rénqiān followed Emperor Zhuāngzōng into Biàn,
his former residence had been occupied by Lǐ Bīn, the Six Residences Commissioner (Liùzhái Shǐ) of the Liáng court.
(Lǐ Bīn,
originally written as
"Lǐ Bīn" (李彬) in the text,
now corrected according to the Cèfǔ Yuánguī.
(Yǐngkù Běn Niánqiān)). At that time, Bīn had gone far away,
and Rénqiān regained his residence.
Someone reported that
Bīn's family members had hidden a large amount of gold and silk within the residence.
Rénqiān immediately ordered Bīn's relatives to take all their hidden possessions out before he entered.
Commentators praised this act.
Zǐ Zhèng
served as the Ménxià Shìláng and Píngzhāngshì of the Imperial Court.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 21367.)
Xiāo Yuàn,
courtesy name Wéigōng,
was the son of Liáng Chancellor Qǐng.
Qǐng,
during the reign of Míngzōng, ultimately served as Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo,
and has a biography in the Táng History.
Initially,
Yuàn's great-grandfather, Fǎng,
became chancellor during the reign of Emperor Xīzōng of Táng.
During an occasion when he was receiving guests,
Yuàn, as a child, playfully
imitated the sounds of announcing visitors.
Fǎng said to his guests:
"How dare I rejoice at having obtained office,
but I am fortunate to have long-lived descendants through the generations,
and now I even have a great-grandson right before my eyes."
When Yuàn reached adulthood, he passed the imperial examination,
and was appointed 校書郎 (Jiàoshū Láng) upon taking off his coarse clothes.
He was later transferred to Jīwèi, Zhí Shǐguǎn, and Jiānchá Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ.
He was promoted to Bǐbù Yuánwài, Yòusī Lángzhōng, and Tàicháng Shǎoqīng.
During the reign of Míngzōng, when sacrifices were made at Tàiwēi Palace,
Yuàn, while drunk, joined the ranks of the high officials,
and was impeached by the Censor.
He was demoted to Yòu Zànshàn Dàfū.
Not long after,
he was appointed Bīngbù Lángzhōng,
and regained his golden and purple robes.
After observing mourning for his mother,
and when the period of mourning ended,
he was appointed Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū from Zuǒsī Lángzhōng.
He successively held the positions of Jǐshìzhōng, Yòu Chángshì, and Mìshū Jiān,
and was later transferred to Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
He died in the spring of Guǎngshùn first year.
He was posthumously granted Lǐbù Shàngshū.
Yuàn was naturally pure and cautious.
When serving his parents,
he always wore his belt and appeared before them.
However, he was excessively fond of alcohol,
and his duties were neglected.
When he was Bīngbù Lángzhōng,
he often held the seal for official appointments.
During an amnesty,
he was rather remiss in his duties.
His father, Qǐng, then Lìbù Shàngshū,
took his place to oversee the seal.
Such was his laxity.
Yuàn died at over seventy years old.
His mother was still alive.
His entire family enjoyed longevity,
a rare feat for others.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 5225.)
Lú Sǔn
was originally from Fànyáng,
but his recent ancestors served in Lǐngbiǎo.
His father, Yǐng,
traveled and served as an official in the capital.
Sǔn began studying literature at a young age.
In the early Jiākāipíng era of Liáng,
he passed the imperial examination.
He had a rather resolute and upright character,
and prided himself on his noble sentiments and refined demeanor.
He passed the examination in the same year as Rèn Zàn, Liú Chāngsù, Xuē Jūn, and Gāo Zǒng.
They often mocked each other wherever they went,
and people at the time
called them the "Mutual Insult List" (Xiāngmà Bǎng).
When Rèn Zàn and Liú Chāngsù held important positions,
Sǔn distinguished himself
and did not associate closely with them.
At that time, Zuǒ Chéng Lǐ Qí, who had always disdained Liú Chāngsù's character,
always treated Sǔn kindly.
Qí had a younger sister who was blind in one eye,
and had remained unmarried into old age.
He therefore married her to Sǔn.
Sǔn admired Qí's reputation and accepted the marriage.
When Qí became a chancellor,
he helped Sǔn advance in his career.
During the Zhēnmíng era of Liáng,
he was successively promoted to Yòusī Yuánwàiláng.
In the early Tiānchéng era of Táng,
he was transferred from Bīngbù Lángzhōng and Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn to Jiànyì Dàfū.
He frequently submitted memorials on affairs of state,
but his words and reasoning were superficial and lacking,
and he was not recognized by eminent scholars.
During the Qīngtài era,
Lú Wénjì became chancellor,
and secretly consulted Sǔn on current political affairs.
Initially,
during the Chángxīng era,
when the Last Emperor of Táng was garrisoned in Hézhōng,
Sǔn once served as a deputy for the Jiā'ēn Shǐ.
When the Last Emperor ascended the throne,
he appointed Sǔn as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
On the day he accepted the appointment,
he declared that the previous Censorate had failed to uphold principles
and caused the customs to deteriorate.
He then made extensive proposals,
which included the phrase:
"Release the keys at dawn,
and guard the principle when the sun rises."
This greatly
ridiculed by scholars.
A short while later,
he mistakenly reviewed an amnesty decree,
allowing a criminal to be released,
and was suspended from office.
During the Tiānfú era of Jìn,
he was reinstated as Yòu Sànqí Chángshì,
and then transferred to Mìshū Jiān.
Greatly disappointed,
he immediately submitted a memorial resigning from his position.
He was then appointed Hùbù Shàngshū and retired,
residing in Yǐngchuān.
At that time, Shǎobǎo Lǐ Lín, nearly eighty years old,
was skilled in breathing exercises and qìgōng.
Sǔn, seeing Lín's advanced age and mastery of Daoist arts,
greatly admired him.
As Yǐngchuān was too close to the city,
he decided to settle in Yángzhái,
clearing weeds and planting herbs,
wearing rustic clothes,
and living leisurely among the woods and gardens.
When he went out, he used a rustic cart and wore a crane cloak,
calling himself the Jùcí Shānréng.
In his later years, with five or six peers,
he channeled a spring and dug a cave in Dàkuí Mountain as a hermitage,
vowing never to leave the mountain again.
After a long time,
his teeth and hair showed no signs of aging,
as if he had achieved something.
He died in the autumn of Guǎngshùn third year,
at over eighty years old.
He was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Shǎofù.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 2212.)
Wáng Rényù,
courtesy name Déliǎn,
was from Tiānshuǐ.
He was orphaned young
and did not follow teachers' instructions.
At twenty-five,
he finally decided to study.
One night, he dreamed of having his intestines opened,
and drawing water from the Xījiāng River to wash them.
He also saw sand and stones in the water,
all bearing seal script.
He then took and swallowed them.
When he awoke,
his mind was suddenly clear,
and from then on, his natural intelligence was exceptionally high.
(Note: There is missing text here.
The Yúdì Jìshèng states: When Wáng Rényù was in charge of the imperial examinations,
the thirty-three jinshì he selected
were all renowned high officials of their time,
with Lǐ Fǎng and Wáng Pǔ at the forefront.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì)) He composed over ten thousand poems,
compiled into a hundred volumes,
titled Xījiāng Jí,
because he once dreamed of swallowing inscribed stones from Xījiāng,
and thus named it.
Later, he became Bīngbù Shàngshū and Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo,
and died.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī, Volume 893.
Wǔdài Shǐ Bǔ: Minister Wáng Rényù,
in the early Qiányòu era,
released a list of two hundred and fourteen successful candidates,
and then composed a poem:
"Two hundred and fourteen disciples,
their feathers light as spring breeze begins to stir,
they exchange gold for the cassia in the sky,
and steal their names from the list by digging through walls."
Táo Gǔ, then a Minister,
was known for his humor.
Upon seeing the poem, he pretended to exclaim:
"Amazing,
amazing!
I didn't expect Wáng Rényù to be a bandit chief today!"
All who heard burst into laughter.
(Note in Yúdì Jìshèng: Rényù's works include Zǐní Jí, Xījiāng Jí, and Rùluò Jì,
totaling one hundred volumes.
(Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì))
Qí Zàngzhēn,
from a young age served in various internal posts,
and was successively promoted to various General of the Guards (zhūwèi jiāngjūn) positions.
Before and after, he supervised and led troops outside,
and was quite praised as a capable official.
However, he was treacherous and immoral,
cruel and eloquent,
and everyone feared his sharp tongue.
During the Guǎngshùn reign,
he was ordered to patrol and protect the river dikes in Huázhōu prefecture,
but due to his slackness, the river breached.
He was stripped of his official title
and exiled to Shāmén Dǎo.
When Shìzōng was in the western ranks,
he was among the same cohort as Zàngzhēn.
Whenever he listened to his discussions,
or his analyses of current affairs,
it seemed there was something worth adopting.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was recalled from exile.
During the campaigns in Qín and Fèng,
he was ordered to oversee a detached force.
And when troops were deployed on the Huái River,
he was again entrusted with supervision,
leading troops with military commander Hé Chāo to capture Guāngzhōu.
Zàngzhēn defrauded and concealed many public properties.
Hé Chāo considered this unacceptable,
to which Zàngzhēn said:
"I already have several rooms on Shāmén Dǎo,
so going back there wouldn't be a problem."
Such was his disregard for the law.
After Shìzōng broke the Zǐjīnshān stockade,
he pursued the Wú bandits to Guōkǒu.
(Guōkǒu
was originally written as
"Tóngkǒu";
it has now been corrected according to the Tōngjiàn.
(Sticky note in the photographic copy)) He then spoke with Zàngzhēn about the victory.
He replied:
"Your Majesty's divine martial achievements
are unparalleled in recent times,
but in terms of civilian virtue, they have not yet fully shone."
Shìzōng nodded in agreement.
He then asked about the matter of Yángzhōu.
He replied:
"Yángzhōu is indeed low and damp,
and its food is usually fishy and rotten.
When I was there last year,
people offered me eel.
Looking at the coiled shape in the plate,
it was exactly like a poisonous snake (huī).
Even if a crane (guànquè) had knowledge,
it wouldn't eat it,
let alone a human!"
His memorials were mostly of this kind,
and those who heard them were invariably startled.
One day,
he again memorialized, saying:
"Táng Jǐngsī has already become a Cìshǐ,
but I have not yet received Your Majesty's favor."
Shìzōng bowed his head and complied.
At that time, Háo Liáng had not yet been captured,
but he immediately appointed him as the acting Cìshǐ of Háozhōu.
When Zhāng Yǒngdé and Lǐ Chóngjìn had a dispute,
Zàngzhēn often tried to persuade Chóngjìn.
When the troops returned from Shòuyáng,
some of the generals reported Zàngzhēn's words to the emperor.
Shìzōng was enraged
and immediately summoned him to the capital.
In the summer of the fourth year,
on the charge of falsely claiming an Inspector (jiǎnjiào) official title,
he was tried and executed for his deeds,
presumably because the emperor did not wish to expose his other evil acts.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 18133.)
Wáng Huán
was originally from Zhēndìng.
In the early Tiānchéng reign of the Táng dynasty,
Mèng Zhīxiáng garrisoned Xīchuān.
Wáng Huán went to serve him.
When Zhīxiáng established his reign title,
Huán commanded the military guards.
When Mèng Chǎng succeeded to the throne,
Huán concurrently held the positions of Left and Right Guards.
In the autumn of the second year of Xiǎndé,
the imperial army campaigned westward.
At that time, Huán was the Jiédùshǐ of Fèngzhōu.
Initially,
a detached force besieged the city,
but was defeated by Huán,
and their副将 (píjiàng) Hú Lì was captured by Huán.
That winter,
the imperial army gathered in large numbers
and fiercely attacked the city.
The Shǔ reinforcements successively retreated in defeat.
Upon hearing this, Huán
strengthened his defenses even further.
The imperial army attacked for several months before finally capturing it.
When the city fell,
Huán was captured.
When he arrived at the capital,
Shìzōng, recognizing his loyalty to his former lord,
pardoned his crime
and appointed him as Right Xiāowèi Dàjiāngjūn.
In the winter of the fourth year,
Shìzōng launched a southern campaign.
Huán followed the emperor to Sìzhōu,
where he fell ill and died.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 18133.)
Zhāng Yànchāo
was originally from the Shātuó tribe.
He had long suffered from a debilitating illness,
and was at the time known as
"The Lame One" (bǒzi).
Initially,
he served Táng Zhuāngzōng with his equestrian and archery skills as a Mǎzhí Jūnsǐ.
When Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
he was appointed Shénwǔ Zhǐhuīshǐ.
(Shénwǔ
was originally written as
"Zhòngwǔ";
it has now been corrected according to the Tōngjiàn.
(Sticky note in the photographic copy)) Míngzōng once adopted him as a foster son.
During the Tiānchéng reign,
he was promoted to Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu.
He had always been at odds with the Jìn Gāozǔ.
When the latter was in charge of the army in Tàiyuán,
he surrendered his city to the Qìdān,
who then appointed him as Jiédùshǐ of Yúnzhōu.
When the Qìdān invaded the south,
Yànchāo led his troops,
causing considerable trouble for Zhèn and Wèi.
When the Qìdān entered Biàn,
he was promoted to Shìwèi Mǎjūn Dūxiào;
soon after, he was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Jìnchāng Commandery.
When Hàn Gāozǔ entered Luò,
Yànchāo immediately sent a memorial expressing his loyalty
and was transferred to be Jiédùshǐ of Bǎodà Commandery.
In the early Qiányòu reign,
he was recalled to the capital by imperial decree,
and merely served as a court attendee (zhāoqǐng) thereafter.
When Tàizǔ entered Yè to quell the internal strife,
Yǐndì ordered Yànchāo to command the cavalry to resist.
During the mutiny at Liú Zǐpí,
Yànchāo first went to meet Tàizǔ.
During the Guǎngshùn reign,
he was appointed Shénwǔ Tǒngjūn.
In the winter of the third year of Xiǎndé,
he died of illness at his residence.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Tàizǐ Tàishī.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 5360.)
Tài Zǔ鎮Yè,
concurrently holding command over the northern forces,
Jùn served as supervising general,
remaining stationed in Yèchéng.
When the palace coup of Yǐndì broke out,
Jùn was also framed by various small-minded individuals,
and his entire family was harmed.
From the time he accompanied Tài Zǔ to the capital,
weaving strategies in the war council,
and contributing to important matters,
Jùn was foremost among them.
After the capital was pacified,
he received an order from the Hàn Empress Dowager
to serve as Privy Council Commissioner (Shūmìshǐ).
When Tài Zǔ marched north,
arriving at Chánzhōu,
and was pressured by various armies,
Jùn and Wáng Yīn, upon hearing the news in the capital,
immediately dispatched Gūo Chóng, the Grand Commander of the Palace Cavalry, to Sòngzhōu,
and Mǎ Duó, the former Prefect of Shēnzhōu, to Xǔzhōu,
to guard against other changes.
The two prefectures remained peaceful,
which was also due to Jùn's planning.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Pingzhāngshì,
and soon after also held the posts of Yòupúshè, Ménxià Shìláng, and Pingzhāngshì,
overseeing the compilation of the National History.
At that time, the court was newly established,
and there were many troubles across the four directions.
Jùn served day and night,
doing everything he knew how to do.
Whenever he attended Tài Zǔ to discuss military affairs,
he never left without spending a long time,
proving to be of great benefit.
However, his nature was impetuous,
his actions often reckless.
He took all affairs of the world upon himself.
Whenever he made a request,
he often acted on his own will.
If Tài Zǔ followed and assented to him,
he would withdraw happily.
If it was not readily approved,
he would immediately become displeased,
and disrespectful words would often be uttered according to the situation.
Tài Zǔ had always known his character,
and also because of his assistance in establishing the dynasty,
he always treated him with leniency.
Jùn was two years older than Tài Zǔ.
Although Tài Zǔ held the highest position,
he sometimes called him "elder brother,"
and sometimes called him by his courtesy name,
not forgetting their friendship from their humble days.
Jùn became even more conceited because of this.
In the winter of the first year of Guǎngshùn,
Liú Chóng and the Qìdān besieged Jìnzhōu.
Jùn requested to lead an expedition to reinforce it.
Tài Zǔ appointed him Grand Commander of the Field Army,
with Wáng Yànchāo, the Military Governor of Xúzhōu, as his deputy.
An edict ordered all armies to be under Jùn's command,
allowing Jùn to act as he saw fit.
Funds for military operations
were to be supplied by the government,
and accompanying generals and officials
could be chosen by him.
Before his departure,
a banquet was held for him at Zīdé Diàn,
where Tài Zǔ presented female musicians to honor him.
On the day he took his leave,
he received generous favors,
not bound by ordinary regulations.
When he departed,
Tài Zǔ went to Xīzhuāng,
personally attending the farewell banquet,
and separately bestowed an imperial horse and a jade belt,
bidding him farewell with a handshake.
Jùn reached Shǎn and stayed there for several nights.
Liú Chóng's attack on Jìnzhōu was very urgent,
and Tài Zǔ worried it could not be held.
He considered leading a personal expedition,
entering via the Zézhōu route,
to rendezvous with Jùn,
first sending a message to Jùn.
Jùn sent an urgent dispatch
requesting the imperial carriage not to proceed.
At that time, an imperial edict had already been issued,
and the departure date was set.
When Jùn's memorial arrived,
it was stopped.
After Jùn's army passed Jiàngjùn,
and was one day's march from Píngyáng,
the enemy burned their camps
and fled in disarray.
Jùn entered Jìnzhōu.
Some requested to pursue the enemy,
believing there would be great advantage.
Jùn hesitated for a long time.
Only the next day did he dispatch cavalry to raid the enemy,
returning after two nights.
Had Jùn pursued with all his might,
then the scourge of Bīng and Fén
would have been completely wiped out.
Jùn was also deeply ashamed of his lack of achievement,
and so he planned to expand and repair the old city of Píngyáng before returning.
At that time, Lǐ Hóngxìn, the Military Governor of Yǒngxīngjūn,
was a close relative of the Hàn imperial house.
Since Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he constantly harbored feelings of worry and dejection.
And the troops in his city numbered less than a thousand.
When Jùn went on expedition to Shǎnzhōu,
using the rescue of Jìnzhōu as a pretext,
he drew several hundred men.
And when Liú Chóng fled north,
he also sent over a thousand imperial guards
to garrison Jīngzhào.
Hóngxìn, fearing,
then requested to come to court.
When Jùn's army returned,
Tài Zǔ bestowed generous rewards.
At that time, Mùróng Yànchāo rebelled in Yǎnzhōu.
(Yànchāo
was originally written as
"Yànshào,"
now corrected according to the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.

(From the note on the photostatic copy)) Cáo Yīng, the Grand Commander of the Palace Infantry, and Xiàng Xùn, the Director of the Department of Guests, had already been dispatched to lead troops to attack him.
Jùn wished to personally lead troops to suppress the rebels,
repeatedly saying to Tài Zǔ:
"Mùróng is a vicious bandit;
Cáo Yīng is not easily his match."
Tài Zǔ remained silent.
Soon after, he personally led an expedition,
appointing Jùn as the Grand Commander of the Imperial Escort.
On the day the rebels were defeated,
Jùn commanded his troops south of the city,
and his men were the first to scale the walls,
showing considerable pride.
After returning to the capital with the imperial entourage,
he soon submitted a memorial requesting to resign from his pivotal post,
and immediately retired to his private residence.
Jùn was greedy for power and profit,
full of schemes,
fond of dispensing small favors,
and liked people to be attached to him.
In the early days of Tài Zǔ's ascension,
he strove to maintain modesty,
and his former subordinates from before his rise were not yet greatly promoted.
Later, Zhèng Rénhuì, Lǐ Chóngjìn, Xiàng Xùn, and others were gradually promoted to important positions.
Jùn resented them in his heart.
Thus, he sought to retire,
probably to gauge Tài Zǔ's intentions.
Before presenting his request,
he sent many letters to various feudal lords
seeking guarantees.
Within ten days,
messengers from all circuits galloped in to deliver Jùn's letters,
and those who heard about it were astonished.
Jùn submitted three memorials in succession.
Imperial envoys conveying messages were sent daily.
Tài Zǔ prepared his carriage to visit his residence.
Jùn, upon hearing this,
immediately galloped his horse to meet him.
Tài Zǔ comforted him for a long time,
then ordered him to resume his duties.
Jùn also built a separate public office
to the east of his residence,
with corridors and halls for official business,
tall, spacious, and extravagantly decorated.
When the construction was finished,
he invited Tài Zǔ to visit,
and received very generous gifts.
Later, a small new hall was built in the imperial garden.
Jùn saw it
and memorialized, saying:
"There are already many palaces and houses,
what is the use of this one?"
Tài Zǔ replied:
"The Privy Council's offices are not few;
why did you build another one yourself?"
Jùn withdrew in shame and silence.
Yáng Xíngmì,
a native of Lúzhōu.
Orphaned and poor in youth,
he possessed great physical strength
and could travel three hundred *lǐ* a day.
During the chaos of the Zhōnghé reign of Tang,
when the Son of Heaven fled to Shǔ,
the prefect of the commandery dispatched Xíngmì to convey a report on foot,
and he returned as scheduled.
(Note: *Běimèng Suǒyán* states that Zhèng Qǐng once managed Yáng Xíngmì as an official for foot reports in his prefecture.)
In the early Guāngqǐ reign,
Qín Zōngquán harassed Huáinán,
repeatedly attacking Lúzhōu and Shòuzhōu.
The prefect of the commandery recruited those capable of leading an attack and capturing bandits,
rewarding them according to their achievements.
Xíngmì, with his courage and strength, volunteered,
and invariably achieved success wherever he went.
He was appointed as a队长 (duìzhǎng, captain).
Xíngmì then personally recruited over a hundred men,
all fierce and unruly individuals.
He killed the commander,
and assumed authority over the prefectural troops.
The prefect immediately handed over the tally and seal and departed.
The imperial court then formally appointed Xíngmì as the Cìshǐ (刺史, Prefect) of Lúzhōu.
In the third year of Guāngqǐ,
Gāo Pián, the Jiédùshǐ (節度使, Military Governor) of Yángzhōu, misgoverned,
entrusting power to insidious figures like Lǚ Yòngzhī.
His牙将 (yájiàng, adjutant general) Bì Shīduó, fearing slander from Yòngzhī,
raised an army from Gāoyóu to attack Guǎnglǐng.
He was repelled by Yòngzhī,
and so sought aid from Qín Yàn of Xuānzhōu,
promising that if the matter was successful,
he would hand over the governorship of Yángzhōu to him.
Yàn first sent his general Qín Chóu with three thousand soldiers to assist Shīduó in capturing Guǎnglǐng.
Gāo Pián appointed Shīduó as Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬, Assistant Military Commissioner).
Not long after,
Qín Yàn led a large force, including their families, across the river
and entered the military headquarters of Yángzhōu,
claiming the title of Jiédùshǐ for himself.
Initially,
before Yángzhōu fell,
Lǚ Yòngzhī falsely issued a proclamation in Gāo Pián's name,
summoning troops from Lúzhōu.
When the city fell,
Xíngmì arrived abruptly with an army of ten thousand men.
When Bì Shīduó entered Guǎnglǐng,
Lǚ Yòngzhī fled outside,
and at this point pledged allegiance to Xíngmì.
Xíngmì attacked Guǎnglǐng,
setting up camp at Dàmíng Sì.
Qín and Bì led out troops to attack Xíngmì's camp.
As soon as the close combat began,
Xíngmì feigned retreat.
Qín and Bì's troops eagerly rushed into his palisade
to seize gold and silk.
Xíngmì then unleashed his ambush troops to attack them.
Qín and Bì suffered a great defeat,
retreating to their fortifications.
From then on, they did not venture out to fight again.
In the ninth month of that year,
Qín and Bì murdered Gāo Pián in his confinement,
killing both young and old.
They were buried in a common pit beneath the northern wall of the Dàoyuàn (Daoist temple).
Xíngmì's siege became increasingly urgent,
and food in the city ran out.
Rice cost forty thousand (cash) per *dǒu*,
and the inhabitants resorted to cannibalism until almost none were left.
In the tenth month,
the city fell.
Qín and Bì fled to Dōngtáng.
(Dōngtáng,
originally written as
"束唐" (Shùtáng),
is now corrected according to the *Xīn Táng Shū*.)
Xíngmì entered Guǎnglǐng
and transported grain from the outer camps to feed the starving people.
On that very day, the price of rice dropped to three thousand (cash).
In the eleventh month,
Sūn Rú, a bandit from Cài, arrived suddenly from Huáixī with ten thousand men,
and reoccupied the outer camps.
Xíngmì's baggage, cattle, sheep, and military provisions that had not yet entered the city
all fell into Rú's possession.
At this time, Qín and Bì came from Dōngtáng
and joined Rú's army.
From then on, the area outside the west gate
again became enemy territory.
Initially,
Lǚ Yòngzhī met Xíngmì in Tiāncháng
and deceived Xíngmì, saying:
"Yòngzhī has five thousand ingots of white gold
buried under the eaves of his residence.
When the bandits are pacified,
I wish to use it to fund a celebratory feast for the generals and soldiers."
By this time,
as Xíngmì reviewed his troops,
Yòngzhī was at his side.
Xíngmì said to Yòngzhī:
"Púshè (僕射, Minister), you promised these men silver.
How could you break your word!"
He immediately ordered him to be beheaded under the Sānqiáo (Three Bridges)
and his clan exterminated.
Having taken Guǎnglǐng,
Xíngmì dispatched an envoy to Dàliáng
to express his intention of submission.
At this time,
Liáng Zǔ (Ancestor of Liang) concurrently held command of Huáinán.
He therefore sent his adjutant general Zhāng Tíngfàn as an envoy to Huáinán
to form an alliance with Xíngmì.
Soon after, he sent Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Lǐ Fán to temporarily oversee the affairs of the Huáinán Liúhòu (留後, acting military governor),
and ordered commander Guō Yán to escort him with troops.
Xíngmì initially treated Tíngfàn with great courtesy,
but upon hearing of Lǐ Fán's journey,
he abruptly showed an intention to defy the order.
Tíngfàn, fearful,
changed clothes and fled by night.
He met Liáng Zǔ in Sòngzhōu
and fully explained Xíngmì's rebellious intentions,
but considering his military strength, it was not yet feasible to attack him.
Thus, Lǐ Fán and others were recalled.
(Note: *Tōngjiàn* states: Lǐ Fán reached Xūyí,
and Xíngmì dispatched troops to attack him.
Guō Yán fought fiercely and escaped.
This differs from Xuē's history.
(*Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*))
Liáng Zǔ then appointed Xíngmì as the Huáinán Liúhòu.
In the first month of the first year of Wéndé,
Sūn Rú killed Qín Yàn and Bì Shīduó in Gāoyóu,
then led his army to attack Guǎnglǐng
and conquered it. Rú declared himself Jiédùshǐ.
Xíngmì gathered his followers and returned to Lújiāng.
In the eleventh month,
Liáng Zǔ sent his general Páng Shīgǔ from Yǐngshàng across the Huái River
to suppress Sūn Rú's rebellion.
Shīgǔ led his troops deep into the Huáidiàn region,
suffered a defeat,
and returned.
In the first year of Lóngjì,
Sūn Rú marched out to attack Xuānzhōu.
Xíngmì took advantage of the vulnerability to attack and occupy Yángzhōu,
and made contact with Shí Pǔ to the north.
Sūn Rú then led his troops to attack Xíngmì again.
In the first year of Dàshùn,
Xíngmì was in a perilous situation,
and led his forces to flee by night,
taking up position in Xuānzhōu.
Rú re-entered Yángzhōu.
In the second year,
Rú mustered and trained his troops and armor to attack Xíngmì.
However, an epidemic struck Jiāng and Huái,
and many of his soldiers died.
Rú also fell ill,
was captured by his subordinates,
delivered to Xíngmì,
and killed.
Xíngmì marched triumphantly from Xuānchéng into Guǎnglǐng,
acquiring all of Sūn Rú's forces.
From the end of Guāngqǐ,
after Gāo Pián's loss of control,
Xíngmì, Bì Shīduó, Qín Yàn, and Sūn Rú successively coveted and plotted against each other.
For six or seven years,
wars constantly erupted,
and within the eight prefectures,
everything was reduced to desolate wilderness,
for hundreds of *lǐ* around,
human habitation ceased.
After Xíngmì annexed Sūn Rú,
he recruited and gathered the scattered populace
and allowed the people to recuperate.
His governance was lenient and straightforward,
which was beneficial to the common people.
He mustered troops and trained generals
to pursue hegemonistic rule.
The forces he gained from Sūn Rú
were all fierce and courageous warriors from Huáixī.
He selected five thousand men and kept them in his official residence,
providing them generously with clothing and food.
When driven to battle,
none failed to vie for the vanguard.
Their armor and helmets were all adorned with black silk,
and they were named
"Hēiyún Dū" (Black Cloud Troop).
In the second year of Qiánníng,
Xíngmì gained full control of the Huáinán region.

Emperor Zhāozōng then issued an imperial decree appointing Xíngmì as Fùdàshǐ (副大使, Deputy Grand Envoy) of Huáinán Jiédù, acting as Jiédùshǐ, concurrently overseeing all matters of the territory's agriculture, observation, and administration, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司, Grand Commissioner, Minister of the Right, and Duke of the Grand Imperial Family), Jiǎnjiào Tàifù (檢校太傅, acting Grand Tutor), Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (同中書門下平章事, concurrently Minister of the Central Secretariat and Minister of the Chancellery), and concurrently Chángshǐ (長史, Chief Clerk) of Yángzhōu Dàdūdū Fǔ (大都督府, Grand Military Command),
Shàng Zhùguó (上柱國, Pillar of the State), and Hóngnóng Jùnwáng (弘農郡王, Prince of Hóngnóng Commandery),
with an enfeoffment of three thousand households
and a true enfeoffment of one hundred households.
In the first year of Xiǎndé, third month,
Zhōu Shìzōng personally led an expedition.
He fought Chóng at Gāopíng
and utterly defeated him.
Chóng, with a dozen or so personal cavalrymen, fled over the mountains.
In the middle of the night, he was confused and disoriented,
not knowing where to go.
He seized a villager and forced him to act as a guide.
By mistake, they headed towards the Jìnzhōu road,
and only realized their error after traveling over a hundred *lǐ*.
Chóng was enraged
and killed the guide.
He then found another road and departed,
changing his name and title.
He wore a毛褐 (máo hè) and a 張樺笠 (zhāng huà lì) as he traveled.
Upon reaching Qìnzhōu,
he and his three to five followers on horseback stopped at a rural dwelling.
They suffered greatly from cold and hunger.
He secretly ordered a messenger to inform the false Inspector Lǐ Tínghuì.
Lǐ Tínghuì provided him with a meal and took off his own clothes and furs to give to him.
Whenever they reached a subordinate county,
the county officials would offer food.
Before the spoons and chopsticks were even lifted,
they would hear that the Zhōu army was approaching
and would immediately flee in a panic.
Chóng was old and exhausted;
he slumped on his horse,
fleeing day and night,
barely able to sustain himself.
When he was one *shè* from Tàiyuán,
his son Chéngjūn came to welcome him at night with a hundred soldiers and escorted him into the city.
When the Zhōu army reached the city walls,
Chóng was intimidated
and remained shut inside the fortress, not daring to come out.
After more than a month,
Shìzōng then withdrew his army.
In the second year of Xiǎndé, eleventh month,
Chóng died of illness.
His son Chéngjūn inherited the false throne.
The events concerning Jūn
are fully recorded in the *Huángjiā Rìlì*.
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 9999.)
The court historian remarks:
"Shǒuguāng rebelled against Heaven and went against the Way,
something unheard of since ancient times.
Even when facing execution,
he still sought to avoid death.
Not only was this the ultimate evil,
but it was also the height of foolishness.
Liú Shèng occupied the southern extreme to proclaim himself a hegemon
during a time of great turmoil in the Central Plains.
By the time of his descendants,
they encountered our prosperous dynasty,
and though they perished from exhaustion,
their lineage was not extinguished,
which was also their good fortune.
Liú Chóng, a remnant of a fallen state,
usurped the title of a false king;
it is clear that he did not know his own limitations.
Now, although the principal villain has perished,
the remaining evil still exists.
Their power is constrained and their people are suffering;
what else can they await but destruction!"
(Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, Volume 9999.)
Collation Notes
Biographies of Usurpers and Pretenders, Part 3
Wáng Jiàn
(The biography of Wáng Jiàn
is missing from the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn.
However, having examined the *Cèfǔ Yuánguī*'s chapter on Usurpers and Pretenders, which cites Xuē Shǐ,
the events concerning Wáng Jiàn are quite complete from beginning to end.
We have now arranged and connected them,
marking the volume numbers from *Cèfǔ Yuánguī*
for verification.
This is hereby appended as a note.
(Sticky note from the photographic edition)) was a native of Xiàngchéng, Chénzhōu.
In the late Táng dynasty,
he was listed in the Zhōngwǔ Army.
Qín Zōngquán, based in Cáizhōu,
offered heavy rewards to recruit him.
Jiàn initially rose from the ranks to become a military commandant (*jūnhóu*).
During the Guǎngmíng era,
Huáng Cháo captured Cháng'ān,
and Xīzōng fled to Shǔ.
At that time, Liáng Zǔ was a general under Cháo,
leading troops to attack Xiāng and Dèng.
Zōngquán dispatched the junior officer Lù Yànhóng, accompanying Supervisor Yáng Fùguāng, to lead troops to attack them.
Jiàn also participated in this campaign.
That year,
Yáng Fùguāng entered to reinforce the capital,
and the following year, he defeated the rebels and recovered the capital city.
Initially,
Yáng Fùguāng organized 8,000 men from the Zhōngwǔ Army into eight divisions (*bādū*).
Yànhóng and Jiàn were each a division commander (*dūxiào*).
After Yáng Fùguāng's death,
Yànhóng led the eight divisions to escort the emperor in his traveling palace.
Upon reaching Shānnán,
he proceeded to plunder various prefectures and counties like Jīn and Shāng,
amassing tens of thousands of soldiers.
He advanced and pressed towards Xīngyuán.
The military governor (*jiédǔshǐ*) Niú Cóng abandoned the city and fled.
Yànhóng then appointed himself acting military commissioner (*liúhòu*),
appointing Jiàn and others as inspectors (*cìshǐ*) of subordinate prefectures,
but did not allow them to take up their posts.
Soon after, Yànhóng was officially granted the military insignia.
Fearing that his subordinates would plot against him,
he often acted with cruelty.
Because of this, his troops became disloyal.
Jiàn was on good terms with another general, Hán Jiàn.
Yànhóng grew more suspicious of the two Jiàns,
pretending to treat them generously
and inviting them into his private quarters.
The two Jiàns were frightened.
At night, they ascended the city walls to comfort the defenders.
Under the moonlight, they conspired together about their future direction.
Wáng Jiàn said to Hán Jiàn:
"The Lord Protector's sweet words and generous treatment
mean he suspects me.
Disaster is imminent;
we should choose a beneficial course of action soon."
Hán Jiàn replied:
"Good."
Consequently, he led 3,000 men towards the emperor's traveling palace.
Xīzōng praised him
and bestowed upon him immense wealth.
He divided his troops into five divisions,
still led by the old commanders,
namely Jìn Huī, Lǐ Shītài, Zhāng Zào, and the two Jiàns.
They were then called the "Five Divisions Escorting the Emperor,"
and Tián Lìngzī adopted them all as foster sons.
When Xīzōng returned to the palace,
Jiàn and the others were assigned to manage the Shéncè Army,
all holding distant titles of inspectors (*cìshǐ*).
In the third year,
Dégāng (德光) falsely changed the era name to Tiānxiǎn (天顯) first year.
This year,
Wáng Dū (王都) of Dìngzhōu (定州) rebelled,
(Wáng Dū (王都)
was originally written
"Wáng Yù" (王郁),
now corrected according to the Tōngjiàn (通鑑).
(From the sticky note in the Yǐngkù Běn (影庫本))) and sought aid from the Qìdān (契丹).
Dégāng (德光) then captured Píngzhōu (平州),
and sent Tūnèi (禿餒) with five thousand cavalry to assist Dū (都) in Zhōngshān (中山).
Wáng Yànqiú (王晏球), the Commissioner for Recruitment and Suppression, defeated them at Qǔyáng (曲陽).
Tūnèi (禿餒) fled and held the bandit city.
In the seventh month of that year,
he again sent Tìyǐn (惕隱) to lead seven thousand cavalry to relieve Dìngzhōu (定州).
Wáng Yànqiú (王晏球) met them in battle north of the Tánghé (唐河),
and greatly defeated them.
Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) of Yōuzhōu (幽州) used fresh troops to intercept them at a vital pass,
capturing Tìyǐn (惕隱) and over fifty other leaders alive,
and presented them at the imperial court.
The following year,
Wáng Dū (王都) was pacified,
Tūnèi (禿餒) and his remaining forces were captured,
and executed.
From then on, the Qìdān (契丹) suffered a major setback,
and for several years dared not approach the border.
They once sent the envoy Nàkuò Méilǐ (捺括梅里) to request Tūnèi's (禿餒) bones.
Míngzōng (明宗) was angered by their deceit
and executed him.
In the second year of Chángxīng (長興),
Dōngdān Wáng Tūyù (東丹王突欲) was at the imperial court.
His mother Jìfā (繼發) sent an envoy to report,
and the imperial court also treated him leniently.
At the end of Chángxīng (長興),
the Qìdān (契丹) pressed on Yúnzhōu (雲州).
Míngzōng (明宗) appointed Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hédōng (河東) and concurrent Grand Commissioner of Northern Barbarian and Han (Běimiàn Fānhàn Zǒngguǎn 北面蕃漢總管).
In the third year of Qīngtài (清泰),
Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) was besieged by Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) and others,
and sent the Commander Hé Fú (何福) with a memorial to request troops,
willing to become a subject.
Dégāng (德光) told his mother,
"Son dreamed yesterday that Shíláng (石郎) from Tàiyuán (太原) sent an envoy to our country.
Now he has indeed arrived.
(Note: The Qìdān Guózhì (契丹國志) states that Tàizōng (太宗) dreamed of Zhēnwǔ (真武) who told him to save Jìn (晉), which differs slightly from Xuē Shǐ (薛史).
(From Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì (舊五代史考異)))
and we must go."
Dégāng (德光) then personally led fifty thousand cavalry from Yànmén (雁門) to Jìnyáng (晉陽),
and on the same day, greatly defeated Jìngdá's (敬達) forces outside the city.
Soon after, Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) was enfeoffed as the Emperor of Great Jìn (Dà Jìn Huángdì 大晉皇帝),
agreeing to a relationship of father and son states,
and ceded the territory under Yōuzhōu's (幽州) jurisdiction, as well as Xīn (新), Wǔ (武), Yún (雲), Yìng (應), and Shuòzhōu (朔州) to him as a bribe,
and furthermore promised to pay three hundred thousand bolts of silk annually.
At that time, Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) of Yōuzhōu (幽州) was garrisoned in Tuánbǎi Gǔ (團柏谷),
and sent an envoy to the tent,
requesting to be established as emperor,
with the Shí (石) clan inheriting Tàiyuán (太原) for generations.
Dégāng (德光) pointed to a stone in front of the tent and said to the envoy,
"I have already promised Shíláng (石郎) a father-son alliance.
It can only be changed when this stone crumbles."
Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) and others killed Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) and surrendered to the Qìdān (契丹).
Dégāng (德光) jokingly said to Guāngyuǎn (光遠) and the others,
"You are really bad fellows.
You don't need salt or cheese,
you've eaten ten thousand warhorses instead."
Guāngyuǎn (光遠) and the others were greatly ashamed.
When Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) traveled south,
Dégāng (德光) personally escorted him to Lùzhōu (潞州).
At that time, Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) and Zhào Yánshòu (趙延壽) surrendered to the Qìdān (契丹) from Lùzhōu (潞州).
Dégāng (德光) locked them up
and ordered them to follow his imperial tent.
When Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) entered Luò (洛),
he soon sent the chancellor Zhào Yíng (趙瑩) to express gratitude to the Qìdān (契丹).
In the third year of Tiānfú (天福),
he again sent the chancellor Féng Dào (馮道) and the Left Grand Master of Remonstrance Liú Xùn (劉㫬) with credentials to confer honorific titles upon Dégāng (德光) and his mother,
bringing imperial insignia, ceremonial guards, court robes, and imperial carriages to their country to perform the rites.
Dégāng (德光) was greatly pleased,
and soon after sent an envoy to confer upon Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) the title of Yīngwǔ Míngyì Huángdì (英武明義皇帝).
This year,
the Qìdān (契丹) changed Tiānxiǎn (天顯) eleventh year to Huìtóng (會同) first year,
appointed Zhào Yánshòu (趙延壽) as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ 樞密使),
elevated Yōuzhōu (幽州) to Nánjīng (南京),
and appointed Zhào Sīwēn (趙思溫) as Resident Commissioner of Nánjīng (Nánjīng Líushǒu 南京留守).
Soon after, Dégāng (德āng) requested that Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) not refer to himself as a subject,
nor submit memorials,
and that correspondence between them only use family courtesies,
simply referring to himself as
"Er Huángdì" (兒皇帝) (Son Emperor).
Jìn Zǔ (晉祖) generously presented gold and silk to show his gratitude.
Jìn Zǔ (晉祖) served the Qìdān (契丹) with extreme deference,
always ensuring that seasonal greetings,
and rites of celebration and condolence,
were performed with utmost generosity.
Whenever an envoy from the enemy arrived,
he would immediately pay respects in a separate hall.
Whenever Dégāng (德光) made a request,
if it was even slightly unsatisfactory,
he would send blame and reprimand.
Jìn Zǔ (晉祖) always humbled himself to serve him,
and throughout Jìn Zǔ's (晉祖) reign,
there was almost no discord.
When the Young Emperor (Shàodì 少帝) succeeded to the throne,
he sent an envoy to the Qìdān (契丹).
Dégāng (德光) was angered that the Young Emperor (Shàodì 少帝) did not first seek his permission
and arbitrarily assumed the exalted position,
and that the documents he brought
omitted the etiquette of a subject.
His anger was great,
manifesting in blame and reprimand.
When the imperial court's envoy left,
he was immediately subjected to further rebuke and humiliation.
At this time, the Qìdān (契丹) envoy Qíao Róng (喬榮) was returning north.
Jǐng Yánguǎng (景延廣), the Commander-in-chief of the Palace Guard (Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ 侍衞親軍都指揮使), said to Róng (榮),
"The previous emperor was established by the Qìdān (契丹),
but the current ruler was enthroned by China itself.
It is acceptable to call oneself 'grandson,'
but not 'subject.'
China has its own one hundred thousand horizontal-grinding swords.
(Horizontal-grinding sword [Héngmójiàn 橫磨劍],
originally written
"grinding-horizontal sword" [Móhéngjiàn 磨橫劍],
now corrected according to the Tōngjiàn (通鑑).
(From the sticky note in the Yǐngkù Běn (影庫本)))
When Róng (榮) returned to his country,
he fully reported the matter.
Dégāng (德光) was greatly enraged.
At that time, Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) of Qīngzhōu (青州) rebelled,
and Dégāng (德光) sent an envoy to incite him.
In the winter of the following year,
Dégāng (德光) led his various tribes south.
In the spring of the first year of Kāiyùn (開運),
he captured Qízhōu (祁州),
and advanced directly to the Great River.
The Young Emperor (Shàodì 少帝) went to Chánzhōu (澶州) to resist them.
In the third month of that year,
Dégāng (德光) was defeated at Yángchéng (陽城),
abandoned his chariots and tents,
and rode a single mule to Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Because of his anger at the disorder,
all leaders from the grand chieftains downwards were flogged several hundred times,
except for Zhào Yánshòu (趙延壽).
At this time,
the Qìdān (契丹) had been invading for successive years,
the Jìn (晉) clan was exhausted by the constant rushing to battle,
and the border people suffered greatly,
having almost no day of peace.
Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰), the Jìn (晉) chancellor, advised the Young Emperor (Shàodì 少帝) to seek peace with the Qìdān (契丹)
to relieve the national crisis.
The Young Emperor (Shàodì 少帝) agreed,
and then sent an envoy with a memorial to declare himself a subject,
using humble words to admit fault.
When the envoy returned,
Dégāng (德光) replied,
"Only if Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) and Jǐng Yánguǎng (景延廣) come themselves,
and you cede Zhèn (鎮) and Dìng (定) to me,
then peace can be established."
The imperial court knew this was impossible,
and so stopped.
At this time, the various Qìdān (契丹) tribes had been campaigning for many years,
and the monarch and ministers of the tribal state were somewhat weary of war.
Dégāng's (德光) mother once said to the Han and tribal officials,
"How can the Han people of the Southern Dynasty simply lie down and do nothing?
From ancient times until now,
we have only heard of the Han coming to make peace with the barbarians,
never of the barbarians going to make peace with the Han.
When those Han people truly have a change of heart,
then I too will not be unwilling to establish good relations."
From the time of
Xuān-Huáng, who first established the celestial
mandate, when the year star was in
xīn-mǎo, the calendar system was perfected.
Thus, the Huáng-Dì first used the Xīn-Mǎo Lì,
Zhuān-Xù then used the Yǐ-Mǎo Lì,
Yú used the Wù-Wǔ Lì,
Xià used the Bǐng-Yín Lì,
Shāng used the Jiǎ-Yín Lì,
Zhōu used the Dīng-Sì Lì,
Lǔ used the Gēng-Zǐ Lì,
Qín used the Yǐ-Mǎo Lì.
The Hàn used the Tài-Chū Lì, the Sì-Fēn Lì, and the Sān-Tǒng Lì,
a total of three systems.
The Wèi used the Huáng-Chū Lì and the Jǐng-Chū Lì,
a total of two systems.
The Jìn used the Yuán-Shǐ Lì and the Hé-Yuán-Wàn-Fēn Lì,
a total of two systems.
The Sòng used the Dà-Míng Lì and the Yuán-Jiā Lì,
a total of two systems.
The Qí used the Tiān-Bǎo Lì, the Tóng-Zhāng Lì, and the Zhèng-Xiàng Lì,
a total of three systems.

In the second year, second month, on the *Xīnhài* day,
an edict stated:
"I, though of humble person,
have been entrusted with this great enterprise.
I think of those who are weary and distressed,
toiling in their waking and sleeping hours.
I sometimes worry that officials are not the right people,
thus causing disorder;
I sometimes worry that punishments are not commensurate with crimes,
leading to complaints and lamentations.
Where the King's transforming influence arises,
lawsuits and prisons are fundamental.
If there is no instruction and encouragement,
there will surely be delays and detentions.
Recently, the common people in various circuits
either violate laws excessively,
or engage in minor disputes.
Officials and their clerks manipulate the system,
cunningly seeking out flaws and pretexts.
Initially, they proliferate regulations and details,
creating laws to imprison people;
ultimately, they extort wealth and property,
buying favor for release.
Outwardly, they uphold public justice;
inwardly, they follow private feelings.
Those without reason are made to procrastinate further,
while those with reason reconsider and retreat.
This accumulates into errors and malpractices,
gradually losing the principles of governance.
From now on, it is strictly enjoined upon all local officials, *Zhōumù*, and *Xiànzǎi*,
to deeply understand Our mind,
and each perform their duties.
All investigations that are lacking
should be promptly and decisively resolved.
If anyone dares to negligently delay and prevaricate,
thus creating injustice and excess,
and a grievance is brought to the Censorate,
or a complaint is submitted to the suggestion box,
and the inquiry proves it true,
then the original investigating officials and clerks shall all be penalized.
The *Guānchásǐ* and *Cìshǐ* in each locality
shall be separately deliberated for court discipline.
It is fitting to order all circuit and prefectural administrations
to act according to this disposition,
and their subordinate prefectures
shall be strictly commanded by their respective circuits."
In the eighth month, on the *Dīngmǎo* day,
an edict stated:
"Regarding the criminal cases in the three capitals and various circuit prefectures,
recent inquiries reveal
that people detained, as before,
often do not have their cases quickly decided.
All circuits should instruct their respective chief administrators
to conduct thorough and dedicated investigations,
without any delays or detentions."
In the fourth month,
the former *Púzhōu Lùshì Cānjūn*, Cuī Cōng, submitted a memorial: (Note: The original text read
"崔瑽" (Cuī Cōng),
but has been corrected according to *Cèfǔ Yuánguī*.
( *Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*))
"Prisoners in various circuits,
I fear, are not being flogged in accordance with the law,
or they cannot bear the suffering and die,
which is then falsely reported as illness.
I request the establishment of sick prisoner wards,
and the provision of medicine."
The *Zhōngshū* replied, saying:
"If one is guilty and deserves punishment,
one looks to Heaven without regret;
if one dies without illness,
one goes to the underworld harboring a grievance.
Reviving cold ashes certainly requires utmost benevolence,
and shining light under an overturned basin certainly needs extraordinary discernment.
The injunction of 'Be reverent!' is recorded in books,
and the phrase 'It is punishment!' is marked in rituals.
This reveals goodness through weeping over the guilty,
and extends kindness by fanning those suffering from heat.
The request to establish sick prisoner wards
is approved.
Furthermore, the chief administrators in each locality
shall be entrusted with special attention.
Should there be sick prisoners,
physicians should be dispatched at once to examine them.
After treatment,
their cases shall be decided according to the severity of their crimes.
If anyone dares to deliberately violate this,
leading to a sick prisoner dying from injustice,
the officials of that locality
shall all be severely punished.
Additionally, every *Xiàzhì*,
once every five days,
people shall be sent to wash the cangues and fetters."
In the first year of *Yìngshùn*, third month, on the *Wùwǔ* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Regarding prisoners detained in the three capitals and various circuit prefectures,
their cases shall be speedily decided based on the severity of their crimes.
In recent times, delays have occurred because
cases requiring memorialization for decision
are inconvenient to categorize,
thus causing their retention.
Henceforth, for all criminal cases,
decisions shall be made according to reason.
Cases that are subject to imperial investigation and require memorialization
are not subject to this limitation."
In the first year of *Qīngtài*, fifth month, on the *Dīngchǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Regarding the prisoners currently detained in the capital's prisons and in the various prefectures throughout the realm,
it is now the time of poisonous heat,
and they cannot avoid the suffering of confinement.
Although I know they bear guilt,
I am particularly concerned.
I fear that legal officials may act on personal feelings,
delaying decisions.
Upon receipt of this edict,
chief administrators in each locality shall personally conduct inquiries
and speedily decide cases according to their severity,
without delay."
In the second year of *Jìn Tiānfú*, eighth month,
an edict was issued to the *Xíngbù*, *Dàlǐsì*, *Yùshǐtái*, and the three capitals and various circuit prefectures:
"Henceforth, should there be any detained prisoners who fall ill,
all military doctors in each locality shall be ordered to attend to them.
The cost of medicine shall be disbursed from public funds.
For those whose cases are minor,
their family members are also permitted to attend to them."
In the fourth year, ninth month,
Sāng Wéihàn, the *Jiédùshǐ* of Xiàngzhōu (Note: The original text erroneously read
"松州" (Sōngzhōu),
but has been corrected according to *Tōngjiàn*.
( *Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ Kǎoyì*)), reported:
"Regarding the properties seized from captured bandits in my jurisdiction,
it has always been confiscated,
said to be an old custom of Yèdū,
but no clear text is found in the legal codes."
An edict stated:
"Henceforth, for all bandits,
their crimes shall be determined according to the codes,
and their family property shall not be confiscated.
All prefectures throughout the realm
shall act according to this disposition."
In the third month, on the *Gēngwǔ* day,
the *Xiángdìngyuàn* reported:
"Lú Càn, the former *Hóngdòng Xiàn Zhǔbù*, submitted a proposal stating:
'I humbly observe that criminal cases are of utmost importance,
and are difficult for the court.
The *Shàngshūshěng* divides its duties among six departments,
and is called the 'Meeting Prefecture' by the realm.
Furthermore, when various circuits decide criminal cases,
if human lives are involved,
the *Xíngbù* should not be unaware.
I wish to request that after prefectures and circuits decide capital crimes,
they report to the *Xíngbù* quarterly whether there were any such cases.
They should also record the details of the case files,
and submit the names of the presiding officials, the *Mǎbù Dōuyúhòu*, the *Sīfǎ Cānjūn*, and the *Fǎzhíguān*,
so that if there are any irregularities or incompleteness in the case,
the *Xíngbù* can conduct a review.
In this way, the realm will abide by the laws,
and no one will dare to lightly handle criminal cases.
Not only will this prevent grievances,
but it will also encourage those who establish governance.'
We, your ministers, have deliberated and observe that human life is of utmost importance,
and national law must be precise.
Although it is contained in old statutes,
it is even more suitable for clarification and order.
This is truly appropriate,
and we hope it will be granted implementation."
This was adopted.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"The difficulty of criminal cases
has been highly regarded throughout history.
When human lives are involved,
it truly moves the heart of Heaven;
should there be aggrieved souls,
it harms the harmonious *qì*.
All circuits and prefectures,
whenever they have prisoners,
shall fully address each case according to the facts revealed by investigation,
carefully examining the statutes, ordinances, and edicts.
Should there be any doubt,
they shall judge according to the ordinance.
If the *Dàlǐsì* also has doubts,
they shall report to the *Shàngshūshěng*.
Once the *Shàngshūshěng* and *Dàlǐsì* clearly provide guidance,
the prefectures and circuits shall then make their decisions."
In the fifth year, third month, on the *Bǐngzǐ* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Since the sixth year of *Dàzhōng*,
those who mutilate their ears to claim injustice
and are then subjected to flogging and exile,
their complaints, though reasonable,
are not subject to review.
Henceforth, their claims shall be investigated and decided.
The crime of ear mutilation
shall be separately penalized according to the law."
In the fifth month, on the *xīnsì* day, of the first year of Guǎngshùn of the Zhōu dynasty (951 CE),
an edict stated:
“The imperial court establishes titles and appoints officials,
seeking the worthy and selecting gentlemen.
Some advance through accumulated service,
others rise through examination ranks.
There are those who study the classics until their hair turns white
before they achieve a single rank;
some spend half their lives awaiting selection
before finally securing a single office.
This ensures that the nation has no undeserving commoners,
and scholars are not promoted indiscriminately.
In recent years, recommendations from zhōu and jùn
often come from individuals without previous official posts or a proper background.
Some are due to powerful connections and written endorsements,
others are private solicitations and requests.
It becomes difficult to refuse,
and thus true favors are bestowed.
This leads to ambitious and opportunistic individuals
contesting for shortcuts,
while diligent and struggling scholars
are left weeping at a dead end.
To rectify the corrupt and promote the pure,
it is fitting to hold names to account for their reality.
Henceforth, zhōu and fǔ are not permitted to recommend individuals without previous official posts or a proper background.
However, if there are exceptionally talented and uniquely virtuous individuals,
who stand out from the crowd and surpass others,
they may still be reported by name.
They can then proceed to the capital with the memorial,
where the relevant authorities will be ordered to examine them.
I will also personally review and scrutinize them,
deciding their worthiness or unworthiness,
and determining their promotion or demotion.
This is to prevent people from being mistakenly recommended
and to ensure no talent is overlooked in the populace.”
In the sixth month of the second year of Xiǎndé (955 CE),
an edict stated:
“The Liúshǒu Pànguān of the two capitals and all circuits’ zhōu and fǔ, [two or three] the Pànguān of the two commissioners, the Shàoyǐn, and the Pànguān for military defense and training matters,
are henceforth prohibited from making recommendations.
For the defense and training commands, and each Cìshǐ zhōu, one Tuīguān shall be appointed.”
This is a reform.
In the eleventh month of the third year of Tiānfú of the Jìn dynasty (938 CE),
Qǐjūláng Yīn Péng submitted a memorial, stating:
“I have heard that according to the Sīfēng regulations,
when internal and external civil and military officials are newly admitted to the imperial roster,
if their parents are deceased, they are immediately granted posthumous enfeoffment;
if their parents are alive, they are not yet enfeoffed.
In my humble opinion,
this is truly unacceptable.
This practice treats the living lightly and the dead heavily,
abandoning current individuals and honoring past ones.
What honor is there in this?
Where is the reason in this?
It also states,
if parents are alive
and the son’s rank meets the criteria,
then his mother is enfeoffed,
but his father is not,
only an honorary district title is added,
and she is called Tàijūn.
This makes it seem as if the wife has no husband,
and the son has no father above him.
How can the father be lowly while the mother is noble,
or the husband be inferior while the wife is superior?
If it is argued that the father is not yet eligible for favor,
how can the mother receive the賜 (cì, grace)?
If it is argued that the son’s position warrants nobility,
why is his father not enfeoffed first?
([It originally omitted the character
封 (fēng),
‘enfeoffment,’
which has now been added from the Wǔdài Huìyào.
(Attached note in the facsimile edition)])
I humbly submit that the father is superior and the mother is subordinate,
which is the way of Heaven and Earth.
There are no two supremes in honor,
and the state is of one body.
Now, to bestow enfeoffment upon a father without rank
is contrary to the norms of moral education,
and there is no greater impropriety than this.
I humbly request that from now on, for civil and military officials,
if their parents are alive,
and their parents already hold official titles,
their rank and grade should be advanced to meet the criteria,
or if they are unable to hold office with salary,
they may be granted the status of retirement or equivalent to a principal official,
so that their wives may be enfeoffed.
Then both parents will be honored,
and filial sons will not feel any shortcomings.
The household will be mutually illuminated,
and the sagely monarch’s abundant rewards and favors will be extended.
Alas!
Those who have benefited from Your Majesty’s governance through filial piety
and received Your Majesty’s honorific stipends for their parents,
if one quietly counts them on their fingers,
they are no more than a few.
May Your Majesty specifically deliberate and implement this,
codifying it as a standing regulation,
to encourage good deeds throughout the realm,
and set an example for all within the domain.
Naturally, this will rectify the omissions of previous dynasties
and establish a grand institution for our dynasty.
Moreover, a section of the benevolent decree from the first year of Chángxīng of the Táng dynasty states:
‘All internal and external officials in the court
whose parents are alive
shall also be granted favors.’
Sīfēng has not implemented this clear directive,
stubbornly adhering to previous texts.
If a new favor were announced,
while also aligning with the old imperial edict,
it would ensure that serving the ruler and serving one’s parents
always follows a unified standard,
and as sons and ministers,
they would not lose the virtue of achieving both.
I also hear that the Sīfēng regulations state,
for internal and external officials whose official rank reaches the fifth grade and above,
they are granted enfeoffment for their wives and *yīn* privilege for their sons.
This does not distinguish between clean and turbid (i.e., distinguished and common posts),
but only considers their rank.
However, Jiànyì Dàfū, Jìshìzhōng, and Zhōngshū Shèrén
are all fifth grade,
while Zànshàn Dàfū, Xǐmǎ, Zhōngyǔn, and Fèngyù, etc.,
are also fifth grade.
If one considers the court’s appointments,
the chief minister’s deliberations,
the steps of promotion,
and the expectations within and outside the court,
then the disparity is as vast as heaven and earth.
Yet, when it comes to their enfeoffment,
they are treated as one.
This has been continued to this point,
which is gravely incorrect.
Furthermore, the North Secretariat are Your Majesty’s attendant ministers,
the South Palace manages Your Majesty’s affairs of governance,
and the Céntái holds Your Majesty’s disciplinary authority.
They are foremost among all officials,
collectively forming the Three Bureaus.
Their duties are especially weighty,
and the expectations placed upon them are not light.
Thus, some in clean posts serve for ten years
without achieving their desired honor and glory,
while others in miscellaneous posts serve two terms
and immediately receive the favor of enfeoffment and *yīn* privilege.
Such unevenness in affairs
ought to be reformed.
I humbly request that from now on, all officials of the fifth grade and above
shall continue to be treated according to the old system.
However, the clean-stream officials of the Three Bureaus of the sixth grade and above
shall also be granted enfeoffment and *yīn* privilege.
Since the clean and turbid are different,
their ranks should be adjusted.
Furthermore, let this be submitted to the relevant authorities
to be discussed and made into a permanent regulation.”
This was accepted.
In the seventh month of the first year of Qiányòu of the Hàn dynasty (948 CE),
an edict stated:
“The Shàngshū Shěng shall convene a discussion:
For internal and external officials,
if the father is alive,
and the mother receives favor through her son’s *yīn* privilege,
or posthumous enfeoffment,
should the character 太 (Tài)
be added?
Report your findings.”
The Shàngshū Shěng reported its deliberation, stating:
“Upon reviewing previous imperial directives,
all mothers are indeed granted the character 太 (Tài),
whether living or deceased.
This means that if the father has passed away and the mother is alive,
then in her enfeoffment or advancement in enfeoffment, the character 太 (Tài) is added.
If the mother has passed away and is posthumously enfeoffed,
the character 太 (Tài) is also added.
Hence it says ‘living or deceased, both are the same.’
However, if the father is alive,
the imperial regulations do not mention
adding the character 太 (Tài) for the mother.
According to recent imperial edicts,
due to the son’s noble status, the father is appointed to office.
If the father already has his own office,
then the wife’s rank follows that of her husband.
([The original text had
夫石 (fū shí),
‘husband stone,’
which has now been corrected to
夫品 (fū pǐn),
‘husband’s rank,’
from the Wǔdài Huìyào.
(Attached note in the facsimile edition)])
Thus, the wife can be enfeoffed.
If the father is alive, it is not appropriate to add the character 太 (Tài) to the mother’s title
through her son’s privilege.
Even if the father holds an office due to his son,
but his rank is still low
and does not permit enfeoffing his wife,
then the limit of the son’s *yīn* privilege should not be applied either.”
When the Zhōngshū [Office of the Imperial Secretariat] kept secrets and ancient texts flourished,
when the Qǔtái [Bureau of Music] deleted and the Zhōuguān [Rites of Zhōu] was composed,
when gold coinage circulated privately,
when lacquer-written books were exchanged for bribes,
with forks within forks –
such are the types of things that occurred.
Thus, the Yì by Zǐxià [Bǔ Shāng]
differed from that by Zhāng Hú;
the chapters of Sùwèn [The Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon]
were, on the contrary, more numerous than those of the Tàipú [Grand Astrologer].
Now, the texts established by the guǎnchén [scholars of the Imperial Library] are not transmitted,
just as the original classics of the bóshì [erudites] were lost.
A wind comes from an empty cave;
like smearing and sticking,
the guóshī [national preceptors] are adept at forgery.
How can it be guaranteed that beyond Dù, Liú, Jiǎ, and Mǎ,
there will be no Zhāng Bà, Fēng Fáng, Sū Yú, and Méi Zé successively arising to commit forgery?
Alas!
During the Five Dynasties, it was dark, obscure, and blocked.
Even if their historical records do not possess the veneration of the classics,
merely for several decades of contending with the people and plundering,
recorded in this compilation,
the threads are tangled like a skein.
Even if the Sòng woodblock editions still exist today,
it is still difficult to manage and sort them.
One error leads to another error;
what can be followed?
Moreover, misfortunes and chaos have their origins,
often arising from the confusion of right and wrong.
The Ten Kingdoms frequently changed;
who supervised and judged reliably?
The lesson from the Yīn [Dynasty] is not far off;
the coming rut is urgent.
It is especially impossible not to scrutinize and rectify them [the texts]
so as to deter future mistakes!
Disregarding my humble capabilities,
I frequently close the book and pace around,
wishing to write ten thousand copies,
hoping they will circulate widely,
without forgetting the true face [of history].
I now hear that a gentleman,
if he fortunately finds this historical gap barely preserved,
and allows it to contribute to the preservation of this culture,
then regarding the duty of those who come after,
he might have no regrets.
Respectfully recorded by Yìyuán Xióng Luó Sù at the Fēngchéng Nán Guǎn in Jīngshī [the capital], in the fourth month of summer in the Xīnyǒu year
(Recorded from the photographic reproduction of the appendices of the old Wǔdài Shǐ).
Origin of the Photo-printed Manuscript of the Old Wǔdài Shǐ.
Péng Wénqín Gōng, in his postscript to reading the Shèngdào Zhāi, said:
"Among the books compiled from scattered chapters of the Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn,
this is the best,
because it indicates the volume numbers of the Dàdiǎn and the names and volume numbers of the books from which it was collected,
making it clear which chapters and sentences are preserved or missing,
without obscuring the truth.
The Sìmíng Quánshū edition was like this,
but later the Wǔyīngdiàn engraved edition completely deleted them.
I repeatedly argued with the zǒngcái [chief editor],
but was not heard.
Consequently, Xuē's true face [of the text] cannot be traced,
and later generations frequently make errors when citing it.
Fortunately, this manuscript copy is preserved;
it must not be discarded."
Now, I observe that the imperial edition's revisions have
everywhere corrupted the original text.
Some instances involve arbitrary deletions:
in volume 61, the biography of Xīfāng Yè (西方鄴傳),
below the sentence "Yè (鄴) was helpless,"
six characters,
"whereas Míngzōng (明宗) had already reached Biàn (汴),"
were deleted.
Above the sentence "returned to Luòyáng (洛陽) and was assassinated,"
six characters,
"reached west of Biàn (汴) but could not enter,"
were deleted.
In volume 93, the biography of Lǐ Zhuānměi (李專美傳),
"though he was often flogged and chastised (雖行行捶楚)"
was changed to
"though he was flogged and chastised (雖行捶楚)."
In volume 96, after the biography of Lǐ Yù (李郁傳), the entire biography of Zhèng Xuánsù (鄭玄素傳) was deleted.
In volume 98, at the end of the biography of Zhāng Lì (張礪傳), over eighty characters cited in the Cèfǔ Yuánguī (冊府元龜) were deleted. These are all examples.
Some instances involve presumptuous additions:
in volume 3, the Annals of Liáng Tàizǔ (梁太祖紀),

"The Daoist dignitary Zhèng Zhāng (鄭章) reported from Zhèxī (浙西),"

were inserted.

In addition to these, according to the opinion of a humble person,
the words of the *Ěryǎ* were changed;
based on what is generally accepted,
it is said that the preceding text contains errors;
together with the fact that all the Róng kings were made Qìdān,
and all braided hair was changed for avoidance,
such arbitrary and harmful actions
are not easily corrected.
I humbly believe that when examining texts from the Five Dynasties,
Ōu's history is not as authentic as Xuē's history,
so between the new and old versions,
the old book must be considered correct.
How regrettable that after having painstakingly collected what remained of the fragmented texts,
they are still plagued by errors in校刊 [jiàokān]!
Is this not a cause for sorrow?
Therefore, I have specifically taken the original hand-copied text from the Wǔyīngdiàn in my possession,
purchased a machine to photocopy it,
ensuring that it is exactly accurate down to the smallest detail,
as if it were a sacred object.
I have also compiled all the attached notes and annotations
and printed them at the end,
so that readers of this book may see what Wénqín called its "true face."
(Excerpted from the appendix of the photocopied *Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ*)
